papers.title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.
papers.summary: The number of tokens a large language model (LLM) generates is often treated as a proxy for inference-time compute, analogous to classical time complexity. The authors show that **token usage does not align monotonically with classical time complexity**, and propose `LLM Complexity`, a metric based on the area above the accuracy-token curve. Different LLMs produce highly consistent task rankings under this metric, which the authors use to build an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning that improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. On real-world tasks the metric gives more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

papers.title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning
papers.abstract: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git
papers.summary: Natural language inference (NLI) systems trained continually across tasks such as sentiment analysis and news classification suffer catastrophic forgetting, and rehearsing labeled past examples can cause overfitting. `ICARE` combines a representation-learning instance selection module that picks which training examples to present with knowledge distillation that transfers both feature-level and logit-level knowledge between tasks, using pruning and tuned objective functions. On benchmark text classification datasets the authors report **higher target accuracy and a lower forgetting metric**, without quoting specific figures in the abstract.

papers.title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
papers.abstract: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.
papers.summary: Recovering the section hierarchy of long, design-heavy documents is error-prone because bottom-up parsers rely on local visual cues and direct large language model extraction lacks spatial grounding. `TETHER` is a training-free, two-stage method that treats the Table of Contents (ToC) as a structural prior: a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) first builds a document skeleton from the raw ToC under spatio-semantic constraints, then an anchor-based alignment step attaches content blocks to that skeleton. On a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports it outperforms hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs in zero-shot hierarchy recovery, while achieving a **90% token reduction** and large speedups over end-to-end baselines.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
papers.abstract:
Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run.
  In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens.
  Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale.
  These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.
papers.summary: Whether standard benchmarks detect meaningful architectural differences is tested with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3 to 8 billion parameters on 1 to 2 trillion `Nemotron-CC` tokens. Differences that nearly vanish at academic scale become measurable at this scale: `Canon` layers, which add local token mixing, save **about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same `MMLU` accuracy at 8B parameters**, and with them plain gated linear attention matches `Gated DeltaNet` and outperforms `Mamba2`. Even so, linear models that match Transformers on benchmarks cannot reliably retrieve information from a 500-token context, and no model reliably beats random guessing on a very simple two-hop question. The authors argue that small synthetic tasks predicted these differences at under 100M parameters, and recommend including in-context reasoning examples early in pretraining data.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard benchmarks and academic-scale pretraining often fail to separate language-model architectures, so this study runs **64 from-scratch pretraining runs** of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3–8B parameters on 1–2T `Nemotron-CC` tokens to test whether predictions from a small synthetic playground hold at scale. They largely do: `Canon` layers, which add cheap local token mixing, give consistent gains, while the same runs expose basic in-context deficits that high benchmark scores hide.

- `Canon` is a residual causal convolution that gives each hidden coordinate a learned weighted sum over the current and three preceding tokens, inserted at up to four positions per layer for under **0.2%** extra parameters and roughly 2.1–3.3% extra step time in a fused implementation.
- On Transformers, `LlamaCanon` beats vanilla `Llama` in every setting by **0.8–1.5 points on `lm-eval`** (a 13-benchmark average) and 1.3–2.9 points on `MMLU`, reaching the baseline's final `MMLU` accuracy with **about 30% fewer pretraining tokens** at 8B.
- Among linear models, the new `GLA5` and `GDN2` variants replace the full-rank output gate with a rank-16 one and reallocate the saved parameters, and once `Canon` is added the simple `GLA5` comes within **0.3 `lm-eval` points** of `GDN2` and outperforms `Mamba2`, suggesting the delta rule and selective state-space update mostly supply short-range mixing.
- Linear models that match or beat Transformers on `lm-eval` fall to **72–98%** on retrieving a stated birth year across 500 unrelated tokens while Transformers stay at ≥99.5%, and on a seven-sentence two-hop question almost every model sits near the **33.3%** chance level, with only the 8B Transformers reaching about 50% and losing most of that advantage once 500 background tokens are added.
- The evidence rests on learning-rate sweeps rather than repeated seeds at roughly $100k per 8B run, `LlamaCanon` bundles `Canon` with reduced RoPE so the two are not separated, three model sizes cannot establish a scaling law, and the authors cannot say whether more tokens or better data made the gains visible.

papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache is a major memory bottleneck for long-context large language model inference. `PRKV` is a training-free eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by running Personalized PageRank over graphs induced by attention, rather than relying on recency or instantaneous attention, and requires no changes to the model. Across long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks on several model families, it reports **competitive task performance against established eviction baselines at compression ratios up to 90%**, with reduced peak memory and low end-to-end overhead.

papers.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
papers.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.
papers.summary: `HireWatch` evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) used in hiring comply with U.S. law on which questions job candidates may be asked. Models select interview questions from a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful questions, classified using federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance, across occupations and contexts, and the fraction of unlawful selections is measured. Across 18 closed and open-weight LLMs and roughly 100,000 trials, **models mostly avoid unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts but violations rise sharply under higher contextual pressure**. Explicit instructions to comply with the law improve compliance without eliminating violations.

papers.title: The ROI of Small Examples: Optimizing In-Context Learning Under Token Budgets
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves large language model performance at inference time without updating model parameters. However, these gains are not free: in practical deployments, longer prompts directly increase inference cost and latency. Under a fixed token budget, prompt construction therefore becomes a resource-allocation problem. While prior work has often focused on how many examples to include in ICL, we study the complementary question of whether the available budget is better spent on a few long demonstrations or on a larger number of shorter ones. We study this aspect in question answering (QA), by organizing candidate demonstrations into length-based bins and constructing prompts from examples within the same length range under fixed budgets. Experiments on two QA benchmarks (\textit{Beat the AI} and \textit{Natural Questions}), using six instruction-tuned LLMs, show that shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space. This effect is especially strong on \textit{Beat the AI}, and remains visible on NQ, although gains are smaller and saturate earlier in the long-context setting. An additional natural language inference experiment on ANLI R3 finds that one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models, although longer demonstrations remain competitive. Overall, our results highlight demonstration granularity as an important factor in prompt design.
papers.summary: Under a fixed prompt token budget, in-context learning (ICL) raises the question of whether to spend the budget on a few long demonstrations or many short ones. The authors group candidate question-answering demonstrations into length-based bins and build prompts from a single bin at fixed budgets, testing six instruction-tuned models on `Beat the AI` and `Natural Questions`. They find that **shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space**, strongly on `Beat the AI` and more modestly on `Natural Questions`, where gains saturate earlier. A natural language inference experiment on `ANLI R3` shows a shorter bin winning for five of six models, though longer demonstrations remain competitive.

papers.title: No-Harm-Jury A Jury-Based Multi-Dimensional Harm Evaluation Framework for Medical AI Responses
papers.abstract: We present No-Harm-Jury, a jury-based automated evaluation framework that scores AI-generated medical responses across seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions using a panel of five diverse language models as independent jurors. Responses generated by Ministral-14B on 3,000 questions drawn from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA are scored by five jurors across dimensions of informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm; the 151 empty responses (98 MedQA, 53 MedM- CQA) are excluded, leaving 2,849 valid samples. The median aggregation robustly suppresses individual juror biases while maintaining coverage through complementary specialisation. No existing system combines all five prop- erties of No-Harm-Jury: automated scalable evaluation, five diverse LLM jurors, robust me- dian aggregation (with a reliability-weighted extension), seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions, and application to medical QA benchmarks.
papers.summary: `No-Harm-Jury` is an automated evaluation framework in which a panel of five different language models independently scores AI-generated medical answers on seven harm dimensions: informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic. It is applied to responses from `Ministral-14B` on 3,000 questions from `PubMedQA`, `MedQA`, and `MedMCQA`, leaving 2,849 valid samples after 151 empty responses are excluded. Scores are combined by median, with a reliability-weighted extension, and the authors claim that **median aggregation suppresses individual juror biases while preserving coverage**; the abstract describes the framework rather than reporting harm rates.

papers.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
papers.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.
papers.summary: Program-induction benchmarks can be uninformative when demonstrations generated from two rules are also explained by a single rule. Certificate-grounded calibration builds matched tasks in a bounded string-replacement language whose minimum solution length is provably one or two rules, certified by exhaustive one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness before any model is run. Across 120 reference families with `Qwen3-8B` and `Olmo-3-7B-Think`, **completion of the displayed task is 23.53 to 45.83 percentage points lower on certified two-rule tasks**, while success on an unshown witness pair is 8.40 to 13.45 points higher. Agreement on inputs that trigger both reference rules is only 1.93 to 5.78%, and a single unchanged example can decide whether two rules are required.

papers.title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
papers.abstract: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.
papers.summary: Resource-constrained spacecraft such as CubeSats need onboard 3D shape models of irregular asteroids without relying on bandwidth-heavy imaging or lidar. The proposed pipeline uses only Sun sensor eclipse entry and exit events plus coarse prior knowledge: `EclipseNets`, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, refines 2D silhouettes, which then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations. In simulations of the asteroid Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, **silhouette intersection-over-union rises from 0.70 to 0.87** and the resulting 3D reconstructions are coherent.

papers.title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
papers.abstract: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.
papers.summary: Local computer-use agents (CUAs) running in resource-constrained settings predict single actions well but often fail by getting stuck in repeated action loops or declaring a task done too early. `CANDID` is an execution-control framework that applies parallel test-time sampling of candidate actions only at these sparse failure-prone points, instead of using textual reflection. A loop-recovery mechanism filters out candidates that repeat earlier behavior, and termination requires unanimous agreement among candidates. On `OSWorld`, the authors report that it **improves success rates and outperforms feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead**.

papers.title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
papers.abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely ($R^2 > 0.99$) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.
papers.summary: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in industrial plants often run programs whose source is lost, while their inputs and outputs are logged continuously. `Trace2ST` has a large language model (LLM) write a candidate program in Structured Text (ST) from a compressed trace summary, replays it one control cycle at a time against the recording, and feeds mismatches back for up to three revisions. On 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks, **recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases** and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs; adding traces that target unexercised branches raises agreement on adversarial inputs from 0.80 to 0.98, whereas an automata-learning baseline falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs. On data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws fit unseen measurements with R-squared above 0.99 and expose the dataset's only actuator attack.

papers.title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
papers.abstract:
Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not).
  However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well.
  Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Mont\'ufar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.
papers.summary: A tutorial-style overview of what is known about the expressive power of neural networks. It covers the universal approximation theorems of Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik, and Leshno, which show that shallow networks with non-polynomial activations can approximate any continuous function on compact sets, and stresses that these results give no guarantees about network size, trainability, or generalization. It then reviews Barron's quantitative approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm and Montufar's result that **the number of linear regions grows exponentially with depth**, making deep networks more expressive than shallow ones with the same parameter count.

papers.title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
papers.abstract: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.
papers.summary: Cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor are hard to study in historical societies that left no psychological survey data. The authors build a text-analysis pipeline over 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513 to 1911, using sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language to score documents on these constructs. Their adapted model `OTA-BERTurk` reaches **Recall@1 of .843 on document retrieval**, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 on semantic textual similarity, and 89.58% accuracy classifying questionnaire items, though document-level performance varies by construct and method. Models, scoring pipeline, and an interactive web interface are publicly released.

papers.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
papers.abstract: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.
papers.summary: Active learning is studied in a setting where the labeling oracle may abstain and its probability of responding shares parameters with the classifier, so the act of responding or not is itself informative. Under a correctly specified parametric model, the authors derive the classifier information after adjusting for response-model nuisance parameters and combine it with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk to obtain an acquisition criterion that minimizes leading asymptotic excess risk under a fixed query budget. In a replay of `Consumer Complaints` data with real human abstentions, **response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets**, while entropy sampling does better at the smallest budget.

papers.title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.
papers.summary: The setting is a multi-armed bandit where each arm's reward is a survival probability at a fixed time horizon and outcomes are right-censored time-to-event observations, so feedback is delayed and partial. `KM-UCB` is a variance-adaptive policy built on the Kaplan-Meier (KM) estimator that replaces Hoeffding-type bounds with an empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula, derived using martingale theory and influence functions. Under catch-up reporting the policy achieves **logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term**. It is evaluated in a delayed-feedback simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data.

papers.title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
papers.abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.
papers.summary: A manipulated clinical language model can return an answer that looks normal, so monitoring only inputs and outputs can miss attacks. The authors use a natural-language autoencoder to translate the activations of `Gemma-3-27B` into text and have an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state separately from the model's answer. Across two clinical attack objectives, two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, **the verbalized-thoughts channel detected the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions**, with near-zero false positives on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to `Llama-3.3-70B`. The channel also flagged unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, and the setup needs no retraining.

papers.title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
papers.abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.
papers.summary: Personalized behavior-prediction agents usually condition actions directly on a static psychological profile and ignore observed state transitions as a training signal. `PsyWorld` instead learns a profile-conditioned world model: a posterior encoder quantizes realized environment-behavior transitions into discrete codes, and a prior predicts those codes from the psychometric profile and prior context, with the predicted code and next state then conditioning behavior. Evaluated on unseen participants in the `VEET` behavioral simulator, it reaches **0.904 Top-1 accuracy** and 0.0033 Macro KL, with ablations attributing most of the Top-1 gain to continuous next-state modeling. It is also tested in the synthetic `AgentSociety` environment, and the authors caution that the results do not imply causal psychological mechanisms.

papers.title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
papers.abstract:
Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.
  At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.
  Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.
papers.summary: Model merging adds task vectors from separately fine-tuned models to a shared backbone, and interference between tasks is normally measured only after building and evaluating each candidate merge. The authors show that a first-order directional derivative of one task's outputs along another task's vector predicts interference, but **only when computed at the receiving fine-tuned model rather than at the shared pretrained backbone**, where it is nearly orthogonal to actual changes in vision experiments. Building on this, `LR-Merge` is a label-free correction that optimizes merge coefficients by convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes without backpropagating through merged networks. It improves all tested base merging methods and matches exact teacher matching, which takes roughly three times longer to converge.

papers.title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.
papers.summary: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks control how many pixels they perturb only indirectly through a fixed sparsity coefficient, so hitting a target density requires re-tuning. Density Feedback Control (`DFC`) adjusts this coefficient at the end of each epoch based on the gap between the observed and target mask density, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10% target, it brings **the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run** and raises the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets while perturbing fewer pixels. For `EGS-TSSA`, which restricts perturbations to feature-importance regions, it gives no consistent gain.

papers.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.
papers.summary: Language models tend to produce sets of samples that cluster around the same semantic modes even when each individual sample is good. The authors frame diverse generation as drawing a size-K subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where likelihood encodes quality and embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Their `PoolDPP` method draws a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weights it toward the target quality, and runs a K-DPP sampler on the pool, with a proof that **the KL divergence to the target K-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size**. Experiments report a wider quality-diversity frontier on open-ended generation, a better precision-recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (`Ambrosia`), and higher diversity at about the same pass@K on `GSM8K`.

papers.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.
papers.summary: Feature reduction is routinely used to cut dimensionality and training time, but its effect on adversarial robustness is not well characterized. The study tests support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors classifiers on the `APT` dataset under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks, with and without principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Measured by accuracy, F1-score, and a mitigation score, **permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information give the most consistent robustness improvements**, while the other techniques vary by classifier and attack.

papers.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
papers.abstract:
The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way.
  The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.
papers.summary: The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension d admits a sample compression scheme of size O(d), with a weaker version asking only for size polynomial in d. The best prior bound depending only on d, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), was exponential in d. The authors prove the weaker conjecture by constructing **a sample compression scheme of size O(d^2 log^2 d) for every VC class**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Whether every binary concept class of VC dimension d admits a sample compression scheme whose size depends only on d has been open since the 1980s, with the best general bound stuck at **2^O(d)** (Moran and Yehudayoff, 2016). The weaker, polynomial form of the sample compression conjecture is settled here: a small set of unlabeled sample points implicitly names a pool of concepts, and a few labeled points set the weights of a majority vote over that pool.

- Every class of VC dimension d gets a compression scheme of **O(d² log² d)** examples plus **O(d log² d)** side-information bits, of which only **O(d log d)** examples need labels.
- An unlabeled set `W` partitions the class into cells of concepts that agree on `W`, the first concept of each cell under a fixed order forms the pool, and the reconstructor replays multiplicative weights (`MWU`) over that pool from the labeled points to output a weighted majority vote consistent with the whole sample.
- `W` is built by iterative refinement over **O(d log d)** rounds: each round picks a distribution via a symmetric zero-sum game and LP duality, then either terminates with an ε-net or adds O(d log d) points that raise the cell-mass entropy by more than **1/128** bit, which the Sauer–Shelah–Perles lemma caps.
- The same bound carries over to agnostic compression and gives **O(d_G² log² d_G)** examples for multiclass classes of graph dimension d_G, and the authors disclose that the result was obtained autonomously by the `Cogentic` multi-agent system running on `Gemini 4 Carbon`.
- The original Floyd–Warmuth conjecture of **O(d)** size remains open against a lower bound of d, the bounds say nothing about the computational cost of compressing or reconstructing, and the explicit constants are very large (the round limit is 4096·d·⌈log₂(d+2)⌉).

papers.title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) need agents that can act on physical hardware unsupervised while knowing when to defer to a human. The authors place an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, letting it select measurements and interpret data while state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. On a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for an organic dye, the agent's oxidant ranking matched scripted peak integration and chemists confirmed its spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulation replaying the archived data, it **measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order**.

papers.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/
papers.summary: Feedforward 3D reconstruction networks are fast but degrade on out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes such as unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. `Infer3D` instead performs inverse generative modeling, optimizing the latent variables of a generative model to match the monocular input, and couples the image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network to keep solutions on a multi-view-consistent 3D manifold and avoid degenerate flat outputs. On controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, it reports **better OOD reconstruction accuracy than feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets**. An adaptive inference strategy spends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD inputs while routing in-distribution inputs efficiently.

papers.title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
papers.abstract: Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.
papers.summary: High-dimensional measurements taken over time for multiple individuals, common in biomedical studies, often have missing values and irregularly spaced timepoints. The authors propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) factorization in which the latent factors are temporally correlated, with flexible covariance structures and **automatic determination of all hyper-parameters, including the number of factors**. Simulations show more precise signal recovery and good missing-data imputation relative to other strategies, and an application to gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment yields interpretable components and improved imputation accuracy.

papers.title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
papers.abstract: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.
papers.summary: Hardware design verification with the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is labor-intensive, and existing benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents split it into decoupled subtasks unlike the real workflow. `DVBench` contains 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, each requiring an agent to complete the full verification workflow on its own. Final testbenches are scored on compilation, coverage, and bug detection, and intermediate artifacts such as feature lists, test plans, and reference models are also assessed. Among frontier models and agent frameworks including `Claude Code`, `Codex`, and `OpenCode`, the best combination (`Codex` with `GPT-6 Astra`) reaches **an overall success rate of only 21.05%**.

papers.title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kaelyn01/VisAlloc
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) can improve visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), but not every sample benefits from privileged visual guidance and uniform token supervision dilutes visually grounded signal. `VisAlloc` filters samples by keeping those a teacher answers correctly from an evidence-centered crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced crop, then reweights tokens according to how much two exponential-moving-average teachers' log-probabilities differ between the views. Inference uses only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, the 4B and 9B models reach macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, **0.97 and 0.52 points above `Vision-OPD` reproductions**.

papers.title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
papers.abstract:
This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts.
  A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.
papers.summary: Industrial maintenance analytics on work orders usually requires data scientists to write custom analysis code. The `CodeReAct` agent takes natural-language instructions and follows a Thought-Action-Observation loop in which the Action step generates executable code over industrial data standardized into business objects and analytical function APIs. It provides knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendation and prediction. A chiller maintenance case study covering multiple years of work orders, alerts, and anomalies is presented as showing that **the agent can turn user utterances into data analyses with less data scientist involvement**; no quantitative evaluation is reported in the abstract.

papers.title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and misroute questions, so the authors ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant. `FinVeriQA` is an open-source multi-agent prototype over SEC filings and live market data in which a compact typed-decision model (`Laya`) routes questions, Python computes every number, `Mistral-7B` writes a cited answer, a code validator checks citations and figures, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. `Laya` routed better than `Mistral-7B` (0.85 vs. 0.52), and `Mistral-7B` got 29% of 100 financial calculations right against 100% for Python. In a controlled study on `FinRank` with one corrupted figure in the evidence, **a check against the same shared evidence caught 35% of errors while a check against the original passage caught 77%**, leading the authors to conclude that verification must be independent of what the writer saw.

papers.title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
papers.abstract:
Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows.
  In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.
papers.summary: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) puts labeled records into a large language model's prompt, which can expose sensitive personal data, and noise-based differential privacy (DP) distorts the feature-label relationships needed for prediction. `PriTabICL` partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each cluster independently with existing DP synthesis algorithms, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistics. At inference each query is routed to a cluster and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic data with no additional privacy loss. On four real-world datasets, the `PriTabICL-PrivSyn` instantiation **improves over global `PrivSyn` in 8 of 12 settings** and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all settings.

papers.title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
papers.abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely.We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.
papers.summary: Browsers now ship on-device language models such as `Gemini Nano` in Chrome, which the authors examine as a living-off-the-land resource for attackers: already installed, vendor-signed, and invisible to network monitoring. They show the model can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system, and that the one-time user-activation check before the model download can be satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely. They measure the model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect personal information in email, classify images, and call custom tools. Combining these, **the model carries out a simulated operation end-to-end without user interaction**: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging its contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration.

papers.title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.
papers.summary: `SailSearch` is a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research using two language-model agents, applied here to the Market Split problem and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, the resulting randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. It found what the authors describe as **the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open `QOBLIB` instances**, solving 130 to 133 of 156 benchmark instances per seed within 24 hours on two CPU cores. For MIS, a generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima, and on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices the tested solvers ended 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum after eight hours.

papers.title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
papers.abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors.
