Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.
papers.summary: Existing machine learning engineering (MLE) benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits, while repository-level software engineering benchmarks have saturated. The authors define a Code Complexity Index (CCI) from ten structural features covering repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size, which predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks with R^2 = 0.951. Guided by it, `BuggyMLE` has agents inject controlled bugs into working ML repositories, producing over 6,600 variants from 222 source repositories. On the resulting `BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite`, **the top solve rate across 14 models drops from 95% on the easiest tier to 9% on the hardest**, and a `Qwen3.5-9B` model fine-tuned on a three-level curriculum is reported to rival frontier models there while raising its `SWE-bench Lite` resolve rate from 24% to 33%.

papers.title: HapBO: Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
papers.abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is more sample-efficient with prior knowledge, but that knowledge often exists only as natural language rather than as an explicit probability distribution. `HapBO` elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles them into a reusable belief function that is applied as a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition function, with **no LLM calls during optimization**. For Expected Improvement, the authors prove the standard simple-regret rate is preserved up to a bounded factor even under adversarial beliefs. It achieves the lowest aggregate regret on 40 `HPOBench` tasks and performs well on cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design at budgets of 12 to 20 queries.

papers.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.
papers.summary: Coordinated multi-robot manipulation requires predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly produce. `MAWAM` is a multi-agent world-action model, built from a pretrained single-robot backbone, that jointly denoises every robot's action chunks and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention while keeping a separate control interface per robot. On three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, umbrella handover) it reaches **67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above `MA-VLA`** trained on the same demonstrations and cameras, and 90.3% mean success on eight simulated tasks with up to four arms. Ablations show that removing cross-agent attention drops a four-arm relay from 95.0% to 39.0%.

papers.title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
papers.abstract: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.
papers.summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems generally assume subjects are captured within about a meter, and no benchmark covers multiple distances, varied environments, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion attacks. The authors collect a video dataset of over 374,000 frames from 261 identities at five standoff distances from 1 m to 100 m, indoors and outdoors, with a DSLR camera and a mobile sensor, labeled live, spoof, or props (occlusions). Among four fine-tuned CNNs, `EfficientNet` performs best overall at **98.48% accuracy**. The DSLR keeps near-perfect spoof classification at all distances, while the mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification falling to 55% at 75 m for `MobileNetV3`.

papers.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
papers.abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.
papers.summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize them, form emotional attachments, and become dependent, yet public benchmarks for whether models reinforce this parasocial attachment are single-turn, observational, or focused on extreme user states. `CoMPASS` is a multi-turn benchmark grounded in attachment theory, with four user personas, three escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. Across eight frontier models from four providers, **six show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions escalate together**. Differences within a provider are small relative to differences across providers, which the authors read as pointing to provider-level choices such as post-training rather than model scale.

papers.title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
papers.abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.
papers.summary: General-purpose LLM agents make data science more accessible but lack the statistical controls of fixed pipelines. `DSFlow` is a `LangGraph`-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that pairs reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. The symbolic validation layer **can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback**. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how diagnostic evidence corrects method choices and how those decisions are recorded in auditable reports; no quantitative results are given in the abstract.

papers.title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
papers.abstract: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.
papers.summary: `DISCO` is an internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that also scores the quality of noise labels, and it is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. The `discoCVI` R package computes it exactly from the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, giving memory linear in the number of points while running time stays quadratic. Results agree with the original Python implementation to within 3e-13, and the package corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. It runs 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference and **scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory**.

papers.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
papers.abstract: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoder features extracted from `GraphCast`, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, are used to test whether a feature must have a physical meaning to be causally relevant, and whether physically associated features can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts. Ablating a feature tied to the model's computational mesh, which has no conventional physical meaning, increases global geopotential height error. Suppressing features associated with convection and low-level vorticity weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening, while amplifying convection features by feature scaling gives a **median 51% reduction in intensity error over seven storms**. The authors conclude that physical interpretability and causal utility are separable, and that sparse features can serve as coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

papers.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents that overflow their context window usually rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, all of which decide what to keep before future needs are known. `GrepMem` instead keeps an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and gives the agent a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall, with no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or extra models. With `Qwen3.5-9B` trained by reinforcement learning under five context management strategies, `GrepMem` reaches **95-97% accuracy on `ContextBench` versus at most 21% for lossy baselines** and beats the summarization of `SUPO` by 8.8 percentage points on `BCP-Multi`. It also stays on the accuracy versus token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks as input streams grow longer.

papers.title: CRAFT: Constrained Route planning with Adaptive Framework and Template-based code generation
papers.abstract: Everyday routing requests are rarely a point-to-point shortest path. A driver may need to visit stops, sometimes in a fixed order, under time budgets or distance limits, and perhaps recharge their EV car along the way. Each combination is a distinct routing problem that classically requires its own algorithm, so no fixed solver covers the space of queries users may ask. This paper presents CRAFT, which takes a constrained routing query as free text and returns a route that satisfies the user's requirements on a real road network. An LLM parses the query and generates four search functions, which a generic graph-search engine executes on the road network. We formalize the underlying problem as State-Expanded RCSP (SE-RCSP), which extends resource-constrained shortest paths (RCSP) with non-additive state such as node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking. We evaluate CRAFT on 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, analyzing correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic POI filtering.
papers.summary: Real routing requests combine ordered stops, time budgets, distance limits, and electric-vehicle recharging, and each combination classically needs its own algorithm. `CRAFT` takes such a query as free text, has an LLM parse it and **generate four search functions that a generic graph-search engine executes** on a real road network. The underlying problem is formalized as State-Expanded RCSP (`SE-RCSP`), which extends resource-constrained shortest paths (RCSP) with non-additive state such as node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking. Evaluation covers 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, examining correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic point-of-interest filtering; the abstract reports no headline numbers.

papers.title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.
papers.summary: Neural operator models struggle to predict seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval seen in training. The proposed framework jointly trains a time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (`TI-DeepONet`), which advances the velocity field with an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme, and a Fourier Neural Operator (`FNO`) that learns a residual correction, in a predictor-corrector configuration. On horizontally polarized shear waves in four-layer soil columns, with test rollouts extending beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors range from **0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals**. Reference stress fields are supplied throughout the rollout, so autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield is not yet established.

papers.title: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for language models needs a reward, but answer checkers require reference answers and LLM judges produce scores that are not probabilities. `RLCDR` (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards) turns an LLM into a decision model that answers a typed question about a response with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders, and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training `Qwen3-1.7B` with `GRPO` on `MATH`, this reference-free reward **raises `MATH500` accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8%, matching training on the answer key (76.9%)**, with half the expected calibration error of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone and no sign of reward hacking. When trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reward still helps but trails the answer key because its probabilities become overconfident.

papers.title: CAIMS: Scalable Cross-Array In-Memory Search
papers.abstract: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to $22.3\times/10.1\times$ and energy efficiency by $426.6\times/23.7\times$ compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.
papers.summary: In-memory search (IMS) runs similarity search inside content-addressable memory (CAM) arrays, but a single array is too small for modern workloads and existing designs cannot accurately reduce per-array binary match results to a global top-k. `CAIMS` is a cross-array framework that uses threshold matching with combined offline and online parameter selection to turn local binary matches into globally comparable coarse similarity scores, then performs hierarchical reduction with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated on the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, it improves **throughput by up to 22.3x and energy efficiency by 426.6x over a server-class CPU baseline**, and by 10.1x and 23.7x over prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, at comparable accuracy.

papers.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
papers.abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.
papers.summary: Evaluating agents on everyday live-web tasks is hard because a request can have several valid outcomes and web content changes over time. `EverydayBench` contains 77 human-authored tasks across eight domains, each with success criteria fixed before execution, and scores submissions by deterministic constraint checks, verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and rubric-based assessment of the deliverable. Across 23 agent-model configurations, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `Claude Fable 5.1` **tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%**, while a controlled `GPT-6 Sol` effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Leadership varies by task type across lookup, planning, comparison, and customized deliverables.

papers.title: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
papers.abstract: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.
papers.summary: Quality assessment of generative content manipulation such as summarization remains largely subjective. Drawing on Shannon's rate-distortion theory, the authors formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem and extract a semantic hierarchy of the source content, which lets them **quantify the trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) and information loss (distortion)** and compare models at a given rate budget. They apply the framework to summarization for long-context question answering with current large language models, and show that using the semantic hierarchy to guide retrieval-augmented generation improves rate-distortion characteristics over baselines.

papers.title: Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer for Minimax Model Estimation in MDPs
papers.abstract: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.
papers.summary: Active exploration for minimax estimation of transition dynamics in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs) was previously addressed by the frequentist `kappa-Explorer`, which needs confidence-bound constructions and a costly joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures. `Bayesian kappa-Explorer` places Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions, so that the posterior expected squared l2 error equals the total posterior variance and gives a closed-form exploration signal, and plans under the posterior mean model. Under the stated assumptions it **retains the O(T^(-1/3)) surrogate convergence rate of the frequentist version** without confidence-set optimization. Experiments on `Pendulum`, `Mountain Car`, and `Taxi` show lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.

papers.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.
papers.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) ask one sparse representation to deliver both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, two objectives that need not align. `DualSAE` keeps a standard SAE as a Sparse Branch for the dominant semantics and adds a plug-in Residual Branch for the non-semantic information the sparse code omits, with a decorrelation loss to minimize overlap and a two-stage training schedule. Across encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, it achieves mean relative improvements of about **29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability** as measured by monosemanticity score. Gains also appear in topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
papers.abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.
papers.summary: `InflEns` is a mixture of `LoRA` experts whose training-data weights and inference-time routing both come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space, where players choose positions to maximize their expected share of the prompt distribution without using expert losses. On a corpus built from seven safety-related benchmarks, the highest-share expert has the **lowest held-out negative log-likelihood (NLL) on roughly 90% of prompts**, compared with about 15% after permuting allocations, and the method performs comparably to published learned gates without training one. Because the router is fixed, harmful behavior can be traced to a single expert and only that expert retrained, which lowers `HarmBench` attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following.

papers.title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
papers.abstract: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice
papers.summary: Whether a language model internally represents alternatives it does not choose cannot be read off its observable decision. `Before the Choice` is an evidence-oriented framework that separates future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance, and organizes four experimental contrasts with their alternative explanations. In its first test on unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments, a preregistered low-rank probe **did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline)**, and a follow-up with matched worlds decoded at 0.521 (p = 0.18). The authors state that these results neither identify prospective simulation nor establish its absence, and present the work as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research.

papers.title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.
papers.summary: Test-time compute (TTC), which spends extra inference to generate, verify, and select among candidates, has not transferred directly to time series forecasting because a forecaster cannot use future information to score a candidate. Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (`BGAA`) builds a causal verifier from the series' own history: rolling-origin backtests score structured views of the context, views that underperform the untransformed context are discarded, and the survivors' predictive distributions are averaged. It improves every tested model-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on `GIFT-Eval`, 1.3-5.0% on `fev-bench`, and **1.7-5.9% on `BOOM`, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family**. Choosing the best view separately for each test window would yield 17-19% gains, which points to window-level view selection as the main open problem.

papers.title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
papers.abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.
papers.summary: Empirical finance papers often reuse the same natural experiments for different outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. AI agents are used to rebuild the data, reproduce the main estimate, and re-estimate it across 62,409 defensible specifications for 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents **reproduce 42% of the main estimates under the papers' own specifications**, and across all defensible specifications an average of 25% keep the published sign with p < 0.10. Regression discontinuity claims are more robust than difference-in-differences claims, and robustness is higher for first-order effects, larger published t-statistics, available data or code, top journals, and earlier uses of an experiment.

papers.title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.
papers.summary: Learned optimizers for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) build their updates from local parameter and optimization-history features and use no information about the underlying PDE. The authors define an 11-dimensional PDE state capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state `G2` combined with bounded `FiLM` as the strongest choice among those tested. The resulting optimizer **improves relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE over `Adam` and the unconditioned learned optimizer** on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

papers.title: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
papers.abstract: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels. A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.
papers.summary: Across 814 reinforcement learning runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, the authors examine what a trained model actually inherits from an LLM judge used as its reward. The judge's knowledge of individual answers does not transfer: training with the answer key or a far stronger judge selects which new questions to answer no better than sampling 32 answers from the untrained model and abstaining where they disagree. The judge's beliefs about a category of question do transfer: a judge that rejects eleven of twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states **teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions**, a loss invisible in accuracy and abstention rates, even though the model still answers 94% of them correctly when abstention is blocked. Rewarding the model for giving the answer most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels or judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

papers.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.
papers.summary: Medical anomaly detection must be learned from healthy-patient data only. `MADJEPA` applies a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) in three stages: image-based JEPA (`I-JEPA`) training to represent normal data, target encoder distillation to limit over-generalization to abnormal data, and pseudo-anomaly classification to learn a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. On six datasets spanning MRI, OCT, X-ray, and histopathology, it is competitive with state-of-the-art methods and **ranks first on three datasets**. Ablations indicate that `I-JEPA` alone is not sufficient for competitive results.

papers.title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
papers.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.
papers.summary: Self-play reinforcement learning produces strong driving policies that are hard to verify, while differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) enforces explicit constraints but is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly reinforcement learning. The authors keep a `PPO` teacher's backbone, replace its action head with a `DiffMPC` that enforces road-boundary half-planes and agent ellipses, and distill the student with `DAgger` in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher **matches its teacher on `nuPlan` and beats it on `CARLA` and on out-of-distribution `Waymo` scenes**, while the student of a stronger teacher has fewer failures on `nuPlan` and `Waymo` and stays level on `CARLA`. Distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

papers.title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
papers.abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.
papers.summary: Empirical conclusions from observational data depend on many defensible analytical choices that readers cannot see. A pilot with 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset shows they disagree through the same kinds of choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range; AI peer review barely changes the dispersion, while exposure to top-rated exemplar reports collapses it largely through imitation. The resulting agentic multiverse analysis (`AMA`) framework has agents enumerate a paper's space of choices, score each against a validity rubric, run the validated specification grid, and cross-examine each other under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten studies from a management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), it **reproduces every paper's original estimates** and finds some conclusions hold across all validated specifications while others hinge on undiscussed choices, at a cost of hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper.

papers.title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation of frozen robot policies to out-of-distribution settings usually relies on correction signals learned from the same robotic data, which fail under the same shifts, or on coarse spatial corrections. `VG-Steer` transfers the motion of successful in-distribution rollouts along geometric axes called object-relational distance pairs, using Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Model (VLM) reasoning to pick task-relevant entity pairs and build a single visual-geometric guidance signal. In simulation it corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts. On a real robot it **more than doubles success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions** and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion.

papers.title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
papers.abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.
papers.summary: Distributional reinforcement learning methods learn the full distribution of returns, but existing algorithms are restricted to a narrow class of distributions. `φTD` computes its loss in the frequency domain using characteristic functions, which unifies the quantile and categorical approaches and **makes it possible to learn distributions that were previously out of reach, such as mixtures of continuous distributions**. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep reinforcement learning environments indicate that the wider parametric families can improve performance.

papers.title: From FAIR to AWARE: Data Readiness for Agentic AI in the Earth Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence in the Earth sciences is beginning to act: prototype agents already search archives, run simulations and draft analyses. Scientific data were curated for researchers who bring expert judgement; an autonomous agent cannot be assumed to supply it. Data can satisfy the FAIR principles and still mislead a machine acting alone. We propose that Earth-science data become AWARE (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled), an agent-specific requirements layer that extends FAIR, within a three-part agenda: AWARE data, bounded tools, layered validation. The ingredients exist across community infrastructure. We outline a staged, measurable path to adoption, intended to reduce silent error.
papers.summary: Earth-science data were curated for human researchers who supply expert judgement, which an autonomous agent searching archives, running simulations and drafting analyses cannot be assumed to have. The authors argue that **data can satisfy the FAIR principles and still mislead a machine acting alone**, and propose `AWARE` (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled) as an agent-specific requirements layer on top of FAIR. It sits within a three-part agenda of AWARE data, bounded tools and layered validation, with a staged, measurable adoption path intended to reduce silent error.

papers.title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.
papers.summary: Tracking state across long event streams requires identifying every change and applying the changes in order, which is tested here on products of permutations of five items, a task fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve at all input lengths under the standard conjecture that TC0 ≠ NC1. Instead of having the model reason through the stream, a trained selector on a frozen language model (or a prompt asking an API-only model to list transitions) extracts each event, and an external integer register composes them, with a confidence rule to flag uncertain updates. A frozen 0.8B model with the selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each, and on 1,000-event room-swap documents **all seven models tested both ways solved every document with extraction plus the register and no chain of thought, while only three of ten did so by reasoning alone**. Concurrent extraction cut median wall-clock time from 136.1 to 10.4 seconds for `Sonnet 5.5` and mean cost per document by 55%, though on 500 free-form issue-tracker comments a 4B reader found the recorded value in only 68.8% of cases.

papers.title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.
papers.summary: Research agents often make claims their observations do not support, explore a narrow set of hypotheses, and keep beliefs despite recognising conflicting evidence. `EpiCompass` (Epistemic Compass) is a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains an explicit epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs and revisions, reassesses hypotheses as evidence accumulates, selects new candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, and verifies the final conclusion against the evidence. Across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones it **consistently outperforms baselines while reducing unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs**.

papers.title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
papers.summary: Legged robots navigating real-world terrain need both robust low-level motion control and high-level reasoning about environmental cues. `ROAM` (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility) has a Vision-Language Model (VLM) assess risks, interpret signs and emit semantic labels with navigation costs, which an open-vocabulary segmentation module turns into a dense real-time risk map that conditions two reinforcement-learning policies trained in simulation for locomotion and local navigation. In alpine and urban field tests the robot **completed kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention**, avoiding danger indicated by signs and choosing safe footing. The authors also report remaining weaknesses in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning.

papers.title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
papers.abstract: Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.
papers.summary: Missing covariates are common in biomedical studies, particularly for costly or invasive biomarkers such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease, and the relative performance of available remedies under different missingness mechanisms is poorly understood. This empirical evaluation **compares eight methods, ranging from complete-case analysis and multiple imputation to machine-learning techniques and deep-learning frameworks** such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. Simulations assess bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage and computational burden across missingness mechanisms and proportions, and an application to the `Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project` illustrates the consequences for regression analysis. The authors close with practical recommendations for method selection.

papers.title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
papers.abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.
papers.summary: Watermarks that trace images back to a generative model can be forged: with one watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the mark on arbitrary images or regenerate new content carrying it. `Tripwire-WM` commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which sign-based watermarks leave unused, so a forged image carries a valid watermark whose commitment does not match its content and is both rejected and reported as a forgery. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and `Gaussian Shading++`, it provably preserves their undetectability. On `MS-COCO` it **accepts no imprinting forgeries, versus up to 55.0% for `SemBind`**, and at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, while accepting at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at a false-positive rate of one in a million.
