papers.title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
papers.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.
papers.summary: The Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark (`MKA`) measures how well autonomous agents complete end-to-end professional tasks that depend on visual understanding, such as combining information from CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, charts and maps into a standalone spreadsheet, slide deck or document. It contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors, graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments, and scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by earlier models (Climb-WSR). `Claude Fable 5.2` (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% overall) and `Gemini 4 Carbon` (54.3%, 71.9%) score highest, with Carbon using 5.7× fewer tokens, and **even the strongest models stay below 57% Climb-WSR**. The authors also note that removing image-viewing tools leaves Carbon's `GDPval` score unchanged, indicating that existing benchmarks barely test this capability.

papers.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
papers.abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
papers.summary: Storing user memories directly in model weights is usually framed as continual learning, which aims to retain everything indefinitely, whereas a memory system must keep stable facts, reinforce recurring ones, update changed beliefs and let transient information fade. The proposed system pairs a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter, whose k-hot rank combinations store facts without catastrophic interference and decay on independently controlled schedules, with a lightweight learned controller that decides what to remember, how deeply and for how long for each incoming user event. On a new dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with probes for both recall while a fact is valid and abstention after it expires, the policy **reaches 86% of oracle performance**, whereas continual-learning and retrieval-augmented baselines mostly default to either recalling or abstaining.

papers.title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
papers.abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.
papers.summary: Models predicting unplanned 30-day readmission of diabetic patients typically use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore clinical notes, which can include code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models handle poorly. The framework fuses engineered structured features, compressed `Bio_ClinicalBERT` note embeddings, and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model through a hybrid retrieval-augmented pipeline with negation auditing, then classifies with cost-sensitive `XGBoost`. On the `Diabetes 130-US Hospitals` test cohort the multimodal model **raised sensitivity from 0.5839 to 0.6667** and achieved the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.6375 versus 0.6477 for the structured baseline). On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval lifted Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and cut entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

papers.title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
papers.abstract: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2\beta_i\beta_j\sigma_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.
papers.summary: Shapley-value attributions give a single number per feature and do not indicate whether a coalition of features that jointly explains more than it is credited with could contest the allocation. Treating attribution as an explained-variance cooperative game, the authors report for each feature a stability band (its range of shares over the core or least core), the nucleolus as a distinguished point, and a certificate that no justified objection exists. They prove that for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive and that **in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value**, so stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. In a gradient-boosting retail forecaster the core is empty and the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares.

papers.title: Beyond Restoration: Content-Degradation Factor Unfolding for Real-World Concealed Object Segmentation
papers.abstract: Reliable visual perception under degradation requires distinguishing task-relevant content from degradation-induced variations, especially in concealed object segmentation (COS), where foreground cues are inherently weak. The central challenge is not merely improving visibility, but identifying reliable content evidence amid degradation-induced variations. RGB-space segmentation often entangles content and degradation cues, while restoration-based methods primarily focus on image recovery and task interaction. This motivates explicit factorization to distinguish content evidence from degradation effects and assess its reliability. Retinex provides a spatially aligned basis for this separation but remains illumination-centric. We therefore extend it to content-degradation formation with task-asymmetric factor roles. The Factor Unfolding Network (FUN) uses the content factor R as the sole source of direct semantic evidence for segmentation, while the degradation factor L captures degradation-related variations and generates a spatial reliability map to calibrate this evidence. A unified energy couples observation formation with reliability-weighted foreground-background separation, and its alternating updates yield a coarse-to-fine network without clean-image supervision. In this way, FUN factorizes degradation for perception rather than removing it. Extensive experiments across clean and degraded conditions and diverse segmentation tasks demonstrate robust performance and generalization. Code will be released.
papers.summary: Concealed object segmentation (COS) under image degradation is difficult because weak foreground cues become entangled with degradation effects, and restoration-based pipelines focus on recovering the image instead of judging which evidence is reliable. The Factor Unfolding Network (`FUN`) extends Retinex decomposition into a content factor, used as the sole source of semantic evidence for segmentation, and a degradation factor that produces a spatial reliability map to calibrate that evidence. A unified energy function couples the two, and unrolling its alternating updates yields **a coarse-to-fine network that needs no clean-image supervision**. Experiments across clean and degraded conditions and several segmentation tasks are reported to show robust performance and generalization.

papers.title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
papers.abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.
papers.summary: The letters of the Swiss Reformer Heinrich Bullinger contain many appeals to the Church Fathers, and detecting such patristic references computationally is largely unexplored. A comparison of lexical (`BM25`), dense bi-encoder and hybrid retrieval finds that **`BM25` reaches 94% Recall@20 on explicit citations, ahead of the best dense model at 82%**, while implicit references remain hard (16% for the best bi-encoder). Because the two approaches recover disjoint implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit recall to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking at 26% without its inference cost. A seed-guided extension of `FASTopic` for topic modelling yields minimal coherence gains and topics too diffuse to inform retrieval.

papers.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
papers.abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
papers.summary: The question examined is whether generality should live in a coding agent that builds a bespoke model per task instead of in a single general model, studied in prognostics and health management (PHM), where models must work on unseen equipment. On `NextUnit-Bench`, covering 24 public datasets in 58 folds with held-out units or operating conditions, each agent gets two hours to deliver an executable predictor; frontier agents beat AutoML, **which reaches less than half the best agent's score**, and only 6 of 30 faithful implementations of published methods beat the strongest agent's own design. The agents' edge comes from a design made on each machine's data: a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and the strongest agent given a weaker agent's plan drops to that agent's level. A locally deployable open-weight model given the strongest agent's designs delivers half as often and scores no higher than without them.

papers.title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
papers.abstract: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.
papers.summary: Robots adapting to changing conditions must revise both their task plans and their architectural configurations, and the two are interdependent because configurations determine available actions while plans determine required capabilities. `PLANTA` represents architectural alternatives and their functional and quality requirements in a Web Ontology Language ontology, defines task actions and goals in the Planning Domain Definition Language, and automatically translates and merges the two so that task and reconfiguration actions are planned jointly, replanning when execution invalidates the plan. In underwater inspection and ground navigation scenarios it proved feasible at runtime, and in the navigation scenario it **used less planning time and memory than optimal-policy generation while producing plans of similar quality**.

papers.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.
papers.summary: Small reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) such as `Qwen3.5` often fall into repetition loops in thinking mode, exhausting the token budget and losing the answer. `Keel` has a frontier multimodal LLM act as an agentic editor that is told only the symptom, then locates the cause in the weights, edits them and tests the result, with a harness that keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on held-out questions. Independent editors traced the loops to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and on `Qwen3.5-0.8B` and `Qwen3.5-2B` across six image benchmarks **the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and makes the models significantly more accurate on average**, with no training and no change in model size or per-token cost. The repair also combines with budget forcing, giving the best average accuracy on both models.

papers.title: When Objectives and Evaluators Disagree: Evaluating Transfer for Post-hoc Demographic Framing Mitigation
papers.abstract: Post-hoc rewriting is used to reduce demographic disparities in LLM-generated text when the source model is inaccessible. A rewrite can look successful merely because it improved its own target or satisfied its selector. We study this as a transfer problem on 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of demographic-conditioned climate messages. A rewriter proposes edits, a selection model chooses among constraint-satisfying candidates, and an independent evaluator uninvolved in either rates pairwise framing disparity. A fixed policy that always targets the message with the lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transfers inconsistently across axes and outcome aggregations. An adaptive policy that proposes edits on both sides but accepts at most one significantly improves on that rule, applied to the same candidates, in seven of eight comparisons across two evaluator families, mostly by editing more pairs, not by guided direction choice, at higher preservation risk. A policy editing both messages gives the largest point reductions on fewer pairs. These two policies reduce disparity across a preservation-threshold sweep; absolute ratings vary across evaluator families and prompts. Shrinking the PBI gap increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families. Mitigation should be reported as transfer across objectives, evaluators and their prompts, and editing policies.
papers.summary: Post-hoc rewriting is used to reduce demographic disparities in LLM-generated text when the source model is inaccessible, but a rewrite can look successful only because it improved its own target metric or satisfied its selector. Using 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of demographic-conditioned climate messages, the study separates a rewriter, a selection model and an independent evaluator, and compares editing policies. A fixed policy targeting the message with the lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transfers inconsistently, an adaptive policy improves on it in seven of eight comparisons mostly by editing more pairs, and **shrinking the PBI gap actually increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families**. The authors recommend reporting mitigation as transfer across objectives, evaluators, prompts and editing policies.

papers.title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
papers.abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.
papers.summary: Porous printed layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the best layout depends on how process settings shape the deposit, yet a generator that ignores those settings samples the same distribution every time. The proposed latent diffusion generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent space, a topology U-Net, a `ControlNet` branch for the design domain, and a separately trained regressor whose gradient steers denoising toward a process-dependent utilization score, applied to aerosol jet printing. Across seven modeled flow settings the lowest-scoring candidate layout differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains, and strong guidance **lowered the mean score from 0.642 to 0.450** (lower is better).

papers.title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection
papers.abstract: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.
papers.summary: Adversarial example detectors often fail against attackers who explicitly try to bypass them. The proposed dual-model approach keeps the classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier, using class-specific patterns of internal activations (activation signatures) to generate hard adversarial examples that fool the classifier, challenge the verifier and internally resemble the target class, while knowledge distillation preserves clean performance. Against adaptive L-infinity attacks, including ones unseen in training, the verifier substantially outperforms confidence-based and feature-based detectors, and ablations show that **adaptive verifier training is the main source of the gain while signature guidance mainly helps clean accuracy**. Evaluations under L2 attacks reveal limited robustness across perturbation types.

papers.title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
papers.abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.
papers.summary: Graph coloring with a fixed palette is NP-hard, which motivates learned methods that exploit recurring structure across instances. Because the validity of a coloring is unchanged by permuting colors, the authors show that exploiting this symmetry shrinks the effective state space a policy must learn over, while the solver still has to break node symmetries such as adjacent nodes in the same automorphism orbit. `Scone` uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to build colorings sequentially so earlier assignments propagate and break those symmetries. It **achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks**, including `sudoku_extreme` and register allocation, and generalizes to graph families not seen in training.

papers.title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
papers.abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.
papers.summary: Continuous-time neural state-space identification, as in `SUBNET`, trains slowly because numerical integration requires many successive neural-network evaluations. Deep structured state space models (`DS3M`) instead combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series, and use custom GPU kernels written in `Triton` to **cut the launch and memory overhead of evaluating those components sequentially**. The authors also describe a port-Hamiltonian variant and report benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

papers.title: MS-Point: Multi-Modal Hierarchical Spectral Learning for Point Cloud Understanding
papers.abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.
papers.summary: Point-image alignment pretraining can give the same alignment signal to different local feature patterns, because they collapse to the same pooled descriptor. `MS-Point` addresses this by supervising intermediate point features directly: at selected encoder stages it computes neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and aligns each branch with image features, with cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinating the branches. The design works with both graph encoders and point Transformers, and evaluations cover object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning. Same-backbone, capacity-matched and computation-matched controls **attribute the gains to the structure of supervision rather than to added capacity**.

papers.title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.
papers.summary: Sparse embedding tables dominate memory in large recommendation models, and in-training embedding pruning (`ITEP`) can hurt accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. `FI-ITEP` sets those ratios from feature importance instead, pruning tables tied to less important features more aggressively. Across three large-scale recommendation models it achieves **20–40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy** relative to percentile-based `ITEP`, which lets the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (for example 112 down to 80) and saves over 1,000 GPU-hours per model launch. The trends are reproduced on the open-source `DLRM` with `Criteo 1TB`, including the cost of computing feature importance.

papers.title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
papers.abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.
papers.summary: Labels from zero-shot large language model (LLM) classifiers are only useful if their trustworthiness can be estimated, so this study compares black-box confidence methods (verbalised confidence, sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (`P(True)` and several logit-scoring variants with constrained generation). Across eleven open-weight models of 1B–32B parameters and five datasets with 3 to 151 labels, the choice of method rarely changes accuracy, but **logit-based scoring separates correct from incorrect predictions far better (AUROC 0.74–0.77) than black-box methods (0.57–0.66)**. A proposed decision-only scoring scheme, which scores only the positions where labels diverge in a prefix tree, cuts decode steps by 88–96% on the three largest label sets with comparable performance. The best configurations, using `Gemma 4 31B` and `Qwen 3.5 9B`, are competitive with the commercial `Jev 1.13.0` classifier.

papers.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.
papers.summary: Large language models are often post-trained to report confidence by rewarding each answer individually toward 1 if correct and 0 if incorrect, which leaves confidences uninformative for ranking answers when a user tolerates some risk and wants the model to abstain selectively. `CARE` (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation) instead computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: at several risk tolerances the set's confidences induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for falling on the correct side of it. On math benchmarks (`MATH-500`, `GSM8K`, `Big-Math-Digits`), **coverage at 5% risk rises from 0.8% to 42.4%** compared with pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on `HotpotQA`, coverage at 5% risk on out-of-distribution benchmarks such as `CommonsenseQA`, `GPQA`, `SimpleQA`, and `TriviaQA` improves from 12.3% to 23.6%.

papers.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: https://github.com/armanbolatov/fedmars_drivaernet
papers.summary: Neural surrogates can predict car aerodynamics in seconds rather than the hours a computational fluid dynamics simulation takes, but the training data is proprietary to manufacturers, which motivates federated training. Using a `Transolver` surrogate on `DrivAerNet++` split across six clients that each hold a single body type, the authors compare spectral optimizers that orthogonalize each weight-matrix update (`FedMuon` and the newly proposed `FedMARS-M` and `FedOLion`) against `FedAvg`, `SCAFFOLD-Adam`, and `FedLion`. `FedMuon` and `FedMARS-M` reach a **drag error within 2% of centralized training** using two to four local epochs per round, while the non-spectral methods remain 17–37% worse than `FedMARS-M` even with sixteen local epochs. The gap is attributed to the low stable rank of weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step gives roughly twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm.

papers.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
papers.abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.
papers.summary: Split federated learning divides a network between clients and a server, which entangles class-specific knowledge across both parts and makes it hard to forget a class while preserving accuracy on the rest. `SplitReAlign` builds endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, realigns the forgotten class's representations, and penalizes changes outside the active subspaces. It supports client-only, server-only, and joint update modes. On `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` with heterogeneous client data it achieves **the lowest average gap to full retraining among compared methods across six settings**, with the server-only mode agreeing most closely with retraining.

papers.title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.
papers.summary: Existing 3D medical imaging foundation models tend to need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, are limited to one modality, or depend on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. `VoxForge` is a single encoder trained with self-distillation and cross-modal curricula on permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes, and is evaluated strictly frozen on segmentation, classification, and registration across MRI, CT, and PET, a modality it never sees in training. It attains **the best or tied-best average rank in every task group** against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models. It also matches top-performing models on `TotalSegmentator` CT using a tenth of the labels.

papers.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
papers.abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.
papers.summary: A Bayesian learner that pays a charge each time it revises an issued action faces a trade-off between predictive loss and adjustment costs. Under assumptions including population curvature and an order-1/n lower bound on posterior uncertainty, with sample losses allowed to be unbounded or nonconvex, the authors characterize exactly when a target rate of cumulative expected excess loss can be achieved together with a finite expected lifetime charge. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, and adaptive timing or private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For excess of order (log T)^r with 0<r<1, **every policy needs on the order of (log T)^(2-r) revisions in expectation**, and a charge-independent schedule matches this bound; the assumptions are verified for logistic decision models.

papers.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.
papers.summary: This doctoral thesis studies three forms of explanation for language model predictions — highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning — judged by faithfulness to the model's computation, plausibility to users, and practical utility. It contributes two evaluation frameworks for highlight explanations and **a meta-evaluation framework that examines how reliable existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations are**. It also proposes two techniques for generating natural language explanations intended to be faithful while remaining concise and coherent. A human-AI interaction study examines how evidence and explanations help users validate model verdicts in fact-checking.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
papers.summary: Deployed motor-imagery EEG decoders must decide when adapting to distribution shift is worth the cost, not just how to adapt. The authors place a control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder running from the factory model to a closed-form Bayesian head, then an affine map, with full fine-tuning as a last resort, governed by a gate that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. A clean-referenced gate reduces unnecessary adaptation on field-like sessions from a rate of 0.56 to 0.11, and under severe synthetic stress a lightweight `LDA` head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures at **about 23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning**. In two unperturbed `BNCI` session checks the factory model transferred without intervention, so the demonstrated benefit under natural drift is cost-efficiency rather than accuracy.

papers.title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.
papers.summary: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained policy with a limited interaction budget, and in multi-phase tasks the phase where failures occur is not necessarily the phase where a correction most improves task completion. The authors define a completion gain — the change in full-task completion probability when a state-feedback controller replaces selected action components during a single phase — estimate it from paired episodes, and use it to choose which action components to correct and how to split training episodes across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking, most failures occurred in the final docking phase but the largest gain was in the preceding channel phase, and gain-based allocation beat allocation proportional to failure counts. In simulated bimanual assembly, a residual policy trained in the release phase **improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%**, even though few failures occurred there.

papers.title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
papers.abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.
papers.summary: AI agents built by coupling a fixed language model to a general-purpose computing device are shown to have **undecidable safety**: given a dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run a semantically equivalent one. As a consequence, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists, and certifications can only provide imperfect protection. With bounded context, values, and running time the problem becomes decidable but remains PSPACE-complete, even when the agent's description is known. Safety is also not compositional, since agents individually proven safe can produce unsafe behavior together, and the authors discuss relaxed notions of safety usable in practice.

papers.title: RE-CAM: Readout-Enhanced Content-Addressable Memory for Quantitative Similarity Search
papers.abstract: Similarity search is essential to many applications but incurs massive data movement when executed on conventional architectures. Content-addressable memory (CAM) is a promising hardware substrate, as it allows similarity search directly in the CAM array, minimizing data movement and offering both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, conventional CAM array readout produces only binary match results, discarding quantitative similarity information that could be further exploited. Extracting this information requires interpreting the CAM array output voltage that evolves during a CAM search, making the sensing timestamp a crucial design variable alongside the reference voltage and decoding parameter. In this work, we propose RE-CAM, a readout enhancement framework for CAM that is agnostic to memory technology and application, enabling CAM array readout to approximate linear and nonlinear functions with one CAM search. By reusing the comparators to sense the time-varying output voltage multiple times, jointly optimizing the three design variables under system constraints and hardware nonidealities, and co-designing the optimization algorithm and reconfigurable hardware, RE-CAM achieves accurate approximation with low energy and area overhead without introducing a readout throughput bottleneck. Across linear, piecewise-linear, sigmoid, and exponential functions, RE-CAM reduces normalized root mean square error by 10.89% to 24.34% for general approximation and 29.43% to 46.73% when exploiting dataset distribution, compared to a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline with the same comparison budget. Relative to the same baseline, RE-CAM also achieves $8\times$ higher search throughput while reducing energy per search and area by 47% and 39%, respectively.
papers.summary: Content-addressable memory (CAM) performs similarity search inside the memory array, but conventional readout returns only binary match results and discards quantitative similarity information. `RE-CAM` is a technology-agnostic readout framework that reuses comparators to sense the array's time-varying output voltage several times, jointly optimizing the sensing timestamp, reference voltage, and decoding parameter so that a single search approximates linear and nonlinear functions. Compared with a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline using the same comparison budget, it lowers normalized root mean square error by 10.89–24.34% for general approximation and 29.43–46.73% when exploiting the dataset distribution. It also delivers **8x higher search throughput while cutting energy per search by 47% and area by 39%**.

papers.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
papers.abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).
papers.summary: In regulated domains such as lending, disparate treatment — using demographic information or proxies for it in decisions — has fewer quantitative detection and mitigation tools than disparate impact, and features flagged as proxies are usually just removed at a cost to predictive performance. The proposed two-part framework first applies a quantitative test for proxy capacity, checking whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a demographic group, and then applies a pre-processing step that adjusts such features to reduce that capacity. On synthetic and public datasets, the framework identifies proxy features and reduces their proxy capacity while **the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal, giving better predictive performance than removing it**.

papers.title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
papers.abstract: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.
papers.summary: Analog layout generators enable design reuse and migration between manufacturing processes, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. `ReLay` translates in both directions between layouts and generator code: it recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling portability across process design kits (PDKs) and parametric resizing, and promotes recurring constructions to library functions so the library grows as layouts accumulate. The authors also release a benchmark of 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs. Learned functions account for 53–66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, and frontier LLM agents using `ReLay` produce new layouts at **64–77% lower API cost per completed task** than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

papers.title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: https://github.com/opatil31/SEANA
papers.summary: Self-supervised learning on noisy scientific images such as microscopy can take a shortcut: because both augmented views come from the same noisy image, the encoder can raise view agreement by encoding noise patterns instead of semantic content. Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (`SEANA`) is a drop-in module that learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform from noisy data, estimates the clean signal, and resamples independent noise in the transformed space, with no clean targets, no denoiser at inference, and no change to the objective or encoder. It improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy on `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-100` under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise across contrastive and non-contrastive methods. On real fluorescence imaging it improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by **up to 28.6 percentage points over standard self-supervised learning** and 27.5 points over denoiser-preprocessed baselines.

papers.title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.
papers.summary: When LLM agents write hardware designs along with the tests and reviews that validate them, the resulting evidence is self-generated and may be weak. The authors describe a seven-stage verification-gated workflow used to port an `ML-KEM-768`/`ML-DSA-65` post-quantum cryptography accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ card, then audit its evidence with netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The design is byte-exact on the board and passes all 85 applicable NIST ACVP cases, yet **existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants**. In replays, undirected whole-design LLM review caught two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions while module-scoped review caught every known flaw in all 54 sessions, but even scoped review found planted key-custody flaws in just 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks flagged every one.

papers.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance
papers.abstract: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.
papers.summary: Automated checkers for ICAO/ISO passport-photo compliance give pass/fail verdicts per criterion without quantifying uncertainty for accept, reject, or retake decisions. The authors add conformal prediction as a triage layer on the `BioGaze` analyser, fitting per-criterion logistic classifiers and comparing marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules on the synthetic `TONO` benchmark across 14 criteria. Marginal conformal prediction reached about 0.90 overall coverage but covered violations as poorly as 0.37 for one criterion, whereas **Mondrian coverage of violations ranged from 0.89 to 0.92**. Most of the false-positive reduction came from the logistic layer itself, tuned abstention rules beat Mondrian on false positives at comparable retake rates, and a Bonferroni correction for joint coverage required retaking nearly all images.

papers.title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
papers.abstract: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS).
