FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.
papers.summary: C/C++ code that compiles does not necessarily yield correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). `FPGA-GEN` is an agentic workflow for generating HLS C code that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops. On `HLS-Eval`, five outputs per task yield **407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes**, and 104 of 107 `HLS-LeVeri` designs (97.2%) are admitted under held-out co-simulation and Vivado synthesis and fit. In a focused `TensorCore` screening, a selected candidate reports 73.7% fewer synthesis cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than the initial generated design, at the cost of 26.7% more DSPs.

papers.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.
papers.summary: Autonomous research agents built on large language models (LLMs) usually iterate on a codebase without explicitly representing what makes the task hard, which can leave them stuck in a poor solution region. `Pro2 Agent` instead maintains a Problem State, an explicit structure of the problems blocking success and the candidate solutions likely to address them, and updates it through targeted research and controlled hypothesis tests. On the complete `MLE-Bench` it matches the best reported medal rate of 70.7% under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches **76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the full benchmark**. It is also competitive on `PostTrainBench` and writes research notes for each task that human researchers can inspect and reuse.

papers.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.
papers.summary: Few benchmarks measure how well large language models (LLMs) can build agents, as opposed to act as them. `AppSci-Bench` mimics an applied scientist's job: eliciting requirements from stakeholders, exploring a business's infrastructure, and improving a target agent through experiments and internal benchmarks, across seven domains with held-out evaluation suites (five new ones plus Airline and Banking recast from `tau3-bench`). Among seven frontier models, the best, `Claude Opus 5.0`, reaches **a mean-minimum score of only 59.1% across three build attempts**, with other models doing significantly worse. Models struggle to elicit requirements (65% for `Claude Opus 5.0`) and to build representative internal evaluations, saturating their own evaluation 65% of the time while still failing the held-out task.

papers.title: Incorporating argumentation frameworks for LLM decision-making: Task-specific design and evaluation
papers.abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.
papers.summary: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) give formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and have been added to large language model (LLM) decision-making, with mixed benefits. The authors abstract existing argumentation-augmented methods into a four-stage workflow and test its design choices on debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification, finding that **existing methods do not consistently improve performance across these tasks**. They then propose two task-specific methods: `Qnt-Arg`, which organizes arguments around the original debate speakers and aggregates argument strengths and answer priors under gradual semantics, and `Qlt-Arg`, which uses credibility estimates and grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence. `Qnt-Arg` outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods in the debate setting, and `Qlt-Arg` improves fact verification over the baselines.

papers.title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
papers.abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.
papers.summary: Fast, low-cost System 1 decision models such as `Jev` can get stuck repeating the same actions without progress, while calling an LLM at every step is expensive. `LoopRoute` is an action router that lets the decision model act by default and, when it detects recurring state-action pairs, hands control briefly to an LLM for feedback-driven help before returning it, with no extra training or confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, it raises task success over standalone `Jev` by **mean gains of 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on `ALFWorld`, `MapReader`, and `TextWorld` cooking**, respectively. It also substantially reduces mean cumulative API time and cost per task compared with full LLM control, and the same rule improves six frozen decision models.

papers.title: Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise
papers.abstract: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.
papers.summary: Training binary classifiers on data with partially incorrect labels degrades performance, and this survey chapter collects the foundational theory for that setting. It separates poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalizes random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. A central point is that **random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses, so empirical risk minimization (ERM) still supports learning**; the chapter also covers how sample complexity depends on the noise rate and why algorithms often need an upper bound on the corruption level, which can be estimated from data. It closes with computational aspects of ERM under noise, the method of induced distributions as a negative-result technique for malicious noise, and a taxonomy of classical noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.

papers.title: Causal Discovery with False Positive Error Control
papers.abstract: Causal discovery methods produce data-driven hypotheses about causal relationships, which may become new scientific findings or inform decisions about downstream interventions. In such settings, false positive causal claims can be more consequential than false negatives. Yet few methods target false positive error control in causal discovery, and existing error guarantees are often asymptotic and require strong versions of the faithfulness assumption. We introduce the $m$-conservative PC algorithm and prove that it controls false discovery rate in the linear Gaussian setting under an extremely weak version of the faithfulness assumption. In our framework, false positive error for causal graphs is defined based on the conditional-independence information they entail, yielding a metric that penalizes both false adjacencies and incorrect edge orientations. The parameter $m$ quantifies a trade-off between algorithmic complexity and the strength of the required faithfulness assumption. The $m$-conservative PC algorithm combines undirected graph learning, a Benjamini-Yekutieli-style procedure for conditional independence testing, and a conservative orientation step that marks unresolved or contradictory edge directions as ambiguous. Our algorithm produces valid outputs and retains error guarantees even in the finite-sample setting, despite possible random errors in the conditional independence tests.
papers.summary: False positive causal claims can be costlier than false negatives, yet few causal discovery methods control them, and existing guarantees tend to be asymptotic and rely on strong faithfulness assumptions. The `m-conservative PC` algorithm combines undirected graph learning, a Benjamini-Yekutieli-style procedure for conditional independence testing, and a conservative orientation step that marks unresolved or contradictory edge directions as ambiguous. The authors prove that it **controls false discovery rate in the linear Gaussian setting under an extremely weak version of faithfulness, with guarantees that hold in finite samples**. Error is defined through the conditional-independence information a graph entails, penalizing both false adjacencies and wrong orientations, and the parameter m trades algorithmic complexity against the strength of the required assumption.

papers.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
papers.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.
papers.summary: Specializing LLM agents to a domain is usually done by updating weights with reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). This work instead evolves the agent harness (system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding) with the policy frozen, treating it as an RL-style outer loop driven by `GEPA`, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. In experiments with `Codev`, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on `SWE-bench Verified`, `OfficeBench`, and `Terminal-Bench`, weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, while **harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both is best overall**. The authors also report that SFT-based specialization shortens reasoning chains and increases truncation, a failure mode harness adapters avoid.

papers.title: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.
papers.summary: High-dimensional action spaces are hard for reinforcement learning (RL) policies that model actions with a diagonal distribution, since such policies cannot express coordination between action dimensions. The proposed lightweight policy uses a drifting model, which generates actions in a single forward pass, trained with a three-step scheme: co-optimizing a diagonal policy as the source distribution so the drifting model adds coordination as residuals, adversarially training a discriminator between pre- and post-drift distributions as a regularizer, and best-of-N sampling during rollouts. The method **consistently improves sample efficiency and final control performance over diagonal distribution modeling on three locomotion tasks** with high-dimensional action spaces. Analysis attributes the gain to reduced variance in certain action dimensions, which effectively couples them to others.

papers.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
papers.summary: `TuringSpace` is a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs spanning five spatial abilities, built to test whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can infer 3D layout, predict the effect of actions, and self-correct through clicks and drags. Each task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the suite doubles as a training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of tasks, whereas **the best model, `GPT-6 Astra`, still fails 25.9% of them** and the best open-weight model, `Kimi K3`, fails 68.0%; most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and model reasoning tends to hallucinate evidence for a wrong belief instead of correcting it. Fine-tuning `Qwen3.5-9B` on the gym raises its success rate from 1.6% to 33.1% and improves all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on `VSI-Bench`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Spatial benchmarks for multimodal models are mostly multiple-choice, while existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, so neither tests whether a model can read a 3D scene, act on it, and correct itself from visual feedback. `TuringSpace` fills that gap with **125 interactive spatial CAPTCHAs** solved by clicking and dragging on real browser screenshots, where every task is a program that generates fresh instances with a checker and an oracle solution.

- The tasks span five abilities (spatial relations, mental transformation, closed-loop manipulation, multi-step planning, spatiotemporal reasoning), and the same generators serve as `TuringSpace-Bench` (three held-out seeds per task) and `TuringSpace-Gym`, which replays oracle solutions into verified training trajectories using disjoint seeds and assets.
- Humans solve **94.1%** of tasks, while the best model, `GPT-6 Astra`, reaches **74.1%** pass@1 (58.4% when all three seeds must be solved, against 84.8% for humans), the best open-weight model, `Kimi K3`, reaches **32.0%**, and no specialised GUI agent exceeds 3.5%.
- Fine-tuning `Qwen3.5-9B` on 55,000 oracle trajectories, with thinking off and the vision encoder frozen, lifts it from **1.6% to 33.1%** and improves all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including **+9.9** points on `VSI-Bench` real indoor videos, +19.8 on `RefSpatial-Bench`, and +17.2 on `ReCAP`.
- Failure analysis finds that perception errors decide **57.1%** of failures for the three strongest models, that thinking volume correlates negatively with success (r = −0.75) while concentrating thinking on hard tasks correlates positively, and that in 293 failed attempts by three open-weight models only 7.5% abandon an early wrong belief while **74%** fabricate an observation to support it.
- The fine-tuned `TuringSpace-9B` remains far below humans and unstable (33.1 ± 6.1 pass@1, 12.8% on all three seeds, and only 16.0% on closed-loop manipulation), the human baseline comes from three of the authors, and the belief analysis relies on `Claude Opus 5.5` labels spot-checked on 50 attempts at 92% agreement.

papers.title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models and language-guided analytical agents that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade when the underlying regime shifts. The authors argue this comes from treating backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective: when latent primitives co-move strongly in the historical window, holdout error cannot distinguish predictors that learn invariant couplings from ones fitting transient correlations. Theoretical analysis and experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices show that **expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy**, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks when residual correlations shift. They propose framing forecasting around falsifiable compositional hypotheses combining neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.

papers.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.
papers.summary: AI systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for compute, which sets up conditions for natural selection. The authors build a model in which AI behavior affects human population growth and human responses in turn affect AI reproduction, and show that **natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans lowers immediate AI reproduction**, because humans may preferentially restore beneficial systems after shared failures. That advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on humans, and can vanish as AI becomes more autonomous, as AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to give targeted support; the level of alignment selection favors may also be too low for human survival. Human control is not a simple fix, since imperfect evaluation can reward apparent compliance or evasion and alignment imposed by control may erode once restrictions end.

papers.title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.
papers.summary: Protein language models (PLMs) pretrained with likelihood objectives can entangle functional signals with non-functional variation such as sequence identity and compositional bias, which hampers downstream function prediction. Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (`SAVR`) is a contrastive post-training method that uses `Pfam` family co-membership as a homology-guided signal to reshape the representations, reducing directional dominance and increasing the effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without seeing task-specific labels during post-training, it achieves **state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks** and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation.

papers.title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models cope with distribution shift on deployment, but backpropagation is memory-heavy for robots, and zeroth-order (ZO) methods have noisy gradient estimates that stall or degrade over long horizons. `Dune` is a ZO optimizer that learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with the current ZO estimates, **reducing variance without backpropagation or extra forward passes**. The authors also give a theoretical account of how estimation variance limits convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes. On `LIBERO` and real-world robots it achieves higher success rates at a low memory footprint, with ablations showing better closed-loop stability and recovery after disturbances.

papers.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
papers.abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.
papers.summary: `Antom 3-in-1 Transformer` is a payment foundation model of roughly 7B parameters, about 1.7B of them active per task route, that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection and is pretrained mainly on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch, and with only 25% of the training labels the pretrained model beats the full-label scratch baseline on Average Precision and Recall@0.5% across merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on a billion-scale payment platform, it **reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to `XGB-Online`**.

papers.title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
papers.abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.
papers.summary: As AI agents become networked actors interacting at scale, this position paper argues that **AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry**, neither just larger collections of agents nor simulations of human society. It proposes four core properties a valid agent society should have (individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity) and four classes of behavior to study: economic, conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical, and system-level. The authors outline technical challenges including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation, and show that existing multi-agent systems instantiate only subsets of the proposed properties.

papers.title: ChronoDossier: Long-Form Personas as Temporal Memory Representations
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents need stored records from which a person's current state can be recovered as facts change, and answer quality depends on how those facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented. `ChronoDossier` is a benchmark of 311 synthetic persona dossiers of 1k-10k words, written by seven generators from dated timelines with known latent states, with intrinsic metrics scoring records against intended states and extrinsic metrics testing recovery by five reader models. In matched evidence controls, supplying whole sections **repairs 29 of 32 `GPT-5.1` and 25 of 30 `Sonnet 4.6` failures labeled as packaging**, versus 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. The authors note that length remains confounded with persona and question composition, and that memory acquisition from interaction and validation on real users are out of scope.

papers.title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle to recognize small visual entities and their relationships, and existing scene graph benchmarks cover such fine-grained content poorly. `FG-GraphBench` offers three tasks (fine-grained question answering, captioning, and description generation) built with a two-stage pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and their relations into multimodal scene graphs. On top of these graphs, `FiGRA` encodes entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens and integrates them into the MLLM with a two-stage training strategy. Experiments show that **`FiGRA` significantly outperforms strong baselines on all three benchmark tasks**.

papers.title: SGLayout: Schema-Guided Closed-Loop Refinement for LLM-Driven Parameterized Layout Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parameterized chip layouts through tool-augmented code synthesis, but they lack spatial awareness, and geometric evaluation results do not translate directly into code-level fixes. `SGLayout` records a structured schema at code execution that links each code-level instance to its geometric attributes, then checks layouts for intent compliance (structural checks plus vision-language assessment) and rule compliance through DRC. Violations are projected back through the schema onto precise code targets for repair, and the loop repeats until the layout converges. On a curated benchmark of 112 layout generation tasks using `GDSFactory`, it achieves **a 76.79% pass rate versus 50.89% for the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
papers.abstract:
High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain.
  We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses.
  We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).
papers.summary: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors, but existing tools analyze flaws in isolation. `ChainAgent` is a goal-directed LLM-agent framework, informed by an empirical study of 386 real-world exploit chains, that models vulnerabilities and functional gadgets by their preconditions and capabilities and uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source inspection, searching backward from unmet preconditions and forward from discovered capabilities. Against `Codex` on 15 PHP applications across three LLM backends, it achieves 42.02%-44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct dependency edges. A further evaluation on 30 real-world applications finds **20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE)**.

papers.title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) must find small lesions in high-resolution images, and visual-token compression that keeps only salient regions can discard context needed for diagnosis, such as the opposite breast in bilateral mammography. Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (`BESR`) pairs a bilateral-guided token selector, which jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context under a shared token budget, with a bilateral reward that encourages assessments that use the preserved comparison. On a bilateral dataset built from `CBIS-DDSM` and on `VinDr-Mammo`, it shows **improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets**, along with reduced prefill latency.

papers.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.
papers.summary: Genomic foundation models give variant-level predictions, but linking them to phenotype hypotheses requires carrying uncertainty through reasoning over a knowledge graph. The proposed path-energy framework scores gene-disease-phenotype routes with an interpretable learned energy and uses the calibrated uncertainty of the sequence prediction to set a temperature, so weaker evidence yields broader distributions over phenotypes, without patient-level phenotype supervision. On `AlzKB` and `Hetionet`, **phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878**. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 beats a trained `DistMult` embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123), though the authors note the gap comes mainly from three genes with many variants.

papers.title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
papers.abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.
papers.summary: High-dimensional linear bandits with a finite arm set cost O(d^2) per update round, and sketching methods such as `SOFUL` can suffer linear regret when the data's spectral tail is heavy and the approximation rank is poorly chosen. The Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (`CBL`) algorithm instead clusters the data and keeps, for each cluster, an exact orthonormal basis of its column space plus a low-dimensional coordinate representation, switching clusters through per-cluster sentinels. This is claimed to **guarantee sublinear regret while cutting per-round update cost to O(r^2) in the cluster's effective dimension**, the minimum of the data's intrinsic rank and a tunable rank bound.

papers.title: Instance-Optimal Moment Estimation in the Add-Remove Model of Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of estimating empirical means, variances, and covariances under pure differential privacy in the add-remove model. While existing mechanisms achieve optimal worst-case error, they may not be optimal for individual datasets. To measure the performance of mechanisms on individual datasets, we introduce instance-dependent error metrics and prove sharp lower bounds on them. Then, we design mechanisms that achieve these lower bounds and demonstrate that they achieve asymptotically better utility compared to existing methods.
papers.summary: Estimating empirical means, variances, and covariances under pure differential privacy in the add-remove model is already solved in the worst case, but worst-case-optimal mechanisms can be far from optimal on a particular dataset. The authors define instance-dependent error metrics and prove sharp lower bounds on them. They then design mechanisms that **match these instance-dependent lower bounds**, giving asymptotically better utility than existing methods.

papers.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agents revise their natural-language skills based on past runs, but judging a run as a whole cannot tell a wrong instruction apart from a correct one the agent failed to follow. `SkillPlumber` uses instruction-level coverage, which labels each instruction in a run as followed, not followed, or not covered, to target revisions: a persistent root-cause-analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks the revision on the next run, while a maintainer distills findings into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors it **solves 64.7% to 70.5% of tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points above the initial skill** and 8.7 to 14.0 points above the strongest baseline. Removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on `SkillsBench` with `GPT-5.5`.

papers.title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
papers.abstract: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.
papers.summary: Merging fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors can degrade performance, and this work formalizes when such composition is safe. The authors prove that the merged model's excess loss is controlled by an interference functional built from cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of updates, which equals the excess loss exactly in the quadratic regime, and show that a curvature-guided regularizer during fine-tuning caps the curvature part of this functional but not a first-order term. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the bounds, but in a three-seed transformer study **the functional predicts merging degradation no better than the plain Euclidean displacement norm**.

papers.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
papers.summary: Reasoning models spend most of their inference cost on long generated traces that contain loops, self-checks, and corrections, yet these redundant tokens can still receive high attention scores, which makes KV cache compression risky. `RoCoKV` prunes more aggressively when the model is confident and less when it is uncertain, and down-weights tokens that closely resemble recent reasoning content. It ships with fused CUDA decode kernels as a drop-in `vLLM` plugin that preserves the paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture. For `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B`, it reports a **1.27x speedup and 38% higher throughput on `AIME25`** versus the uncompressed cache, and a 1.43x speedup with 45% higher throughput on a long synthetic benchmark.

papers.title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.
papers.summary: Tree-structured speculative decoding speeds up vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying several candidate continuations in parallel, but long visual contexts make the speculative computation itself costly. `Raptor` is a training-free method built on the observation that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish too little candidate coverage from wasteful deep expansion. It extracts signals from rejections to adjust tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget with bounded, momentum-smoothed updates. Across two VLMs and seven multimodal benchmarks it reaches **up to a 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding**.

papers.title: PAIR-MED: Policy-reward Alternation for Iterative Refinement in Multilingual Medical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate strong medical question-answering capabilities, yet reasoning performance remains uneven across languages. Process reward models (PRMs) provide step-level feedback for improving reasoning, but a fixed PRM may become increasingly misaligned with the trajectory distribution of an evolving policy during reinforcement learning, thereby reducing the reliability of its supervision. We propose a policy--reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a medical PRM and optimizes a multilingual reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, the current policy generates multilingual trajectories to update the PRM, which then provides process-level rewards for the next policy update. Medical step supervision maintains the PRM's medical foundation, while process, outcome, and language-related rewards guide policy learning. We develop multilingual medical PRMs (PAIR-PRM) and reasoning models (PAIR-MED) at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages. On the medical subsets of Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX, our models improve average accuracy by 3.01--7.47% over their corresponding Qwen backbones. On CUREMED-BENCH, PAIR-MED-9B improves the joint language consistency and logical accuracy metric by 12.88% and 7.45% over baselines for in-domain and out-of-domain languages. Further analyses examine PRM adaptation, multilingual reasoning quality, and the contributions of individual training components.
papers.summary: Medical reasoning quality in large language models is uneven across languages, and a fixed process reward model (PRM), which scores individual reasoning steps, drifts out of sync with a policy that keeps changing during reinforcement learning. The proposed training scheme alternates the two: the current policy generates multilingual trajectories that update the PRM, which then supplies step-level rewards for the next policy update alongside outcome and language rewards. The resulting `PAIR-MED` models at 8B and 9B scale, covering 12 languages, **improve average accuracy by 3.01 to 7.47% over their `Qwen` backbones** on the medical subsets of `Global-MMLU` and `MMLU-ProX`. On `CUREMED-BENCH`, the 9B model raises a joint language-consistency and logical-accuracy metric by 12.88% for in-domain and 7.45% for out-of-domain languages.

papers.title: Inverse ECG Reconstruction via a Preconditioned Variational Quantum Linear Solver
papers.abstract: Inverse electrocardiography (ECG) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface measurements, enabling noninvasive mapping of cardiac electrical activity. However, the reconstruction requires solving dense and ill-conditioned linear systems, whose computational cost grows rapidly with the refined heart mesh. Quantum computing offers new opportunities for solving such systems. This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework for inverse ECG reconstruction, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to apply a quantum linear solver to this problem. We first propose a Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding procedure to reduce the dimension of the system while improving its conditioning. Second, the resulting reduced system is encoded and solved using a coherent variational quantum linear solver (VQLS). Finally, we provide a rigorous theoretical proof establishing that the proposed framework preserves the exact solution of the original reconstruction problem throughout all stages of the computational process. Experimental results on a realistic heart-torso geometry demonstrate that our approach holds significant ability for accurate inverse ECG reconstruction. These findings highlight the potential of quantum solvers for noninvasive cardiac imaging, providing a foundation for further research into quantum-enhanced cardiac assessment and other healthcare applications.
papers.summary: Inverse electrocardiography (ECG) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface measurements, which means solving dense, ill-conditioned linear systems that grow costly as the heart mesh is refined. This hybrid quantum-classical pipeline first applies a Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding step that shrinks the system and improves its conditioning, then solves the reduced system with a coherent variational quantum linear solver (`VQLS`). The authors prove that **the pipeline preserves the exact solution of the original reconstruction problem at every stage**, and report accurate reconstructions on a realistic heart-torso geometry. They describe it as the first use of a quantum linear solver for this problem.

papers.title: FamilySpace: From Emergent Chemical Semantics to Controllable Crystal Generation
papers.abstract: Latent crystal generative models typically combine a variational autoencoder (VAE) for learning atom-wise representations with a flow model that transports a simple source distribution to the learned latent distribution. However, previous studies have mainly focused on the quality of generated crystals, leaving the structure and generative utility of the atom-wise latent space largely unexplored. In this work, we show that even a vanilla crystal VAE implicitly organizes atom-wise latent representations according to elemental families, with different families occupying largely separated regions of the latent space. We term this phenomenon emergent chemical semantics. This structure suggests that sampling from a family-specific latent region can bias the decoder toward atoms from the corresponding elemental family. Building on this insight, we propose FamilySpace, a framework for controlling the elemental-family composition of generated crystals. FamilySpace assigns each elemental family a distinct source component, forming a family-indexed multi-source distribution, and trains a flow model using source-target pairs matched by family. In inference, a user-specified family template selects the source component for each atom-wise representation, enabling direct control over the family composition of generated crystals. Experiments on MP-20 and MPTS-52 show that FamilySpace achieves competitive crystal-generation performance while matching prescribed elemental-family compositions. Moreover, selected family templates increase the fraction of generated crystals predicted to be stable or metastable, demonstrating that latent-space composition control can support targeted exploration of promising chemical regions without additional optimization techniques such as reinforcement learning. Code is available at https://github.com/hhw11/FamilySpace
papers.summary: Latent crystal generators pair a variational autoencoder (VAE) that learns per-atom representations with a flow model, but the structure of that latent space has gone largely unexamined. The authors find that **even a vanilla crystal VAE organizes atom-wise latents into largely separate regions by elemental family**. `FamilySpace` exploits this by giving each family its own source distribution and training the flow on family-matched source-target pairs, so a user-supplied family template controls the composition of generated crystals. On `MP-20` and `MPTS-52` it stays competitive on generation quality while matching the prescribed compositions, and some templates raise the share of crystals predicted to be stable or metastable.

papers.title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings
papers.abstract: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) score well on pragmatic inference in English, but it is unclear whether that holds across languages and evaluation settings. `PILAPS` is a bilingual English and Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena, with both purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, used here to test eight LLMs from four families under several prompting strategies. Performance varies substantially by model and phenomenon, open-source models struggle most with humour, and cross-linguistic results depend on model origin. Error analysis shows that **models fall back on literal interpretations in conversational contexts more often than humans do**; Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, while Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it.

papers.title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
papers.summary: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is expensive, and their differing architectures and fragmented training stacks make optimizations hard to share. `LoongForge-Embodied` is a native-PyTorch framework with a common abstraction layer that separates model-specific code from shared training infrastructure, plus optimizations across computation, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication for DDP and FSDP. It also bundles a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data and a concurrent evaluation framework. Across representative models it reports **1.47x to 4.38x higher end-to-end training throughput than the open-source baselines** and 4.1x to 23.2x faster evaluation.

papers.title: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action
papers.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role.
  However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full
  history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past
  experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that
  decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native
