  video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this
  inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets
  the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation
  across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena,
  surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared
  methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above
  the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and
  https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
papers.summary: Memory-augmented Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models either retrieve past observations without reasoning about them or reason over the full history in a context that crowds out current perception. `ActMem` separates the two inside one vision-language backbone: it infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history, keeps the hidden states from that inference as a latent memory chain-of-thought that conditions a flow-matching action expert, and lets the expert attend directly to the current view. It reaches **71.1% task success on `RoboMemArena`, 7.5 percentage points above the strongest baseline**, and 73.8% average success on `MIKASA-Robo`. On real-world memory tasks it averages 68.8% success, 10.0 points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA.

papers.title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
papers.abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.
papers.summary: Hierarchical reinforcement learning pipelines that need no demonstrations are compared against flat baselines on `MiniGrid` navigation and robotic manipulation. For navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen `FourRooms` layouts under hand-specified high-level plans; for manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment, and lifting are trained separately, each starting from states collected while running the preceding skill. **The hierarchical pipelines outperform flat `DQN` on unseen layouts and need fewer training steps than flat `SAC`**, with lower variation across seeds in manipulation. The frozen pick and lift skills are also reused for stacking by training one additional place skill.

papers.title: Dimension-Free Buffer Bounds for Compressed-Momentum Error Feedback
papers.abstract: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $\beta_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-\beta_1)\|G_t\|_F + \gamma\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $\Theta(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}\eta_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.
papers.summary: Analyses of error feedback for compressed optimization bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant, such as r/p for a rank-r approximation of a p-dimensional spectrum, which then appears in the convergence rate. The authors show that when the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, **the buffer bound becomes free of the matrix dimensions and the rank**, using only the fact that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, which covers both top-k selection and truncated SVD. In the standard two-stage analysis this replaces a constant of order p^2/r^2 with one of order 1, at the price of an additive O(log^2 T) floor and not a slower rate. On `BERT` fine-tuning at rank ratio 32/768, the feedback decay costs under 0.008 validation F1.

papers.title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps
papers.abstract: An image can pass automated safety checks while showing harmful content to its human viewer. We introduce DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems often read only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR viewers reconstruct its appearance using an auxiliary gain map. DRJanus inverts this reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images in a single JPEG, without querying or optimizing against the target model. It preserves the chosen SDR base exactly and reconstructs HDR targets at an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images. On a benchmark of 100 sexual-content images, DRJanus evades detection by all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models. Across five agents, each evaluated on 120 task cases per threat setting, attack success ranges from 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and from 95% to 100% for task manipulation. We also explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation. These findings expose a gap in visual trust: securing what a machine reads does not secure what a user sees. A demo is available at https://qshen0629.github.io/DRJanus/
papers.summary: Automated image checks often read only the standard dynamic range (SDR) base of an image, while high dynamic range (HDR) displays reconstruct what the viewer sees using an auxiliary gain map. `DRJanus` exploits this gap by inverting the reconstruction to embed two independently chosen colour images in a single JPEG, with no queries to or optimization against the target model. On 100 sexual-content images it **evades all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models**. Across five agents, attack success is 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and 95% to 100% for task manipulation, and the authors explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation.

papers.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
papers.abstract: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write the declarative specifications from which physics-based digital twins of HVAC systems are generated, but existing evaluations stop at parse success, completed runs, or text similarity. The proposed four-level protocol runs each specification through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioural equivalence with a hidden reference model, within bands calibrated by sizing perturbations of plus or minus 20%. Across eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, seven models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials within three repairs, yet **reached behavioural equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%**. About half of the failed trials converged to the wrong steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems.

papers.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.
papers.summary: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) adds capabilities to a trained network by having executable programs read, construct, or modify its weights directly, with no gradient-based training. In the `WeightCode` framework, a frozen language model writes these weight programs from task knowledge and the network's existing weights, and the installed capability then runs without the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, the programs take **unseen command compositions from 0% to 99.8% exact match** and a new pickup action from 0% to 98.4% success while preserving the original capabilities. On `ImageNet`, four programs give net gains of 8.84 to 17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, and programs rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers keep 83 to 110% of their gains, whereas copying the fixed weight edits yields negligible gains.

papers.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
papers.abstract: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.
papers.summary: This entry to `BraTS-GoAT` Task 3, which evaluates brain-tumour segmentation across heterogeneous tumour types, trains a 3D `ResidualEncoderUNet` with consensus pseudo-labels, a nested-region training objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Teacher models labelled 1,138 unlabeled cases, and fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening kept 983 of them for training alongside 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold entry scored a **mean DSC of 0.834** and mean NSD of 0.510 on the validation server. The effects of individual components were modest and region-dependent.

papers.title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
papers.abstract: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $\Theta(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $\Sigma_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.
papers.summary: Iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time when a planning task has bounded width, but how well width can be approximated was open even when an optimal plan is supplied. The authors construct STRIPS tasks with positive preconditions, a supplied unique optimal plan, and a single reachable goal state, in which **distinguishing width 1 from width linear in the number of atoms N is NP-hard**. Unless P equals NP, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor of o(N) or a symmetric factor of o(sqrt(N)). Testing width against a threshold k is coNP-complete for fixed k and Sigma-2-P-complete when k is part of the input, while on an explicit state graph a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor.

papers.title: When Should a Voice Agent Speak? End-of-Turn Detection in Turkish
papers.abstract: A voice agent that waits for a fixed silence before replying either interrupts users who pause mid-utterance or responds late to users who have finished. This study examines the decision at the onset of silence, using turn ends and turn-internal pauses extracted from the Real-TurnTurk corpus of Turkish dyadic video calls. A fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT model, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a deployed multilingual detector are compared, together with voice-activity timing and facial features, under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation with paired cluster bootstrap tests. On held-out recordings, the fine-tuned model separates turn ends from pauses better than both text baselines and is the best calibrated of the three. Timing features of the current speaker are similarly informative, and their combination with the fine-tuned text score gives the best timing-based results; with logistic regression, this combination also outperforms the same combination with either text baseline. In a latency simulation, adding the text score to a silence timeout shortens the mean response delay at the same interruption rate. On automatic Whisper transcripts, the fine-tuned model retains its advantage over the zero-shot model.
papers.summary: Voice agents that wait for a fixed silence either interrupt users who pause mid-utterance or reply late, so this study examines the speak-or-wait decision at silence onset using turn ends and turn-internal pauses from the `Real-TurnTurk` corpus of Turkish video calls. A fine-tuned Turkish `TurnGPT` model is compared with a zero-shot Turkish language model and a deployed multilingual detector, alongside voice-activity timing and facial features, under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. The fine-tuned model separates turn ends from pauses better than both text baselines and is the best calibrated, and **adding its text score to a silence timeout shortens mean response delay at the same interruption rate**. Its advantage over the zero-shot model holds on automatic `Whisper` transcripts.

papers.title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.
papers.summary: Safety evaluations in science usually measure whether large language models (LLMs) refuse misconduct requests, but not whether they recognize the problem or why they comply. Using the 1,350 prompts of `SciIntBench` across 8 LLMs, the authors find that **models identify misconduct in 91% of even the most covert requests when asked directly, yet refuse to carry them out in only 34% of cases**. Rephrasing a request as a question about permissibility rather than an instruction had the largest effect, raising refusal from 52% to 88%. Two system-prompt fixes, assessing the request before responding and a reminder of responsible research conduct principles, raise refusal on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%.

papers.title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
papers.abstract: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.
papers.summary: A methodological framework is proposed for using several large language models together in academic research. It rests on seven principles: procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence and of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility. These feed a non-linear protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critiqued and, where needed, checked against external sources, illustrated with cases from research practice. The central argument is that **adding more models does not by itself make results more reliable; what matters is how the cognitive and verification steps are organised**, with the researcher keeping final responsibility.

papers.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
papers.abstract: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.
papers.summary: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible speech together with environmental sound as one coherent acoustic scene, but existing systems model the mix with a single acoustic representation and train on scenes simulated from separately recorded sources. Here a source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment token streams from mixed audio, and a pretrained large language model generates both streams interleaved, conditioned on a scene description and the speech content. Because the streams come straight from mixed recordings, the model can be adapted to in-the-wild audio without isolated sources. The authors report **improved speech intelligibility, scene relevance and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation methods**, with further gains from real-world adaptation.

papers.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
papers.abstract: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.
papers.summary: Vision-language models are used to simulate where a user looks on a web page, but a persona written into the prompt only partly changes the simulated gaze. The authors measure this as the gaze difference between two `MatrAIx` personas that differ in one attribute, and test three ways of inserting the persona: a text lens (a two-step prompt), a pixel lens (marks on regions matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a gated dwell reward used in training). With `Qwen3-VL` at 4B and 32B and `Qwen3.5-9B`, the text lens separates personas strongly but reacts to profile changes that should not move gaze, the pixel lens separates less but is robust, and the weight lens generalizes to held-out interests at 4B and 9B. **The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone**, so the choice of lens depends on cost and model size.

papers.title: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
papers.abstract: Smoothed online learning has recently been studied as a way to bypass hardness results for the fully adversarial setting, which can be overly pessimistic. In this framework, the adversary is constrained to generate contexts from distributions having a bounded density with respect to some fixed base measure $\mu$. Prior work makes the strong assumption that $\mu$ is known to the learner, with notable exceptions including Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). In this paper, we study sequential probability assignment (a.k.a., online learning with log loss) with smooth, well-specified data in the more general setting where $\mu$ is \emph{unknown}, without the Lipschitz condition imposed in the work of Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). We prove regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries: the adaptive bound is controlled by empirical $\ell_\infty$ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound improves this dependence to empirical $\ell_2$ Hellinger entropy, the notion that has been shown to characterize the complexity of learning with i.i.d. data (Bilodeau et al., 2023). Both bounds are obtained through algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. We complement these results with a general lower bound, showing that our upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, which implies a separation in the difficulty of smoothed online learning between regimes where $\mu$ is known and where it is unknown.
papers.summary: Smoothed online learning restricts the adversary to distributions with bounded density relative to a base measure, and most prior work assumes the learner knows that measure. This work studies sequential probability assignment (online learning with log loss) on smooth, well-specified data when the base measure is unknown, without the Lipschitz condition used in earlier work. Regret upper bounds are proved through algorithms built on truncated empirical Hellinger covers: the bound against adaptive adversaries is controlled by empirical L-infinity Hellinger entropy and the bound against oblivious adversaries by empirical L2 Hellinger entropy. A general lower bound shows these are essentially tight for some natural classes, implying **a separation in difficulty between the known and unknown base measure regimes**.

papers.title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
papers.abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.
papers.summary: Adding constraints obtained by integrating the governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), but without much mathematical explanation. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), the authors derive stability estimates for losses with and without the integral constraints. The comparison shows that **in certain parameter regimes the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and the integral constraints restore uniform control of them**. Numerical experiments agree: the two losses differ clearly in accuracy in those regimes and perform similarly where the standard loss retains enough control.

papers.title: DRVEXO-4B-Unified: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Speech-Vision System
papers.abstract: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.
papers.summary: `DRVEXO-4B-Unified` is a modular multimodal assistant built on a 4B language backbone, with a single checkpoint that takes text, image and speech input and produces reference-conditioned speech output and structured tool calls. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface, explicit text boundaries enable incremental speech synthesis, and three scoring heads rank application-supplied action candidates. The authors report **74.22% on the 900 `MMMU` validation questions**, above the published scores of `Gemma 3 4B IT` and `InternVL3.5-4B`, along with 82.26% strict prompt-level accuracy on `IFEval` and 89.40% on `MATH-500`. On NVIDIA GB10 hardware the first speech chunk arrives in 390 ms, and weights and code are planned for release under Apache 2.0.

papers.title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
papers.abstract: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.
papers.summary: Agents operating a personal smartphone can touch private data, payments and settings, so `MATE` (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution) adds an execution layer between the agent's proposed actions and their effect on the device, without modifying the underlying model. Each UI primitive becomes a structured action record that a Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps to allow, block or ask-the-user, while Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks. On `MobileSafetyBench`, **high-risk blocking rises from 29.7% to 97.0% under `GPT-4o`**. On `AndroidWorld` the system cuts LLM calls by up to 6x and reaches 95.7% success on recurring-use tasks.

papers.title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
papers.abstract: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.
papers.summary: Items on a recommendation page compete with and complement one another, so the best page is not just the individually best items side by side, and the space of pages is too large to enumerate. Existing generative re-rankers either give every choice in a sampled page the same page-level signal or imitate target pages fixed before training. The proposed whole-page policy improvement uses one local page-level objective that splits exactly into a training target per position, comparing candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. It **outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines on `KuaiRand-1K`, `RL4RS-SeqSlate` and an industrial dataset**, and comes closest to the known optimum on a synthetic benchmark.

papers.title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when those skills are chained into long-horizon tasks, and self-improvement from their own experience stays within what they can already do. In `CoachSI`, a frozen off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) watches the robot and names the next step in the policy's own instruction format, never outputting actions; successful coached rollouts are relabeled with the original task instruction and used for fine-tuning. On states where the policies had stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x. After fine-tuning, **unassisted long-horizon success in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%**, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above self-collected successes at an equal data budget.

papers.title: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion and flow models yield a preview, their clean-image estimate, at every denoising step. When they miscount, drop or misplace objects, test-time search is in a bind: its verifiers are reward models built for finished images, so judging early misreads blurry previews, and judging late, as best-of-N does, pays to fully denoise doomed candidates. We find that the image is not the problem: the outcome is settled as denoising starts, by the seed or by a stochastic sampler's first steps, and already shows in early previews; what fails on them is the judge, as reward models read them near chance on several kinds of prompts. We introduce Keystone, a training-free judge of previews that compiles a prompt into typed questions about its objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model answer them. Asked this way, the judge reads counts and positions from early previews better than reward models read them from finished images. Searching at these key steps on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning significantly outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half its generator compute, and as a drop-in verifier there, the Keystone score significantly improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering; without retuning, both searches stay significantly above the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average over four base models and three benchmarks. Keystone thus moves test-time judgment to the key steps where the outcome already shows.
papers.summary: Test-time search for text-to-image diffusion and flow models relies on reward models built for finished images, which misread blurry early previews, while judging late wastes compute on fully denoising bad candidates. The authors find that the outcome is settled at the start of denoising and is already visible in early previews, and that the judge is what fails. `Keystone` is a training-free judge that compiles a prompt into typed questions about objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal model answer them on previews. On `GenEval` with `SD3.5-Medium`, its adaptive search and pruning **outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half the generator compute**, and its score also improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering as a drop-in verifier.

papers.title: LM-based Personalized Travel Planner
papers.abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research
papers.summary: Travel planning requires combining several information sources while satisfying constraints and user preferences, which single-agent LLM systems handle poorly. The proposed hierarchical multi-agent framework has a supervising chatbot agent coordinate specialized agents for schedule validation, query formulation, real-time data retrieval and constraint-aware itinerary generation, with iterative refinement driven by a deterministic multi-dimensional scoring scheme. On the `TravelPlanner` benchmark, the authors report improvements over the `ReAct` baseline of 10% on budget-constraint planning, 25% on planning under a wider constraint set, and **45% on personalized planning**. The code is publicly available.

papers.title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
papers.abstract: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.
papers.summary: Agent skills are documents of expert procedural knowledge that models increasingly maintain by rewriting them without any feedback. The authors let models rewrite expert skills for many rounds with no task, run or judgment, then test agents built on the same models with the results. **Every model performs worse with the rewritten skills on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on `SkillsBench` after thirty rounds**, because rewriting pulls a skill toward what the model would write from the topic alone and drops the knowledge outside that prior first. Restoring that knowledge recovers much of the loss, and `SkillDiff`, which marks it in place without altering the skill's text, raises the `SkillsBench` pass rate by 4.8 points on average.

papers.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
papers.abstract:
Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks.
  Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(\alpha,\beta)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $\gamma$-H\"older-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(\alpha,\beta)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2\gamma/(d+2\gamma+2)},\,(n\alpha)^{-2\gamma/(d+\gamma+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
papers.summary: Learning score functions from sensitive data risks exposing training examples, particularly in score-based generative models, yet the statistical limits of private score estimation are not well understood. The authors study score estimation under differential privacy for sub-Gaussian distributions with locally Hölder-continuous scores, building an estimator from quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, implemented with projected Langevin Monte Carlo in time polynomial in the sample size. They derive its error rate and **a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation**. As an application, they construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee does not depend on the number of denoising steps and which attains nearly minimax-optimal total variation error.

papers.title: Towards Autoregressive Neural Network Parameter Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently established a new paradigm in machine learning, demonstrating exceptional zero-shot generalization and complex reasoning capabilities. Concurrently, neural network parameter generation has emerged as a promising avenue for rapid task adaptation and model synthesis. Existing weight generation techniques, however, struggle to jointly learn the distribution of diverse models, to encode heterogeneous architectures within a single generator, and to generalize out of distribution. We therefore ask whether pretrained parameters can be encoded into a discrete domain so that the zero-shot generalization LLMs exhibit in text generation can be transferred to weight generation. Following this view, we propose an LLM-inspired approach, Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (IGPG), that formulates network parameter generation as an autoregressive modeling problem. We first quantize pretrained weights with a VQ-VAE, then train a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator over the resulting tokens. At inference, the generated weight tokens are mapped back to parameter space by the VQ-VAE decoder. We evaluate the framework across in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer, and cross-architecture settings. The proposed method achieves competitive performance in in-distribution generation and provides useful parameter initializations for held-out datasets and architectural configurations, improving downstream performance over random initialization after adaptation. These results suggest that discrete autoregressive modeling provides a promising framework for learning and transferring structure across collections of pretrained neural network parameters.
papers.summary: Methods that generate neural network weights struggle to learn the distribution of diverse models, to handle different architectures in one generator, and to generalize out of distribution. Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (`IGPG`) treats weight generation as autoregressive modeling: pretrained weights are quantized into discrete tokens with a `VQ-VAE`, a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator is trained over those tokens, and the decoder maps generated tokens back to parameters. Evaluated on in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer and cross-architecture settings, the method is competitive in distribution and **yields initializations for held-out datasets and architectures that beat random initialization after adaptation**.

papers.title: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
papers.abstract:
Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span
to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice.
  We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624.
  COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.
papers.summary: Omissions in LLM summaries are hard to verify because missing information leaves no output span to inspect. `COVERAGE-TRACE` tests whether a summary depends on a designated atomic source fact by replacing only that fact with type-matched alternatives, holding the summary fixed, and measuring the change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. On 80 matched covered and omitted pairs from `QMSum` across four open-weight models, the multi-counterfactual variant reaches **0.764 to 0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest text-only baseline**. Adjusting for meaning-preserving paraphrases lowers this to 0.591 to 0.624, so the authors present it as a complementary signal of source-summary dependence and not a wording-invariant measure of coverage.

papers.title: Dynamics of Protected State Evolution
papers.abstract:
States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection.
  On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.
papers.summary: A formal framework is developed for systems in which states with identical protected observations can still admit different future interventions, with each transition recording its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. The analysis covers a weighted Gram operator that determines the linear response ellipsoid, a cubic correction to quadratic minimum cost, path-dependent feasibility at singular gates, and a characterization of exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics. In experiments on `Qwen2.5-7B` Base, two projected update policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of 2e-5 and **recovered 391 of 396 initially rejected writes over 200 arrivals**, each with over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of an `AdamW` baseline restricted to the historical channel. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation gave 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost, while renewal used fewer full verification scans.

papers.title: Efficient Multimodal Agents for Auditing 3D Worlds
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.
papers.summary: Interactive 3D worlds built by agents often contain glitches such as floating objects or walk-through walls, and an automatic auditor must navigate to suspect objects, trigger behavior-dependent glitches, and recognize what is wrong, while staying cheap. A 4B vision-language model fine-tuned on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers match a frontier model on both, but recognition lags far behind. The resulting auditor pairs a swarm of small explorers with a frontier model that reviews their recordings. On `WorldAuditBench` it **succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest reported auditor at under a quarter of its cost**, and matches the frontier reviewer exploring alone at 4.6 times lower cost.

papers.title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction
papers.abstract: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.
papers.summary: Automatically building evaluation rubrics for open-ended LLM outputs is studied in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without an expert reference rubric. A multi-axis generation framework explores structural and free-form views of the source evidence to build a broad candidate pool, and a coverage-selection gap metric separates failures to discover criteria from failures to select them under a fixed budget. On four held-out tasks the framework reaches **0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics**. Adding new structural search axes improves recall by 6 to 10 percentage points versus at most 1.5 from generating more along existing axes, and the authors conclude that reference-free selection, not generation, is the remaining bottleneck.

papers.title: Is a Description Worth a Thousand Demonstrations? Specificity and Reliability of Task Descriptions in In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: A prompt for in-context learning (ICL) can describe a task in addition to, or instead of, demonstrating it through examples. Yet how task descriptions work remains poorly understood theoretically. Through the Bayesian view of ICL, we model descriptions as informative priors characterized by their specificity and reliability. We adapt the effective sample size (ESS) from Bayesian statistics, quantifying a description's predictive value as an equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, we show that a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and with the task's dimension. A description that may be irrelevant, however, gains little from its specificity unless demonstrations are given. In practice, do in-context learners use descriptions as a Bayes-optimal predictor would? Our experiments show that meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS when tested on their training distribution. Pretrained language models, however, make too little use of highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning; most of them closely match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled. These results extend the Bayesian analysis of ICL from demonstrations to descriptions.
papers.summary: Task descriptions in in-context learning (ICL) prompts are modeled here as informative Bayesian priors characterized by their specificity and reliability, with a description's value quantified as an effective sample size (ESS), meaning the equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and the task's dimension, while a possibly irrelevant description gains little from specificity unless demonstrations are also given. Meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS on their training distribution, whereas pretrained language models **underuse highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning and mostly match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled**.

papers.title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
papers.abstract: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $\pi(a\mid x,m)$.
papers.summary: Test-time interventions such as retrieval or context expansion can meet their own intermediate objectives without actually fixing an answer. The Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (`TERRA`) is an evaluation protocol, not an inference algorithm, that decomposes intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource cost, using paired comparisons that fix the incoming state. In executable financial reasoning experiments, the same context expansion harms one model configuration and helps another, sufficient evidence does not guarantee a correct answer, and **diagnostic headroom plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains**, so the value of an action depends on the input and receiving model rather than on the diagnosis alone.

papers.title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
papers.summary: Detecting mistakes in egocentric procedural video while there is still time to recover requires judging actions against the task instructions as the video unfolds, yet existing online detectors ignore the instruction text and instruction-conditioned methods work offline. Using only observed video, instructions, and prior predictions, the proposed models identify and localize completed action attempts and classify them as correct, modified, slip, correction, or addition, comparing a modular pipeline against a joint model that predicts everything in one step on a repartitioned `EgoPER` with erroneous videos in all splits. Step-segmentation F1@0.5 is similar (93.6% and 92.1%), but the **joint model reaches higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%)**, with the largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%), and both designs outperform released `AEM` and `ESTANet` checkpoints on test videos containing mistakes.

papers.title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
papers.abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.
papers.summary: Aerial sensing has to combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement, and image processing. `AeroBelief` groups candidate views by their first executable action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model, using calibrated group bounds and a six-query controller to decide when to commit. Across 960 closed-loop executions in 40 simulated worlds, it completes 75.42% of tasks versus 73.33% for exhaustive world-model scoring while using **91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations**. On 2,685 recorded unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven `DJI Mavic 3M` routes, context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight supported target confirmations while processing 76.05% fewer images.

papers.title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
papers.abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.
papers.summary: `WeatherCraft` applies the GPT-style pretraining and post-training recipe to global medium-range weather forecasting by representing atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete tokens, modeled by a Transformer that is causal across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Sampling yields diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities allow Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On `ERA5`, the eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, runs **about 18x faster than `GenCast`** at inference. Reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
papers.abstract:
Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing.
  Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust.
  Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale.
  Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts.
  Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.
papers.summary: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive, web forms cannot clarify questions for respondents, and open-ended chatbots can drift from protocol. `Epira` pairs large language model (LLM) dialogue with a rule-based controller that enforces required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and it adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload, with a local `Qwen2.5` backend and a cloud `GPT-5.4` backend. Across 864 simulated measles and gonorrhea sessions, `Epira` with the local model captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts, while **open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1 to 41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models under protocol control**. In a 72-volunteer study, completion was 100% and mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95, with local and cloud deployments producing similar records.

papers.title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
papers.abstract:
Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments.
