We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems.
  We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.
papers.summary: Robot policies built on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) generalize poorly out of distribution, and the authors observe that retrieving past successful experiences to warm-start diffusion denoising improves both accuracy and compute cost, at the price of large experience banks that strain edge storage and search. `FlashX` is a NAND flash architecture based on CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA) that performs parallel key search inside the flash with interleaved Compute-in-Flash engines, plus proprioception-aware clustering that allows incremental additions without global reclustering. It improves task success by up to 12.24 percentage points, achieves 2.57x higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture, and delivers a **1.29x to 3.95x end-to-end speedup over SSD-based retrieval** with 1.12x to 2.34x better energy efficiency.

papers.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
papers.summary: `AutoRAGBench` measures how well LLM agents can build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems from scratch in an open code space, across nine development tasks with no starter code or prescribed strategy and a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. Agents analyze task data, implement pipelines, and iteratively refine them from experimental feedback, and nine agent configurations are evaluated on both final system quality and development trajectories. The best configuration, `GPT-6.1 Sol` with `Codex CLI`, reaches an **average score of 56.1 versus 44.4 for a composite human state-of-the-art baseline**. When starting from a human-designed system on seven of the tasks, the same agent improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

papers.title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.
papers.summary: LLM agents with persistent memory are exposed to memory drift, where an adversarial or misleading memory changes the execution path and final outcome, and content-level signals such as perplexity or retrieval relevance cannot tell which retrieved memory is causally responsible. `DriftGuard` builds causal supervision offline by repeatedly replaying the original trajectory and a single-memory-neutralized trajectory from a shared pre-action state, aggregating the results by majority vote into a memory drift score (MDS) covering action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. An online risk model then estimates that score from pre-action information alone, **flagging drift-inducing memories without any counterfactual rollouts at serving time**. The authors report accurate identification of drift-inducing memories and efficient online defense.

papers.title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
papers.abstract:
Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities.
  Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions.
  Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap.
  Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis across heterogeneous cohorts.
papers.summary: Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (`HIT-Fuse`) integrates six data modalities for cancer prognosis, namely copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, protein abundance, and vision-transformer-derived pathology features, across four `TCGA` cohorts. Modality-specific autoencoders compress the inputs before a two-stage CP tensor decomposition, missing modalities are reconstructed from clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts, and a mathematical traceback provides global and local attributions. The method finds latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, and cohort expansion yields a **56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma**. Validation against `DepMap` CRISPR screens and `miRTarBase` supports the decoded drivers, with 71 to 92% of decoded miRNAs having regulatory support.

papers.title: Learning Networked Dynamical Systems via Neural ODE-based Graph Structure Inference
papers.abstract: Inferring the latent interaction graph from multivariate time series is fundamental to understanding complex dynamical systems in neuroscience, biology, and physics. Despite recent progress in neural relational inference, most methods rely on discrete-time modeling, which degrades under sparse and irregular observations and tends to entangle multi-hop dependencies into spurious direct edges. We show that a continuous-time formulation naturally decouples inference from any fixed observation schedule, allowing gradient signals to be integrated continuously between observations for both dynamics and structure learning. We propose NOGI (Neural ODE-based Graph Inference), a framework that couples a deterministic graph learner with an MPNN-based Neural ODE. The two modules are trained end-to-end via the adjoint method. Across four simulated dynamical systems at two scales, NOGI achieves the best structure recovery in 30 out of 32 evaluated cases with highly competitive forecasting performance, remaining robust under observation degradation. On the realistic Netsim fMRI benchmark, it attains an average AUPRC of 0.90 (AUROC 0.96). These results suggest that explicitly decoupling relational interactions from self-dynamics within a continuous-time vector field provides a powerful mechanism for graph structure learning under realistic observation conditions.
papers.summary: Inferring the hidden interaction graph of a dynamical system from multivariate time series usually relies on discrete-time models, which degrade under sparse, irregular observations and tend to turn multi-hop dependencies into spurious direct edges. `NOGI` (Neural ODE-based Graph Inference) couples a deterministic graph learner with a message-passing Neural ODE, trained end-to-end with the adjoint method so that structure and dynamics are learned in continuous time independent of the observation schedule. Across four simulated systems at two scales it achieves the **best structure recovery in 30 of 32 evaluated cases** with competitive forecasting, and on the `Netsim` fMRI benchmark it reaches an average AUPRC of 0.90 and AUROC of 0.96.

papers.title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges
papers.abstract: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.
papers.summary: LLM judges are assumed to score according to a rubric's meaning rather than its numeric scale, an assumption tested here through semantic faithfulness: semantically equivalent rubrics should yield consistent scores. A scale-reversal probe inverts the score anchors without changing the evaluation criteria, and floor normalization calibrates the resulting disagreement against each model's intrinsic variability so that models can be compared fairly. Across five meta-evaluation benchmarks and seven open-weight and proprietary judges, the experiments reveal **widespread violations of semantic faithfulness**, and show that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Averaging scores over both anchor directions reduces dependence on scale direction without hurting alignment with human judgments.

papers.title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.
papers.summary: Hallucinations in LLM outputs for cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks such as summarization and question answering can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. `HalluVision` is a reproducible measurement framework that generates outputs, extracts domain-specific entities with a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and scores factual consistency with multiple similarity metrics, applied to 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles and two commercial plus one open-weight LLM. Validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors, **semantic similarity aligns with human judgments whereas entity-based metrics show limited agreement**. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, and entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.

papers.title: From Data Alignment to Parameter Generation: Few-Shot Cross-City Traffic Prediction with Conditional Diffusion
papers.abstract: Accurate mobile traffic forecasting is crucial for network service management, supporting proactive capacity provisioning, congestion mitigation, and energy-efficient operation. However, many cities and regions are data-scarce (e.g., newly deployed or poorly instrumented areas), thus making traffic prediction a few-shot learning problem and limiting the practicality of standard data-driven models. Existing cross-city solutions primarily rely on data-space alignment to match traffic distributions between data-rich and data-scarce cities, but such alignment is often brittle under real-world distribution shifts, measurement noise, and city-specific bias. To address these limitations, we propose a Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (CDPG) framework. Instead of aligning raw data, CDPG learns the conditional distribution of high-performing predictor parameters for source cities and directly generates node-specific model parameters for the target city. To support reliable adaptation for network traffic prediction, CDPG conditions parameter generation on multi-modal spatio-temporal context. Specifically, CDPG captures spatial environment cues by combining satellite imagery with large language model (LLM)-derived semantic descriptions, and summarizes complex temporal behaviors via unsupervised pattern clustering. These contextual components guide CDPG in producing parameters tailored to each base station's operational context, thereby improving robustness under cross-city and cross-region shifts. Extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets show that CDPG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72% on standard forecasting metrics and remains robust for few-shot multi-step prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LingoodBoy/CDPG.
papers.summary: Mobile traffic forecasting in data-scarce cities is a few-shot problem, and existing cross-city methods that align raw traffic distributions are brittle under distribution shift, noise, and city-specific bias. Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (`CDPG`) instead learns the distribution of well-performing predictor parameters in source cities and directly generates node-specific model parameters for the target city. Generation is conditioned on spatial context from satellite imagery and LLM-derived semantic descriptions, plus temporal patterns from unsupervised clustering. On three large-scale datasets it outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by **up to 9.72%** on standard forecasting metrics.

papers.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
papers.abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.
papers.summary: Language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes are often trained with comparative feedback, where a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened. Fitting that feedback with a Bradley-Terry objective is shown not to recover the true outcome probabilities: on a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, a model that starts accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points) has **33 to 43 percentage points of its probability moved onto outcomes that none of the enumerated branches produces**. The cause is the objective rather than the comparisons, since its optimum computed before training predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The downstream cost is conditional, at about 3 percentage points of utility per decision on trained conditions when physically impossible events are included and under 1 point on average without them.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.
papers.summary: When LLM predictions feed a downstream optimization problem, better prediction accuracy does not necessarily mean lower decision cost. Decision-focused reinforcement learning (`DFRL`) post-trains LLMs using negative downstream decision regret as the reward, requiring neither convexity nor differentiability of the downstream problem. To limit expensive reward evaluation, it uses heuristic warm-starting with cheap approximate rewards and a reward-correction scheme that mixes cheap estimates with randomized exact solves while preserving the expected policy gradient. On inventory planning with `H&M` transactions and product descriptions, the best configuration **reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the supervised fine-tuning baseline** and by 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

papers.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents that run arbitrary shell commands can make unauthorized network requests or persistent malicious changes, and current defenses are either LLM-based monitors without provable guarantees or stateless policy layers that miss multi-step data flows and unmodeled side effects. `Tether` executes each proposed action in an ephemeral isolated sandbox, infers abstract action semantics from the observed system calls, and allows the action only if it complies with a stateful policy. Policies are written in an embedded domain-specific language in `Lean 4` that covers information flow control (IFC), access control, and network rules, which lets global security invariants be formally verified, such as no network access after reading a sensitive file. On realistic coding-agent benchmarks with a single policy shared across all tasks, it **blocks 100% of in-scope attacks with a benign false-positive rate under 5%**.

papers.title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
papers.abstract: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.
papers.summary: Structural stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how far node representations can move when edges change, but they are rarely checked against the simplest alternative, a perturbation-independent bound on the distance between any two outputs. The authors derive stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (`GIN`s) and single-head `GATv1` networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each against such a diameter bound. For `GIN`s they give an exact condition linking perturbation size, depth, and maximum degree under which the stability bound is tighter, which holds with a wide margin on `Cora` but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree `MUTAG` graphs. For `GATv1`, **the stability bound is never tighter than the trivial diameter bound**.

papers.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
papers.abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.
papers.summary: A large-scale empirical study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026 traces AI involvement from bug discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. AI-involved reports become more complete over time and a growing share are confirmed valid; using AI for reproduction and diagnosis is associated with higher validity, whereas using it for report writing is not. Maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes, and spend more effort on AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than on reports of AI-discovered bugs. Following their own guidance on reproducibility, verification, and accountability, the authors submitted 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which **69.81% were accepted by maintainers**.

papers.title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
papers.abstract: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that produce item titles directly may concentrate exposure on already popular news articles, and training-data memorization is examined here as one mechanism behind that. An instruction-tuned `Llama 3 8B` model was continually trained on about 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service to generate the next article title in a session. Its generated titles were more concentrated and less diverse than the titles in the logs, and **frequently repeated target titles were memorized more strongly and then generated in response to a wider range of prompts**. An exploratory deduplication of targets reduced both memorization and output concentration, but substantially cut training-set size and recommendation accuracy.

papers.title: PSTO: A PDE-structured transport operator with shared implicit updates for multiscale CDR systems
papers.abstract: Multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems couple spatial transport with local stiff reaction kinetics, making their numerical simulation computationally demanding. Conventional neural surrogates require costly coupled CDR training data, and their parameter counts scale with the number of transported variables, limiting scalability to high-dimensional CDR systems. Here we propose a PDE-Structured Transport Operator (PSTO) that learns convection--diffusion dynamics solely from reaction-free data. By embedding the PDE structure into the neural architecture, PSTO generalizes to full CDR systems at inference without retraining. A single transport operator block is shared across all transported variables and refined through relaxed fixed-point iterations, performing an implicit-like correction in latent space. This improves stability during recursive multi-step prediction without adding trainable parameters. We evaluate PSTO on three benchmarks: a canonical 2D CDR system, a multiscale Robertson counterflow flame, and a multiscale hydrogen planar jet flame. In every case, PSTO reduces the mean relative $L_2$ error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% compared to the strongest neural baseline. Ablation studies on the fixed-point iterations and detailed error decomposition further confirm that PSTO achieves both high one-step accuracy and long-term stability in coupled rollouts. Time-step sensitivity analysis shows that PSTO maintains accuracy even with a tenfold larger time step, whereas baseline accuracies decay rapidly as the time step increases. This framework enables efficient, modular modeling of multiscale CDR dynamics by separating transport learning from the treatment of local kinetics.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates for multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems usually need expensive coupled training data and grow in parameter count with the number of transported variables. `PSTO` (PDE-Structured Transport Operator) instead learns convection-diffusion dynamics only from reaction-free data, shares a single transport block across all variables, and refines it with relaxed fixed-point iterations that act as an implicit-like correction in latent space. On a canonical 2D CDR system, a Robertson counterflow flame, and a hydrogen planar jet flame, it **cuts mean relative L2 error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% versus the strongest neural baseline**, and stays accurate with a tenfold larger time step.

papers.title: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal World Modeling with Content-Adaptive Spatial Addressing
papers.abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.
papers.summary: Long-horizon world models in partially observable environments need compact memories that keep spatial structure intact despite accumulated localization drift. `HiSTFormer` draws on hippocampal memory and entorhinal grid cells, arranging local temporal `RoPE` and multi-periodic spatial `RoPE` layer by layer, adding content-conditioned address offsets, and using a fixed-capacity memory so storage and per-step attention cost stay bounded. On `MemoryMaze` and `HM3D` it beats strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and **generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen in training**, with a compact model and consistent gains as depth increases.

papers.title: Can an LLM Fix a Language Model Without Training It?
papers.abstract: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.
papers.summary: A controlled study asks whether having an LLM interactively choose weight edits adds value over fixed numerical edits when repairing a faulty Transformer without gradient updates. The LLM editor inspects predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, then selects projection recipes; 20 recorded sessions over five masked and causal language models compare it with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Live selection matches black-box search on `SmolLM2` and `Qwen2.5`, and on `Pythia` reaches **65.62% completion accuracy versus 0% for black-box search but 66.15% for a fixed projection**. Under a compound attention and feed-forward fault, scripted and LLM-guided selection both raise the five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25%, indicating that operator coverage rather than interactive feedback explains much of the recovery.

papers.title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition actions on that prediction, and running them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations, and key-value caches. Existing 4-bit quantizers protect the generated action but let the predicted future degrade, so `LAQ` allocates precision using a reader metric (future error measured by its effect on the action) and a read count (how many denoising steps read each rounding error), plus a second 4-bit pass on the tokens the action attends to. On `LIBERO-Plus` it reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on `Fast-WAM` and `Cosmos-Policy`, **within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models**, while compressing the model 3.8x, cutting peak GPU memory 2.3x, and running 1.66x faster. On a real `AgileX PiPER` arm it achieves 47.0% average success against 52.0% for the 16-bit model.

papers.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
papers.abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.
papers.summary: `Splice-Core` is a hardware general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that mixes temporal-unary and binary computation, minimizing accumulation latency for low-order bits while keeping value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. Two processing element variants are presented: `Splice-BP`, which uses bit planes, and `Splice-LUT`, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Against a binary systolic array in 45nm, they achieve **77.4% and 76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions across 26 INT4 convolutional network and large language model workloads**, and `Splice-LUT` also raises throughput by 44.4% and lowers energy-delay product by 6.13x.

papers.title: Cyber-Physical RSI for AI-RAN: A Case Study
papers.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.
papers.summary: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are typically built in simulation and can shift when they meet real propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment. A cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework links a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent, and is exercised on ping-pong handover with 12 physical executions in six baseline-candidate pairs. Raising time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280 ms changed the observed ping-pong count from three to zero, but on a common three-configuration physical evaluation **the post-feedback model had a higher mean absolute error (1.601 round trips/min) than the pre-feedback model (1.240)**, exposing parameter-dependent generalization limits.

papers.title: DAWN: Robust Neural Blind Deconvolution via Alternating Wiener Guidance
papers.abstract: Blind image deconvolution (BID) is an ill-posed inverse problem that aims to jointly recover a sharp image and blur kernel from a single degraded observation. Under nontrivial and high noise, which is common in photography and scientific imaging such as microscopy, BID remains particularly challenging, as existing methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation. Existing training-data-free learning methods for BID, such as those based on the deep image prior (DIP), often utilize external guidance by including model-based estimates as additional loss terms, which underexploits the information these estimates carry especially under nontrivial noise. To address these challenges, we propose DAWN, a training-data-free DIP framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the model input and refining this imperfect estimate with the network's own prior. To provide more reliable kernel estimates for these injections, we apply autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks. On natural and scientific images under varying levels of Gaussian and Poisson noise, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and kernel quality (achieving up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the Levin dataset at $\sigma = 0.1$). Without any training images, DAWN remains highly competitive with a state-of-the-art diffusion model on FFHQ, despite the latter being trained on a massive number of in-distribution images.
papers.summary: Blind image deconvolution, which jointly recovers a sharp image and blur kernel from one degraded observation, breaks down under heavy noise because existing methods overfit the noise and misestimate the kernel. `DAWN` is a training-data-free deep image prior (DIP) framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the network input and refining them with the network's own prior, with autoencoding regularization on both the image and kernel networks. Across natural and scientific images with Gaussian and Poisson noise it outperforms prior methods in image and kernel quality, reaching **up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the `Levin` dataset at sigma = 0.1**, and stays competitive with a trained diffusion model on `FFHQ`.

papers.title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
papers.abstract: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.
papers.summary: How the neural tangent kernel (NTK) deviates from its infinite-width behavior when depth and width scale together is less understood for convolutional neural networks than for fully-connected, residual, or recurrent ones. Numerical experiments measure NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training, with depth L as the number of convolutional layers and width C as channels per layer. Dispersion grows with L/C in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes but stays small in the ordered regime, and **at critical initialization the dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of L/C**. Kernel rotation during training generally increases with L/C even in the ordered regime, suggesting that concentration at initialization and stability during training scale differently.

papers.title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design
papers.abstract: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.
papers.summary: Designing undersampling masks for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is recast as feature subset selection, with each sampling line a binary feature. Mutual information and conditional mutual information estimated from candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, plus a sampling-count penalty, define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model solved with simulated annealing and quantum annealing. In zero-filled reconstruction simulations on `fastMRI` knee images with patient-disjoint splits, the selected masks give **lower mean root mean square error than four conventional sampling methods at all six target sampling rates from 15% to 40%**.

papers.title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
papers.abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.
papers.summary: Whether video world models learn physical laws or merely imitate motion is probed through nonlinear forced response, in which an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. Six image-to-video backbones are adapted with dual visual-numeric conditioning and trained with only the flow-matching loss, then examined with three tiers of tests built from Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response including resonance, and **five capture higher-order dynamics such as nonlinear softening, even though softening accounts for only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement in training**. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts, and learned dynamics can fail to surface when state estimation or propagation goes wrong.

papers.title: NIMIS: A Structure-Agnostic, Chemically Informed Slot-Attention Framework for Demixing 1D $^1$H-NMR Mixture Spectra
papers.abstract: The products of chemical reactions are usually complex mixtures that must be separated into their components before interpretable $^1$H-NMR spectra can be obtained. Direct analysis of the spectra of crude mixtures would accelerate reaction analysis and facilitate the exploration of new chemical space. We present NIMIS, a structure-agnostic, attention-based deep learning framework that groups the peaks of a 1D $^1$H-NMR mixture spectrum according to the component from which they originate. J-coupling information is introduced directly into the attention mechanism of a multi-head Transformer encoder, and the resulting contextualised peak embeddings are separated into components by slot attention. NIMIS was trained on 158,005 synthetic mixtures constructed from experimental spectra in the NMRexp database, covering molecules of up to 20 heavy atoms composed of C, H, N, O, S, F, Cl, Br and I. On held-out molecules it reaches a peak-to-component assignment accuracy of 82.28% for noise-free input and 77.34% with 10% integral noise, with a mean NIMIS score of 0.83 for correct assignments. NIMIS outperforms a conventional Transformer and simple baselines, and its performance carries over to a scaffold-disjoint evaluation. By grouping peaks into component-level sets, NIMIS provides a foundation for more robust mixture analysis methods, including methods capable of handling overlapping signals.
papers.summary: Crude reaction products are mixtures that normally must be separated before their 1H-NMR spectra can be interpreted. `NIMIS` is a structure-agnostic framework that groups the peaks of a 1D mixture spectrum by originating component, injecting J-coupling information into the attention of a Transformer encoder and separating the resulting peak embeddings with slot attention. Trained on 158,005 synthetic mixtures built from experimental spectra in the `NMRexp` database, it reaches **82.28% peak-to-component assignment accuracy on held-out molecules with noise-free input** and 77.34% with 10% integral noise, outperforming a conventional Transformer and simple baselines.

papers.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
papers.summary: Video generators evaluated as world models can score higher on physics benchmarks with fewer denoising steps even as their videos blur or stop moving. The cause is traced to `Physics-IQ` comparing each generated video with a single recording when a scene has multiple valid futures; an exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures even as the distribution becomes less accurate. `Kernel Physics-IQ` removes this incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition, and two-step sampling lowers it in all five image-to-video models tested. For `CogVideoX`, **the official score rises by 0.055 while the new metric falls by 0.131**.

papers.title: AesDistill: Distilling Generative Aesthetics for Image Color Enhancement
papers.abstract: Image color enhancement aims to improve visual appeal, but previous methods often learn to reproduce ground-truth expert targets. These targets reflect the preferences of a few experts and cover a limited range of aesthetic choices. Matching them does not ensure stronger aesthetic quality across different tastes and scenes. By contrast, large generative models learn rich visual knowledge from large image collections and often produce vivid, appealing image edits. However, direct generation can change the source image's semantic structure along with its colors. In this paper, we introduce AesDistill, a framework for distilling generative aesthetics into image color enhancement. We use 4 leading open-source large generative models to produce 64,644 edited images as teacher targets at a cost of about 3,360 H100 GPU-hours, forming the AesDistill Dataset. AesDistill also includes AesDistill Student, a 1.13M-parameter model that learns teacher color changes through confidence-weighted supervision while preserving the source image's semantic structure. We evaluate AesDistill with 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality assessment models. Every teacher's targets rank above the FiveK and PPR10K expert target means in the joint assessment. Across both datasets, AesDistill Student outperforms all 20 baseline methods and ranks directly behind the 4 teachers. These results demonstrate that distilling aesthetics from generative models enables a compact student to outperform methods trained on expert targets.
papers.summary: Image color enhancement methods usually learn to reproduce targets from a few experts, which cover a narrow range of aesthetic choices, while large generative models produce appealing edits but can alter image content. `AesDistill` uses four open-source generative models to produce 64,644 edited images as teacher targets (about 3,360 H100 GPU-hours) and trains a 1.13M-parameter student to copy the teachers' color changes through confidence-weighted supervision while preserving semantic structure. Evaluated with 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality assessment models on `FiveK` and `PPR10K`, **the student outperforms all 20 baseline methods and ranks directly behind the four teachers**.

papers.title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.
papers.summary: Federated reinforcement learning lets a robot fleet learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience, but standard aggregation ignores that some robots train in much easier environments and stop contributing useful updates once they plateau. `FedDIA` scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by an environment difficulty inferred from the model's own performance, so both signals are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients it reaches **a mean success rate of 75.5% across training and held-out environments versus 68.7% for the strongest federated baseline**, and the advantage persists on hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts and with one defective client.

papers.title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
papers.abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.
papers.summary: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared instead of raw images, and concept-erasure methods are used to hide sensitive attributes at the population level. A proof shows that **when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved**, so global erasure either destroys task signal or leaves leakage within task strata. `TC-LEACE`, a closed-form variant of `LEACE`, enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum instead. Experiments on 85 `CelebA` attribute pairs across four vision foundation models and on hospital chest radiographs confirm that conditional leakage persists after `LEACE`, while `TC-LEACE` recovers most of the lost task utility with conditional leakage within a prespecified margin.

papers.title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding
papers.abstract: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can translate in parallel by denoising tokens at arbitrary positions, but fixed target lengths waste computation on unused positions and confidence-only commitment delays tokens whose predictions have already stabilized. `TRAC` is a training-free decoding method that sets the generation length from source length and translation direction, and commits medium-confidence tokens early when they are stable across steps, judged by top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-K distributions. On Chinese-English translation in both directions across `FLORES-200`, `WMT23`, and `NTREX-128`, it reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves **sentence-level speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over `Fast-dLLM` with only a 0.02-point drop in macro-average `COMET`**.

papers.title: MambaLIFT: Reference-Based Mechanism-Aware Attribution for VMamba
papers.abstract: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models remains challenging because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways. We introduce MambaLIFT, a reference-based, multiplier-first attribution framework for VMamba that propagates contributions through its computational graph using interaction-aware rules for selective-scan injection, recurrent memory, LayerNorm, and shared pathways. MambaLIFT decomposes the reference-relative class-logit difference, \(f_c(x)-f_c(x^0)\), by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and computational mechanism. Experiments on ImageNet-1K evaluate VMamba-T and VMamba-B, with hyperparameters selected on a calibration set and faithfulness assessed on a disjoint held-out evaluation set. MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision across audited attribution interfaces in both configurations. Under mean-colour pixel flipping, it achieves significantly higher mean faithfulness scores than MambaLRP on both configurations and the highest scores among the evaluated methods, including Integrated Gradients with matched references. Under blurred replacement, MambaLIFT is non-inferior to MambaLRP on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B, indicating that its advantage depends on the replacement protocol. Ablations on VMamba-T show that interaction allocation, temporal propagation, and pathway composition affect attribution maps. Mechanism-level analyses further show that exact relevance conservation does not imply additive effects under finite interventions: the mechanism decomposition accounts for the reference-relative logit difference but does not estimate intervention effects or establish causal validity.
papers.summary: Explaining predictions of visual state-space models is difficult because input-dependent selective dynamics entangle feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared pathways. `MambaLIFT` is a reference-based attribution framework for `VMamba` that propagates contributions with interaction-aware rules and decomposes the class-logit difference from a reference input by spatial position, block, scan direction, and mechanism. On `ImageNet-1K` with `VMamba-T` and `VMamba-B`, it conserves relevance to floating-point precision and **achieves significantly higher faithfulness than `MambaLRP` under mean-colour pixel flipping**, though under blurred replacement it is only non-inferior or equivalent. The authors note that exact conservation does not imply additive effects under interventions or establish causal validity.

papers.title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
papers.abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation across various material surfaces.
papers.summary: High-throughput catalyst screening needs fast adsorption energy predictions, but existing approaches trade off evaluation speed against sensitivity to local geometry. `AdsNet` is an equivariant graph neural network that predicts adsorption energy in one forward pass from a local graph containing only the adsorbate atoms and nearby surface neighbors, making cost independent of total system size. Trained on `AdsTraj`, a set of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) structures covering 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates, it achieves **an adsorption energy root-mean-square error of 0.032 eV** and a force error of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces allow structure relaxation by projected gradient descent, and predicted energies decompose into per-atom contributions.

papers.title: Extending Rademacher Complexity-Based Generalization Theory to Domain Generalization
papers.abstract: Domain generalization (DG) aims to train models on multiple source domains with distinct distributions to ensure robust performance on unseen target domains. In doing so, it elevates the concept of generalization from the traditional sample level to the distribution level. Existing theoretical frameworks introduce a domain space endowed with a meta-distribution to extend classical generalization analysis to this new setting. However, these approaches typically treat the domain space as devoid of geometry. In reality, the domain space is an inherently infinite-dimensional, nonlinear abstract space composed of probability distributions, and its complex geometric properties fundamentally determine generalization behavior. Consequently, existing geometry-free theories of domain generalization have a fundamental limitation. They lack a formal characterization of what distinguishes distribution-level generalization from sample-level generalization, leaving the inherent difficulty of generalizing across domains largely unexplained. To bridge this gap, we formalize the domain space as the Wasserstein space over the representation space. Building on the geometric properties of this space (specifically the $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$ curvature theory) we derive a novel, geometry-dependent DG error bound. By introducing an additional curvature-dependent confidence term, this bound formally disentangles the two levels of generalization effects and reveals the essential nature that domain generalization is affected by both the invariance and the curvature of the representation space. Finally, we experimentally validate the effect of curvature on domain generalization.
papers.summary: Existing theories of domain generalization (DG) place a meta-distribution over a domain space but treat that space as having no geometry, leaving unexplained what separates generalizing across distributions from generalizing across samples. Here the domain space is formalized as the Wasserstein space over the representation space, and its CD(K, infinity) curvature properties are used to derive a geometry-dependent error bound. **The bound adds a curvature-dependent confidence term that separates the two levels of generalization**, indicating that DG depends on both the invariance and the curvature of the representation space; experiments are reported to validate the effect of curvature.

papers.title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
papers.abstract: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships.
