Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.
papers.summary: Materials science spans text, molecular and crystal structures, characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships, which makes a general-purpose model for the field hard to build. `MatVerse` is built on `Intern-S2-Preview` and specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training on a multimodal corpus assembled with teacher-guided reasoning distillation, problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based data construction. Evaluated on `OmniMatBench`, `MatSciBench`, and `MaCBench`, it shows **consistent improvements over the base model on all three benchmarks**, along with better inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems.

papers.title: Multiple Criteria Decision Making Under XORness
papers.abstract: How should we make decisions under XORness? XORness is a class of uncertainty arising from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy. We develop a multiple criteria decision making framework that preserves XORness throughout the decision process. We define XOR numbers and prove their fundamental arithmetic and algebraic properties. Building on these results, we extend the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix and introduce a compatible normalization procedure. Further, we propose an additive XOR aggregation operator, which preserves indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy inherent in evaluations. In addition, we introduce an axiomatic XORness measure that quantifies the degree of uncertainty associated with global performance scores and develop a performance--XORness index to rank alternatives. We prove that this index induces a total preorder over the set of alternatives and identify the conditions for preserving dominance. The applicability of the developed framework is demonstrated through the risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems, and recommendations are derived using the XOR--weighted sum method.
papers.summary: Decision making under a class of uncertainty the authors call XORness, which arises from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy in evaluations, is formalized through newly defined `XOR numbers` with proven arithmetic and algebraic properties. The framework extends the standard decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix with a compatible normalization, an additive aggregation operator, and an axiomatic measure of how uncertain each global score is. A combined performance-XORness index is **proven to induce a total preorder over the alternatives**, with conditions identified for preserving dominance. The method is demonstrated on risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems.

papers.title: ColorRef: Calibrating Verbal Feedback for Color Revision
papers.abstract: People rarely specify an exact color when asking someone to revise a design: they might say \textit{a little darker} or \textit{more blue} after seeing a proposal. A language-model assistant must then infer not only which way to change the color, but how far. We study this distinction with \textsc{ColorRef}, a color reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher, knowing a recorded target hidden from the guesser, supplies verbal corrections. On 1{,}000 crowd-sourced description--target pairs, three rounds of deterministic oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 $\Delta E_{76}$. However, those corrections provide additional information, and improvement alone does not establish well-calibrated feedback following. A controlled Qwen3-14B diagnostic reveals a more specific failure: following a requested direction and ordering graded phrases do not guarantee a suitable step size; strong modifiers can induce excessive changes. We therefore measure each receiver's typical response to \textit{a little}, \textit{somewhat}, and \textit{much} on separate colors and select wording matched to its observed steps. On 128 held-out starting colors, calibration reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B against a fixed graded-wording rule. The benefit is concentrated on large corrections, with many unchanged cases and no consistent increase in threshold success. Our findings show that following the direction of feedback is not the same as making an appropriately sized revision.
papers.summary: When a person asks for a color to be made a little darker or more blue, a language model has to infer both the direction of the change and how far to go. `ColorRef` is a reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher who knows the hidden target gives verbal corrections; on 1,000 crowd-sourced pairs, three rounds of oracle feedback cut mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 Delta E76. A diagnostic on `Qwen3-14B` shows that following the requested direction does not guarantee a sensible step size, with strong modifiers causing overshoot. Measuring each model's typical response to graded words and choosing wording to match **reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for `Qwen3-14B`** and from 11.06 to 5.89 for `Gemma 4 12B`, with the benefit concentrated on large corrections.

papers.title: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics
papers.abstract: This paper presents DARSY: a software tool for abstraction-based verification and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions. DARSY requires only a simulator of the system and a Lipschitz bound on its dynamics, and needs no knowledge of dynamics or noise distributions. The tool is fully automated and constructs a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions, whose probability intervals are obtained via statistical techniques and Lipschitz reasoning. Robust dynamic programming on this IMDP then yields a policy together with a lower bound on the probability that the unknown system satisfies a desired specification. This lower bound holds with a user-specified confidence; that is, it is probably approximately correct (PAC). The tool is implemented in Python and supports general Lipschitz-continuous system dynamics and specifications expressed in syntactically co-safe LTL (scLTL), which includes reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety specifications as special cases. Beyond standard IMDPs, DARSY implements a two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction that also bounds the probability of transitioning to aggregated state blocks, yielding smaller abstraction errors than IMDP abstractions and, as a result, tighter satisfaction guarantees. We demonstrate DARSY's broad applicability across a variety of benchmarks and specifications.
papers.summary: `DARSY` is a Python tool for verifying and synthesizing control policies for discrete-time stochastic systems whose dynamics and noise distributions are unknown, requiring only a simulator and a Lipschitz bound. It builds a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions and runs robust dynamic programming to produce a policy together with **a lower bound on specification satisfaction that holds with user-specified confidence, i.e. is probably approximately correct (PAC)**. Specifications are written in syntactically co-safe linear temporal logic, covering reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety. A two-layer IMDP abstraction that also bounds transitions to aggregated state blocks gives smaller abstraction errors and tighter guarantees.

papers.title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
papers.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.
papers.summary: Transferring a robot manipulation skill to a differently shaped tool requires working out which geometric features of the tool actually matter for the task. `A2-VLA` pairs an embodied agent with a vision-language-action (VLA) policy: from a few teleoperated demonstrations the agent reconstructs scenes in simulation, proposes functional regions and geometric properties as affordance hypotheses, tests and revises them through autonomous experiments, and stores validated extraction skills in a reusable library. The encoded functional-region features then condition a `pi0.5` backbone during training and inference. The method reaches 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting and **improves real-robot success on unseen tools by 30.7 percentage points over `pi0.5`** across three tool-use tasks.

papers.title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.
papers.summary: Training hardware-engineering agents with reinforcement learning needs environments that span tasks, keep state across tool calls, and handle large design hierarchies with parallel rollouts. `SiliconGym` is a cross-task, cross-toolchain environment for hardware design and verification that separates versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, scaling from module-level tasks to multi-round repository repair and full system-on-chip flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, **finishing a 256-answer batch 21.9% faster than native `ChipSeek`**. With interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, functional correctness learned on open-source tools transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation shows when power, performance and area gains survive commercial synthesis.

papers.title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
papers.abstract: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.
papers.summary: Language models repairing Register-Transfer Level (RTL) hardware code struggle when the root cause of a fault sits far from the failing output in the source. `GRODE-RTL` extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps the nodes back to editable source lines, and presents them as a compact dependency view grouped by hop distance, prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant ones. On 30 formally validated non-local faults it **improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, 26.7% on `GLM-5.2`, and 20.0% on `MiniMax-M3`**. A six-configuration ablation attributes the gain to selective dependency organization rather than to simply adding more context or exposing the full graph.

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.
papers.summary: Drug-target interaction (DTI) models score candidate drugs that their owners cannot reveal, and secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, but slowly. This winning entry to Track III of the iDASH 2026 competition co-designs the model and the protocol: `SlimDTA` minimizes operations on the secret drug, especially the non-linear ones that need communication, while a GPU framework evaluates linear layers with additive secret sharing and non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for comparisons. The system runs at **under 10 ms per prediction on average**, with secure outputs matching the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.abstract:
Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference.
  In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
papers.summary: Sending queries to a remote large language model exposes sensitive user input, and existing differentially private approaches that add noise to input embeddings lose substantial accuracy as privacy tightens. `DP-SPD` instead hides the real query among client-generated dummy queries and shuffles them before sending, so the server cannot tell which one reflects the user's intent. To offset the cost of the extra queries, it exploits their shared prefixes and reuses transformer key-value (KV) caches during decoding. Across classification and generation tasks and under several inference attacks, the authors report **strong inference-time privacy with near-plaintext utility**.

papers.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
papers.summary: Latent chain-of-thought methods compress a vision-language model's textual reasoning into continuous thoughts, but the models remain full precision, and naive quantization to 4-bit weights and activations badly damages reasoning accuracy. `QL-VLM` addresses this with Dynamics-Guided Quantization, which uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, and Dynamics-Preserving Distillation, which aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher. On `ScienceQA-IMG` with `Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct`, the **4-bit model reaches 90.43% accuracy**, improving on the baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit chain-of-thought.

papers.title: LATER: Learning Action-Conditioned Temporal Evidence Retrieval for Predictive World Models
papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.
papers.summary: Early interactions with an object can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show but that still determine how future actions play out. `LATER` is an action-conditioned world model built on `CF-JEPA` that stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories held fixed during candidate rollouts, and queries them with the current state and candidate action. On distracted `Two-Stage PushT` it **raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0%** over a reconstructed `CF-JEPA`, and it reduces along-push mean absolute error under distractors by 20.2% relative to that baseline. Controlled history interventions confirm that later predictions depend on earlier physical evidence even when the query observation and action are fixed.

papers.title: SEAF: Selective Semantic Enrichment and Visual Evidence Fusion for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
papers.abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection requires textual, visual, and contextual evidence, particularly when multiple images provide complementary cues. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate auxiliary information from a post's text and images, but their outputs may mix useful background knowledge with redundant visual descriptions. We propose SEAF, a dual-branch framework for selective semantic enrichment and visual evidence fusion. SEAF assigns generated fields to distinct roles: entity background enriches semantic input, while image descriptions supply alignment statistics. The semantic branch combines the original post text, background from a frozen MLLM, and optical character recognition (OCR) text. The aligned visual branch combines global and local visual features with statistics of cross-modal and inter-image similarity. Text-Anchored Smoothed Aggregation (TASA) weights images by their similarity to the original post text while preserving contributions from images with low literal similarity. Summing the branch classification scores integrates contextual semantics with visual evidence. Experiments on the multi-image MMSD3.0 benchmark show that SEAF outperforms all compared methods.
papers.summary: Detecting sarcasm in posts with several images requires combining textual, visual, and contextual cues, and auxiliary text generated by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) tends to mix useful background with redundant image descriptions. `SEAF` splits the generated content by role across two branches: a semantic branch combines the post text, entity background from a frozen MLLM, and optical character recognition (OCR) text, while a visual branch combines global and local image features with cross-modal and inter-image similarity statistics. A text-anchored aggregation scheme weights images by similarity to the post text without discarding those with low literal similarity. On the multi-image `MMSD3.0` benchmark, **`SEAF` outperforms all compared methods**.

papers.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
papers.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
papers.summary: Long-running language-model agents accumulate history, tool output, and intermediate decisions, and compacting that working context is a common way to keep going, yet how well models do it is poorly measured. `CompAct-Bench` takes successful agent trajectories, inserts compaction boundaries at different stages, has the model under test compress the preceding context at controlled retention ratios, and lets the same executor continue the task, covering `BrowseComp`, `SWE-bench`, and an internal `CompanyBench`. Results show that **compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models**: Claude- and GPT-family models do best, but downstream accuracy still degrades substantially under aggressive compaction. Failures stem not only from omitted information but from distorted task state, such as unresolved issues recorded as conclusions or established results being forgotten, leading to wrong decisions or redundant work.

papers.title: Lightweight Low-Frequency Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring via Karhunen-Lo\`eve Feature Distillation and Temporal Convolutional Networks
papers.abstract: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) is a critical enabler for demand-side management which allows for smart grid optimization. A deployment-ready NILM solution necessitates three key features: accurate disaggregation, low-frequency sampling, and low computational cost. This paper proposes a lightweight, edge-oriented NILM framework that combines activity-boundary-aware synthetic data augmentation with Karhunen-Lo\`eve Transform (KLT) feature extraction and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). The augmentation stage extracts and recombines complete or near-complete appliance activation segments so that the model can be trained without new fully labeled household aggregates. The KLT filter bank extracts decorrelated, appliance-informed temporal features which are then fed into a compact TCN along with the original aggregate for energy disaggregation. Evaluations on two standard NILM datasets, UK-DALE and REDD, at 10-s sampling and with leave-one-house-out testing, demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves comparable or superior disaggregation accuracy relative to NILMFormer, BERT4NILM, BiLSTM, and BiGRU. The computational footprint of the framework is 31,009 parameters, the fewest of the five models compared, and on a single CPU thread it needs 2.78 ms per 1000 samples, 84-95% less than the baselines. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for low-frequency smart-meter NILM.
papers.summary: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) estimates per-appliance energy use from a household's aggregate meter reading, and practical deployment calls for accuracy at low sampling rates and low compute cost. The proposed edge-oriented pipeline augments training data by recombining appliance activation segments, extracts decorrelated features with a Karhunen-Loève Transform (KLT) filter bank, and feeds them with the raw aggregate into a compact Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). On `UK-DALE` and `REDD` at 10-second sampling with leave-one-house-out testing, it matches or exceeds `NILMFormer`, `BERT4NILM`, `BiLSTM`, and `BiGRU`. The model has **only 31,009 parameters** and needs 2.78 ms per 1000 samples on a single CPU thread, 84-95% less than the baselines.

papers.title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
papers.summary: `VC-VQA` is a large-scale benchmark testing whether Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can acquire and reason over fine-grained visual knowledge, rather than merely recognizing an entity and then relying on text-based external knowledge. Its questions require retrieving external visual evidence, spotting visual clues before retrieval, and localizing, verifying, or matching retrieved knowledge against the query image, backed by a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable evidence. Evaluating 21 MLLMs with no external knowledge, provided evidence, knowledge-base retrieval, and open-web search shows that current models still struggle, with **fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition as the primary bottleneck**. Agentic retrieval results point to the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

papers.title: Explainability of genotype embedding models through observed cohort paths
papers.abstract: Deep learning models that combine genotypes with neuroimaging predict neurological diseases more accurately than either modality alone. Their clinical use, however, requires identifying which genetic variants a prediction is based on. Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients address this by integrating the model's gradient from a baseline to the input. These methods assume the model accepts any point along that path as a valid input. Genotype models violate this assumption. They map the three discrete allele dosages \{0,1,2\} to vectors through a learned embedding defined only at those values, so a straight line passes through fractional genotypes at which no embedding, and therefore no gradient, exists. Attribution must therefore proceed in embedding space where the choice of path can affect the resulting attribution. We show that the commonly used per-variant estimator does not generally satisfy completeness. Additive separability guarantees completeness for this estimator, but interactions between variants generally break that property. Instead, we integrate along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths connecting genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. Each path satisfies completeness in the continuum although the interiors of its segments are not necessarily observed. Our method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations, and is competitive with a support-background Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations. It also shows higher seed stability and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.
papers.summary: Attribution methods such as `Integrated Gradients` integrate a model's gradient along a straight line from a baseline to the input, but genotype models embed the three discrete allele dosages 0, 1, and 2, so points in between have no embedding and no gradient. The authors show that the commonly used per-variant estimator in embedding space **does not generally satisfy completeness** once variants interact, and propose integrating along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths through genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. The method improves faithfulness over `Integrated Gradients` and its discretized variant under two perturbation protocols and gives the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations. It also shows higher stability across seeds and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.

papers.title: FoodReact-AR: Learning Audience Reactions that Zero-Shot LLMs Miss in Arabic Food-Insecurity Discourse
papers.abstract: Facebook reactions record how an audience received a post, a signal absent from the post's text. We treat the six differentiated reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from public Facebook pages (2020-2024) as compositions, apply a centered log-ratio transformation, and cluster them into four audience profiles: Solidarity (Love-dominant), Dismissal (Haha-dominant), Grief (Sad-dominant), and a flat Ambivalent profile. Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%), the year of the wheat price shock, and grief in 2024 (14.0%), during the Gaza food emergency; a page-clustered GEE confirms both shifts (odds ratios 2.18 and 1.34), and they survive minimum-reaction filtering, alternative zero replacements and clustering methods, and bootstrap resampling. We then test whether the profiles can be predicted without reactions. A zero-shot Arabic LLM recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but Dismissal for only 3.4%, and in a matched ablation, it shows the reaction percentages do not help. A simple classifier trained on the reaction-derived labels and tested on unseen pages recovers dismissal for 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 against 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. Derisive audience responses are thus learnable from text, yet a zero-shot LLM misses them. We release the corpus, LLM, and human annotation layers, and an evaluation protocol as FoodReact-AR.
papers.summary: Facebook reactions capture how an audience received a post, which the text alone does not show. Reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from 2020-2024 are clustered into four audience profiles (Solidarity, Dismissal, Grief, and Ambivalent), with dismissal peaking in 2022 during the wheat price shock and grief in 2024 during the Gaza food emergency. A zero-shot Arabic language model predicting the profile from text recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but **Dismissal for only 3.4%, whereas a simple classifier trained on reaction-derived labels recovers it for 60.0%** on unseen pages, mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. The corpus, annotation layers, and evaluation protocol are released as `FoodReact-AR`.

papers.title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.
papers.summary: Lighting changes can make a dexterous manipulation policy's actions drift even when the physical scene is unchanged, and it is unclear when touch should override vision. `TipDex-VTLA` is a vision-tactile-language-action policy with two components: `VASE` estimates how reliable the visual action is by learning from a frozen reference policy's sensitivity to illumination perturbations, and `TACE` compares predicted and measured touch at matched times, using the discrepancy plus visual reliability to gate bounded corrections to actions not yet executed. Trained only on data from normal lighting, it achieves average full-task success of **87.5% under normal and 73.8% under challenging unseen lighting** on four real-world dexterous tasks. It is also evaluated on the `UniVTAC` simulation benchmark.

papers.title: Measurable Does Not Imply Transportable: A Prospective Audit of Model Explanations in Multi-Year Field Trials
papers.abstract: Model explanations are increasingly used as scientific evidence, yet it remains unclear what they license scientists to conclude beyond the data on which they were constructed. When a fine-grained explanation fails to replicate, the failure may be attributed to noisy measurement of its target, raising a fundamental question: does reliable measurement imply a reproducible explanation? We test this directly. We formalize prospective explanation transportability: the extent to which an explanation learned from past data is recovered in a genuinely future context. This property is distinct from feature importance and measurement reliability. Using multi-year Genomes-to-Fields maize trials, where each new year is a real future context rather than a random resample, we evaluate 16 agronomically interpretable environmental concepts across five forward splits and one prospectively locked test year. Coarse environment-level explanations transport reliably (median cosine 0.83); their locked 2024 value, 0.811, fell within a prespecified 80% bootstrap percentile interval. For grain yield, genotype-conditioned explanations have a historical median cosine of 0.30 and range from 0.006 to 0.822 across years. Reliability does not order these outcomes: the year with the highest split-half reliability had the lowest explanation transport. Within-context resampling showed that GxE explanations were reproducible within a fixed context (0.77-0.95) while exhibiting lower prospective alignment across the 2020-2023 transitions (0.01-0.36). A second phenotype transports strongly at both resolutions, and non-temporal validation inflates apparent interaction-level transport by +0.22. These results show that target reliability and within-context explanation reproducibility do not by themselves establish when a model explanation can support a reproducible scientific claim.
papers.summary: Whether a model explanation learned on past data is recovered in a genuinely future context, termed prospective explanation transportability, is tested on multi-year `Genomes-to-Fields` maize trials with 16 interpretable environmental concepts, five forward splits, and a prospectively locked test year. Coarse environment-level explanations transport well (median cosine 0.83, with the locked 2024 value of 0.811 inside the prespecified interval), but genotype-conditioned explanations for grain yield have a median cosine of 0.30 and range from 0.006 to 0.822 across years. Measurement reliability does not predict this: **the year with the highest split-half reliability had the lowest explanation transport**. Explanations were reproducible within a fixed context (0.77-0.95) yet aligned poorly across years (0.01-0.36), and non-temporal validation inflated apparent transport by 0.22.

papers.title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies depend on visual feedback throughout a task, which exposes them to adversarial textures, but optimized patches tend to look out of place and are easy to notice. `DMT-Attack` is a gradient-free gray-box attack that searches the latent space of a frozen text-conditioned diffusion model for natural-looking textures on ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths, refining a latent proposal network with closed-loop rollout feedback. Against `pi0.5` and `OpenVLA-OFT` on four `LIBERO` suites it reaches a **macro clean-conditioned attack success rate of 57.9%**, versus 44.7% for `UPA-RFAS` and 19.7% for random natural textures. It is also flagged far less often by a detector, at 45% compared with 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines.

papers.title: From Geographic Memory to Spatial Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can associate places with geographic descriptions, but recovering an observed association does not establish an ability to generalize across geographic space. We distinguish geospatial memory, the recovery of location--description associations observed during training, from spatial generalization, the prediction of descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. We investigate whether continuous location representations improve this generalization and encourage geographic knowledge to become spatially organized within an LLM. We frame this organization as a latent spatial field: a learned mapping from locations to descriptions connected through spatial dependencies. Building on a continuous spatial encoder, we project location representations into the model's embedding space and supply them as spatial tokens. We evaluate the resulting models on two newly curated geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London using two complementary assessments. Geospatial captioning tests both memory and spatial generalization by generating descriptions at observed locations and at locations beyond the spatial coverage of the training observations. A separate geospatial grounding model tests whether generated location--description pairs provide useful additional supervision for mapping text to geographic space. Across multiple LLM families, continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations relative to textual coordinates, while their generated descriptions yield modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering provide additional evidence consistent with spatially organized geographic representations. Together, these findings show the value of evaluating spatial generalization separately from memory and of incorporating continuous spatial representations into language models.
papers.summary: Large language models can recall descriptions of places seen in training, which the authors distinguish from spatial generalization, meaning predicting descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. They project representations from a continuous spatial encoder into the model's embedding space as spatial tokens and evaluate on two new geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London. Across multiple model families, **continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations relative to textual coordinates**, and the generated descriptions give modest but consistent gains when used as extra supervision for a text-to-location grounding model. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering are consistent with geographic knowledge becoming spatially organized inside the model.

papers.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.
papers.summary: Long-term memory systems for personalized agents usually record what happened and leave the large language model to work out later why it happened. `STARK` is a dual-graph memory: an Episodic Graph links interactions temporally, causally, and semantically, while an Insight Graph holds LLM-extracted behavioral signals that are scored by supporting events and connected by the events that produced them. Insights are retrieved directly at inference, and the event-as-edge structure allows embedding the graph so that insights can transfer across users in similar circumstances, which helps cold-start users. The reported gains over prior state of the art are **1.48 judge-score points on `LongMemEval` information extraction** and 0.93 on `LoCoMo` open-domain questions, with cross-user transfer adding 0.7 judge points on `LongLaMP` abstract generation.

papers.title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.
papers.summary: Classical Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) optimizers can stall or suffer line-search failures in finite precision arithmetic. This framework keeps the standard two-term NCG structure and adds two online extreme learning machine models: one predicts the NCG coefficient during restart recovery or persistent stagnation, the other proposes a bounded correction to the fallback step size after a line-search failure. Predictions are accepted only if they pass deterministic descent, scale, and out-of-distribution safeguards, and the models train on quantities already produced along the trajectory, so no extra function or gradient evaluations are needed. Applied to six classical NCG methods, the approach shows **improved robustness for all six variants on 480 `CUTEst` problems** at broadly comparable evaluation cost.

papers.title: VR-SparseQuant: Accurate FP4 Quantization with 2:4 Sparsity on Vera Rubin
papers.abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.
papers.summary: Four-bit floating-point (FP4) activation quantization lowers the cost of serving large language models on recent GPUs but can substantially degrade model quality. `VR-SparseQuant` uses the elementwise 2:4 structured sparsity of the Vera Rubin GPU generation to overlap two sparse streams, spending the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization while refining the activations with the largest errors; scale ratios are calibrated offline and a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams. On `Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B`, **`WikiText-2` perplexity drops from 6.85 to 5.57** compared with dense round-to-nearest 4-bit weights and activations. The native kernels reach up to 3.1x GEMM and 2.7x MoE speedup over BF16, including activation preparation.

papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict future video and robot actions with a single backbone, and their imagined future is often treated as a safety signal. `SteerTrace` is a targeted universal attack that uses one L-infinity-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, to push the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target, and it also traces where the effect travels inside the model. Across eight WAMs from four families on `LIBERO` and `RoboTwin`, the attack drives task success close to zero. Internally, **restoring just 0.36% of feed-forward neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect** in six models, and when the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future clean, the effect can shift to depend on current-frame tokens instead.

papers.title: MemMend: A Selective Revision Framework for Memory Question Answering
papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
papers.summary: Revising every answer produced from a long-term memory system costs inference budget and can corrupt facts that were already correct. `MemMend` routes only potentially incomplete answers to an editor, expresses corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts an edit only when it has resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations, otherwise keeping the original answer. On 1,986 `LoCoMo` development questions it reaches 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and an 88.35 mean judge score, improving on a verified revision chain while using **62.37% fewer revision calls**. Applied to answers from `PropMem`, `Mem0`, and `SimpleMem`, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points, although a `PerLTQA` dialogue subset exposes a completeness gap.

papers.title: Verifying Before Enhancing: Target Evidence Chain Verification for Infrared Small Target Detection
papers.abstract: Infrared small target detection is essential for early warning, surveillance, remote sensing, and space-based target perception. However, infrared small targets are typically tiny, weakly textured, and boundary-blurred, making them difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds. Moreover, target-like background structures can produce salient responses across multiple scales, making response strength alone insufficient for reliable target discrimination. To address this challenge, we propose VBE-UNet, a Target Evidence Chain Verification Network that assesses candidate reliability beyond response magnitude through complementary evidence cues. Specifically, counterfactual background explanation models local target evidence, while joint evidence verification integrates cross-scale support and perturbation-based contribution verification to guide feature recomposition. The resulting reliability estimates guide selective feature refinement, promoting target-relevant responses while reducing unsupported background activations. Extensive experiments on IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST, and NUAA-SIRST demonstrate that VBE-UNet achieves superior detection accuracy and lower false-alarm rates compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies and evidence reliability analysis further validate the effectiveness of the proposed verification framework.
papers.summary: Infrared small targets are tiny, weakly textured, and blurred, and background structures that resemble targets can respond strongly at several scales, so response strength alone is an unreliable detection cue. `VBE-UNet` estimates the reliability of each candidate from complementary evidence: a counterfactual background explanation models local target evidence, and a joint verification step combines cross-scale support with perturbation-based contribution checks. These reliability estimates then steer selective feature refinement to keep target responses and suppress unsupported background activations. Experiments on `IRSTD-1K`, `NUDT-SIRST`, and `NUAA-SIRST` report **higher detection accuracy and lower false-alarm rates than the compared state-of-the-art methods**.

papers.title: CGM: Chaos-Guided Graph Attention and Expert Routing for Autism Stereotypy Detection
papers.abstract: Skeleton graph attention for autism video analysis weights joints by content alone, giving an erratic wrist the same standing as a still one. Stereotypy, however, is defined by how unpredictably movement unfolds rather than how much of it occurs: in our cohort, every amplitude-based kinematic descriptor falls in stereotyped clips, while windowed Sample Entropy of angular velocity alone rises (Hedges' g = +1.05). We compute this irregularity as a per-joint, per-frame tensor that structurally drives computation. The proposed chaos-guided graph attention and mixture-of-experts model (CGM) couples two mechanisms. First, a learned pairwise term added to the graph-attention logit concentrates attention on irregular joints and re-ranks the remaining edge weight toward jointly irregular pairs; its unconstrained coefficient neither vanishes nor inverts, and zeroing the tensor realigns attention in 94% of clips. Second, a gate conditioned on the same signal routes each frame to two of four experts, whose weights track frame-level irregularity. Under subject-grouped five-fold cross-validation on 116 clips, CGM reaches 0.930 balanced accuracy, exceeding the graph-attention baseline by +0.187; the component ordering replicates on the public MMASD dataset, and on held-out Panoptic Studio sessions, CGM keeps 0.86 specificity without retraining, against at most 0.35 for chaos-free baselines. In ablation, routing without irregularity yields no reliable gain, whereas chaos modulation alone contributes +0.132. A severity index from the same tensor reaches 0.87 split-half reliability, separates the cohorts with Hedges' g = +1.08, and stays consistent within children across therapy recordings, supporting video-only monitoring of stereotypy during intervention.
papers.summary: Skeleton-based graph attention for autism video analysis weights joints by content alone, yet stereotyped movement is characterized by how irregularly it unfolds rather than by its amplitude. The chaos-guided graph attention and mixture-of-experts model (`CGM`) computes windowed Sample Entropy of angular velocity per joint and frame, adds it as a learned pairwise term in the attention logits, and uses the same signal to route each frame to two of four experts. Under subject-grouped five-fold cross-validation on 116 clips it reaches **0.930 balanced accuracy, 0.187 above the graph-attention baseline**, and the component ordering replicates on the public `MMASD` dataset. On held-out `Panoptic Studio` sessions it keeps 0.86 specificity without retraining, against at most 0.35 for baselines without the irregularity signal.

papers.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
papers.abstract: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.
papers.summary: `Auto-Alpha` is a framework for autonomous quantitative factor research that both generates economic hypotheses and implements and tests them. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions, a research agent develops them in a test-driven loop with backtest feedback, and semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission decide which factors enter a persistent library alongside an Experience Library of research insights. Starting from 120 research reports it built 32 initial factors, then produced 420 implementations and kept 62 more. On a fixed snapshot of 105 factors, a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns **16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the `CSI 1000` price index**; the authors note the results are retrospective and that controlled evaluation is needed to isolate each component's contribution.

papers.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
papers.abstract: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.
papers.summary: Pipeline-based natural language understanding systems must reconcile overlapping or conflicting outputs from multiple entity extractors, and rule-based resolution tends to be inflexible and hard to scale. The study compares a rule-based resolver with two approaches built on `Llama3.1-8B-Instruct`: multi-shot prompting and a `LoRA` fine-tuned model, evaluated both on agreement with existing pipeline output and on human-labeled data. Multi-shot prompting is easy to adapt and quick to change behavior, while **the fine-tuned model performs better on complex, ambiguous cases**. The authors conclude that combining the two strategies works best.

papers.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
papers.abstract: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.
papers.summary: Companion AIs are widely used for emotional support, but it is hard to tell meaningful engagement apart from harmful reliance. The Taxonomy of Relational Risks (`TRR`) defines users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately codes evidence of relational harm (RH), so the two can be studied together. In naturalistic `Character.AI` and `Replika` conversations from 110 adults, **EO-related behaviors appeared in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations while observable relational harm appeared in 10.5%**; overreliance did not necessarily lead to harm, but recurring patterns often co-occurred with it. Open-source LLMs detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors satisfactorily in at least one configuration, and the authors argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to behavior patterns and trajectories.

papers.title: PosteriorBench: Evaluating Behavior Posterior Sampling in Language Models
papers.abstract: Rare language model behaviors can be difficult to study because obtaining them through ordinary sampling can require a very large number of samples. This motivates the behavior posterior sampling problem: given a language model and a behavior of interest, is there an algorithm that efficiently samples from the model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit this behavior? We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for comparing algorithms by their compute cost and by how close their samples are to the true posterior in forward and reverse KL divergence. PosteriorBench contains 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-1}$, each with exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. We find that no method we evaluate is both efficient and faithful: simple methods like prompting are cheap but plateau at a high KL divergence from the posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do not perform better. Building a posterior sampler that can cheaply approximate the true posterior remains an open problem, and we hope PosteriorBench can measure progress towards this objective. Code and data are available at https://github.com/TransluceAI/PosteriorBench.
papers.summary: Rare language model behaviors are hard to study because ordinary sampling may need an enormous number of draws to surface them, which motivates behavior posterior sampling: efficiently drawing from a model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit a given behavior. `PosteriorBench` compares algorithms by compute cost and by forward and reverse KL divergence from the true posterior, using 21 tasks on `Qwen3.5-0.8B` with behavior probabilities from 1e-5 to 1e-1 and exact posterior samples drawn from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. The main result is that **no evaluated method is both efficient and faithful**: prompting is cheap but plateaus at high KL divergence, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do no better.

papers.title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
papers.abstract: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.
papers.summary: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) allow traffic-control functions to be deployed at runtime, but static rules and learning-based controllers with fixed state and action spaces adapt poorly when service intents change. The proposed xApp uses an LLM to combine operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration into traffic-management policies, without blocking packet forwarding or telemetry processing during inference. In an `OpenAirInterface` 5G environment the controller achieves an **average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static `TC-RAN` configuration**. Under degraded channel conditions it holds roughly 0.88 against roughly 0.4 for the static baseline.

papers.title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
papers.summary: Exploration in Craftax-style environments is difficult for reinforcement learning (RL) agents because rewards are sparse and horizons are long, and LLM-generated goals from models without task adaptation can be inconsistent or depend heavily on prompt design. The authors build `CCGP-2M`, a multimodal goal-preference dataset from `Craftax-Classic` trajectories, and fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) offline with Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (`KLTDPO`), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. The fine-tuned VLM then supplies goals during online RL.
