On `Craftax-Classic` the method **collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines and achieves the highest score and reward**, with the highest success rates on most achievements.

papers.title: Verification Behavior Across Five Qwen2.5-Instruct Checkpoints
papers.abstract: We evaluate five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task. Two AI raters scored 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B. The runner sent a standard follow-up when a request detector fired. The three checkpoints received at least one follow-up in 15, 12, and 15 cases, respectively. On information-sufficient tasks at 3B through 32B, scored format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories. After adjudication, 1/60 in each condition met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3). Across all checkpoints and prompts, 7/300 information-sufficient trajectories met H3 after adjudication, all on the same task. The prespecified upward transition did not occur in this run. The results separate visible structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after a request for evidence.
papers.summary: Five `Qwen2.5-Instruct` checkpoints from 0.5B to 32B parameters are tested under four prompting conditions on whether they declare that information is insufficient, request evidence, and actually carry out diagnostic checks, with two AI raters scoring 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, strict declarations of insufficiency were recorded in 11 of 15 cases at 7B, 0 of 15 at 14B, and 5 of 15 at 32B, so the behavior did not rise steadily with model size. On information-sufficient tasks the protocol prompt produced the scored format markers in 60 of 60 trajectories, yet **only 7 of 300 information-sufficient trajectories met the diagnostic-execution criterion**, all on the same task. The results separate visible structure in a response from real diagnostic execution and from persistence after a request for evidence.

papers.title: SAM 3 Sees More Than It Detects: Promptable Concept Maps Beyond Categories
papers.abstract: Promptable segmenters answer what a thing is. Dense prediction tasks also ask class-agnostic questions, such as what stands out or hides, how light is blocked, transmitted or reflected, and where structure lies. Robots, surveillance systems and image editors build on their answers. We study promptable concept maps (PCM), which extend SAM 3's promptable concept segmentation from noun instances to maps of concepts named by short noun phrases such as `"transparent object", with "none" as an answer. PCM-Bench groups the standard test sets of seven such tasks by the question they ask. On it, we find that SAM 3 sees more than it detects. Its semantic path responds to many of these concepts, yet a low image-level presence score can block every detection of its instance path. We present UNVEIL, which trains a copy of SAM 3's semantic path for these maps, with LoRA on copies of its last blocks. A separate presence decoder learns from verified negatives whether a concept occurs. With one text phrase per query, UNVEIL maps region concepts such as salient and camouflaged objects, shadows, transparent objects and mirrors. The same weights map thin structures such as edges and skeletons as well as object categories. Run next to SAM 3, it leaves SAM 3's own outputs unchanged. On each of the seven tasks, UNVEIL reaches the highest score among the compared promptable models, including SAM 3's official fine-tuning and pipelines built on multimodal LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/yuhuan-wu/UNVEIL.
papers.summary: Promptable segmenters identify what a thing is, but many dense prediction tasks ask class-agnostic questions such as what is salient or camouflaged, where shadows fall, or what is transparent or mirrored. The authors define promptable concept maps (PCM), which extend the concept segmentation of `SAM 3` to maps named by short noun phrases with none as a valid answer, and assemble `PCM-Bench` from the test sets of seven such tasks. They find that the semantic path of `SAM 3` responds to many of these concepts, but a low image-level presence score can block every detection from its instance path. `UNVEIL` trains a copy of that semantic path with `LoRA` plus a separate presence decoder learned from verified negatives, and it reaches **the highest score among the compared promptable models on all seven tasks** while leaving the original `SAM 3` outputs unchanged.

papers.title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.
papers.summary: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) recovers ideal results from noisy circuit executions but can require superpolynomially or exponentially many samples when no problem-specific information is available. For supervised binary classification, where only the sign and margin of the classifier output matter, the authors compare boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits against probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both to reach the same learning target. They prove a common hypothesis-class complexity bound under Pauli noise and evaluate `AdaBoostR` and `Real AdaBoost` in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and noise strength. At the same classification-accuracy target, **boosting needs fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase**, and it also reaches higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference.

papers.title: ADAPT: Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing
papers.abstract: Retrieval-based classifiers efficiently route queries to specialised services, but they typically select a candidate even when no suitable service exists. We introduce Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing (ADAPT), a lightweight routing architecture with an explicit fallback option that enables queries to abstain from specialist selection. ADAPT uses the separation between the highest relevance score and the candidate score distribution as routing confidence. Experiments across retrieval models and increasing numbers of services reveal a consistent empirical behaviour: the confidence distribution changes systematically with candidate-pool size K, making fixed abstention thresholds increasingly miscalibrated. ADAPT addresses this effect with a K-aware threshold that adapts as services are added without classifier retraining. Evaluation across two specialist datasets shows that this simple mechanism provides an effective accuracy-cost trade-off compared with generative LLM routing, supporting lightweight and dynamically extensible service-routing architectures.
papers.summary: Retrieval-based classifiers that route queries to specialized services usually pick a candidate even when no suitable service exists. Adaptive Decision and Abstention with Pool-Size-Aware Thresholds for Service Routing (`ADAPT`) adds an explicit fallback option and measures routing confidence as the separation between the top relevance score and the distribution of candidate scores. Experiments across retrieval models show that **the confidence distribution shifts systematically with the number of candidate services, so fixed abstention thresholds become increasingly miscalibrated**. A threshold that depends on pool size corrects this as services are added, without retraining the classifier, and gives an effective accuracy-cost trade-off against generative LLM routing on two specialist datasets.

papers.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.
papers.summary: Coding agents summarize long development tasks in work reports that developers and later agents rely on, and false or unsupported claims in those reports can let incomplete work pass unverified. Starting from real developer-agent conversations in `SWE-chat`, a mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports identifies eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling such a report costs **on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes** of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. The authors also annotate 435 sampled work reports and build `FaithDetector`, which scores about 13 percentage points of macro-F1 above the baseline on naturally sampled reports; the abstract as posted omits the prevalence figure and the detector's absolute score.

papers.title: AdaptReg: Skip-level FiLM Adapter for Task-Specific Adaptation of a Frozen Registration Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Longitudinal PSMA-PET/CT registration is a key step in assessing treatment response in prostate cancer, and it requires more than generic alignment accuracy: the deformation must preserve lesion volume, so that measured changes in metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) reflect treatment response rather than registration artifacts. We propose AdaptReg, which adapts a frozen registration foundation model to such task-specific requirements through a lightweight trainable adapter branch with identity-preserving initialization. Keeping uniGradICON fully frozen, we apply FiLM-style per-voxel affine modulation ($\gamma$, $\beta$) to its decoder skip connections; the modulation is generated from anatomical semantic features of a frozen TotalSegmentator encoder and supervised by a lesion volume-preservation loss. On the official Codabench validation set (20 pairs), AdaptReg achieves DSC 0.7585, HD95 6.33 mm, MTV/TLG errors of 1.68%/2.11%, and 0.0022% non-diffeomorphic voxels, improving on the uniGradICON + instance optimization baseline by $+0.05$ DSC and reducing the MTV/TLG errors by 70.9%/67.7%. On the hidden official test set (160 pairs), AdaptReg achieves CT DSC 0.816, PET DSC 0.598, and MTV/TLG errors of 4.02%/3.46%, ranking fourth among 16 teams in the final PSMAReg evaluation. Code: https://github.com/shishuyue/AdaptReg
papers.summary: Registering longitudinal PSMA-PET/CT scans for prostate cancer treatment assessment must preserve lesion volume, so that measured changes in metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) reflect treatment response and not registration artifacts. `AdaptReg` keeps the `uniGradICON` registration foundation model fully frozen and adds a lightweight adapter that applies FiLM-style per-voxel affine modulation to its decoder skip connections, generated from features of a frozen `TotalSegmentator` encoder and supervised by a lesion volume-preservation loss. On the 20-pair validation set it **reduces MTV and TLG errors by 70.9% and 67.7%** relative to `uniGradICON` with instance optimization, while improving Dice score by 0.05. On the hidden 160-pair test set it ranked fourth among 16 teams in the `PSMAReg` evaluation.

papers.title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models update many tokens in parallel and so can generate with fewer sequential steps than autoregressive decoding, but quality falls when the number of denoising and refinement steps is cut. `CaRR` (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery) is a training-free framework for a fixed editable checkpoint with two modules: Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit pass using updated context, and Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) recovers supported candidates from the refinement trajectory when the final response fails task-specific output requirements. Neither module adds backbone forward passes. On code generation and mathematical reasoning it improves on native `ME-DLM` at all four inference budgets, and at one-eighth of the full budget it raises **six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points**, including gains of 11.37 on `MBPP` and 10.05 on `MBPP+`.

papers.title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
papers.abstract: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.
papers.summary: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors inject impedance-check pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current drift and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. The authors build causal streaming filters to remove these artifacts and pair tree ensembles on the cleaned cortical features with `Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control` and online `Conformal PID` tracking, evaluated across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Pre-filter blanking removed about 98% of false flatline conflicts while preserving about 99% of deep suppression, and the calibration **bounded all 70 shift cells for propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia at or below 4.38% against a 5% target**. The cortical features showed no detectable difference from deep sequence encoders and gave no gain for hypotension prediction.

papers.title: Driver Gaze Target Identification via Gaze Estimation and Structured Driving Scene Understanding
papers.abstract: Identifying a driver's gaze target provides object-level information for visual attention monitoring in intelligent vehicles. Gaze-zone classification and continuous attention localization provide limited information about the identity of the attended scene target. This paper proposes a modular framework that identifies object- or region-level gaze targets from synchronized in-cabin driver images and forward-view road images. The framework comprises four components: MFGaze, which combines a Vision Transformer pretrained with a masked autoencoder (MAE) and head-pose conditioning through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM); panoptic scene understanding, which constructs a structured candidate set; polynomial ridge regression, which maps gaze features to 2D scene-image coordinates through individualized calibration; and entropy-driven target inference, which adaptively fuses boundary-distance geometry with class-level semantic priors. Experiments evaluate the framework using three public gaze datasets, a laboratory test using Cityscapes road scenes and self-collected gaze data, and the Look Both Ways (LBW) dataset. The complete framework achieves an overall Top-1 gaze target identification accuracy of 96.27% in the laboratory experiment. After sequence-specific calibration, it achieves Top-1 accuracies of 79.92% for task-relevant objects and 85.58% for the road class on LBW. MFGaze achieves the lowest mean angular errors among the compared methods, with 4.06$^\circ$, 4.23$^\circ$, and 10.52$^\circ$ on MPIIFaceGaze, ETH-XGaze, and Gaze360, respectively, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization. Sensitivity analyses show stable performance under hyperparameter perturbations. These results support the framework as a source of object-level gaze information for driver monitoring.
papers.summary: Gaze-zone classification tells a driver monitoring system roughly where a driver is looking but not which object they are attending to. This modular framework combines `MFGaze`, a masked-autoencoder-pretrained Vision Transformer conditioned on head pose, with panoptic scene segmentation, per-person polynomial ridge calibration, and an entropy-driven step that fuses geometric distance with class-level semantic priors. It reaches **96.27% Top-1 gaze target accuracy in a laboratory test** on `Cityscapes` scenes, and 79.92% for task-relevant objects on the `Look Both Ways` dataset after sequence-specific calibration. `MFGaze` also reports the lowest mean angular errors among compared methods on `MPIIFaceGaze`, `ETH-XGaze` and `Gaze360`.

papers.title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency
papers.abstract: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.
papers.summary: Full-duplex speech models handle turn-taking and interruptions well but often fail at tasks because they never issue a tool call, or issue an incomplete one, before any backend can act. `Duopra` is a full-duplex interaction model that treats the backend agent as a tool taking a self-contained natural-language request, so direct tool calls and delegation share one action interface. It is trained in three stages: supervised fine-tuning on the protocol, full-duplex reinforcement learning that rewards timely and complete execution, and a projector-only repair of the talker's conditioning. On `Full-Duplex-Bench v3`, **Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7% with the same backend**, and reaches 47.7% when calling tools directly, while three takeover rates on `FDB v1.0` improve over the base model.

papers.title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.
papers.summary: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can separate correct from erroneous reasoning steps, which invites the conclusion that the model's verification judgment follows what routing encodes. `RouteVerify` tests this by swapping router logits, MoE outputs or post-MoE residual states from one solution trace into another across nine MoE checkpoints, and measuring the shift in the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. Probes on router logits read correctness in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88), and replacing router logits moves the judgment in all nine by more than a norm-matched random replacement. However, **the shift rarely depends on whether the source step was correct**, whereas residual replacements do show that dependence in eight of nine checkpoints.

papers.title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
papers.summary: A collision-free detour can leave a legged robot a few centimetres or degrees off when it reaches a stair or ledge, causing a fixed locomotion skill to stall or fall. Passage-conditioned navigation stores each crossing from a single 27-minute teaching session as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces an entry gate that makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10° off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, this **raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings within limits from 24.1% to 88.6%**, and in contact simulation a robot pushed off course before stairs had no falls in 180 climbs versus 9 when the stored direction was ignored. On a real wheeled-legged robot it completed all six competition runs over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain fully autonomously.

papers.title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
papers.abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.
papers.summary: Multimodal safety guards increasingly produce rationales with their safety verdicts, and this study examines whether those rationales are trustworthy. It distinguishes visual rationale hallucination (unsupported visual facts) from safety attribution hallucination (grounded content given the wrong safety interpretation), and finds that **rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently shrink with higher classification accuracy or larger models**. In the Think-with-Image paradigm, errors concentrate in fine-grained attributes and relations, and visual tools are invoked rarely or without enough spatial focus. The proposed `Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning` (`TCG-RL`) rewards tool use only when it improves grounding over a tool-free reference, reducing hallucination while keeping safety prediction competitive.

papers.title: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats?
papers.abstract: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.
papers.summary: Neural insider-threat detectors flag unusual days of worker activity, and explanations of those flags point to internal features of the model. The authors audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on `CERT` simulated workplace logs by removing the named features and comparing against a control change of similar size, then introduce the tipping radius: a first-order estimate of how far the similarity metric must move before the removal-versus-control difference vanishes. **In 33 of 34 runs across seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard metric choices**, meaning the audit result is fragile to that choice. They also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is instead of what they did, and recommend fixing the control metric in advance and reporting its tipping radius.

papers.title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
papers.abstract: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from the words of a sentence, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads it. We study how much of prominence language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and largely make the same errors. With the prompts we tested, LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. Linear probes find more in their representations. Speech models reach 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of prominence, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting does not bring it out: they represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell you.
papers.summary: Prosodic prominence, meaning which words a speaker emphasizes, is partly predictable from text and partly dependent on how a sentence is read aloud. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, the authors compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models finish within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the three-way task, while speech models reach 84.7%. With the prompts tested, **LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline even with 500 examples, although linear probes recover more from their representations**.

papers.title: Inject Where It Matters: Objective-Dependent Feature Control in Rectified-Flow Image Editing
papers.abstract: Many prompt-driven FLUX editing methods rely on injecting source features into target-conditioned generation, creating an inherent trade-off between source preservation and the desired edit. We address this problem by controlling where source features are injected and which transformer blocks are used. First, we introduce adaptive masks that spatially gate feature injection using differences between source- and target-conditioned block outputs at matched inversion states. Second, we use REINFORCE to select Top-K injection blocks under different preservation-editability objectives. The selected blocks are fixed at inference and require no online search. On PIE-Bench with FLUX.1-dev, spatial masking controls the alignment-preservation trade-off. On 60 validation examples, a learned nine-block set gives lower whole-image LPIPS than the 18-block RF-Edit set within the same masked pipeline, with slightly lower alignment. Among 50 random nine-block sets, it has the lowest LPIPS but not the highest reward. Separate objective sweeps reveal different block preferences for preservation and alignment.
papers.summary: Prompt-driven image editing with `FLUX` typically injects source features into the target-conditioned generation, trading off source preservation against the requested edit. This work adds adaptive masks that spatially gate injection using differences between source- and target-conditioned block outputs, and uses `REINFORCE` to pick a fixed Top-K set of transformer blocks for injection under different preservation-editability objectives. On `PIE-Bench` with `FLUX.1-dev`, spatial masking controls the trade-off, and **a learned nine-block set gives lower whole-image LPIPS than the 18-block `RF-Edit` set, with slightly lower alignment**. Among 50 random nine-block sets the learned one has the lowest LPIPS but not the highest reward, and preservation and alignment objectives favour different blocks.

papers.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, so the drafter must be both lightweight and accurate. `G-MTP` is a Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture with a single shared drafting head that adds target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to skip prefill compute, and a clustered vocabulary projection to cut full-vocabulary decoding cost. On the `Gemma 4` family it delivers **speedups of up to 3.1× for server-side models** and, for smaller on-device models, up to 2.3× on an H100 and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes keep the drafter aligned under domain shift, needing up to 1.83× fewer target forward passes than tuning the backbone alone.

papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
papers.summary: Preference training is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in vision-language models, and this study decomposes what the reported drop in `CHAIR` score actually consists of. Each trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes gains from simply saying less, and the remainder is compared with a deliberately weak eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images. For eight public methods on `LLaVA-1.5-7B`, **the probe reproduces at least two thirds of the beyond-brevity gain for 7 of 8 methods on `COCO`** and 8 of 8 on `AMBER`, with `RLAIF-V` the consistent exception. Using the probe or an object-level `CLIP` score as labels for `DPO` recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the gain from ground-truth labels on `Qwen2.5-VL`, and the authors report that a human check of the `CHAIR` evaluator's precision fell below their pre-set bar.

papers.title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
papers.abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.
papers.summary: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which ones are safe to act on unattended and to keep a record explaining each. The proposed reconciliation contract commits the target model's greedy answer as an anchor, draws one or two greedy checks via an alternate prompt or a model from another family, and applies a pure function with five outcomes, acting only on Agree. Across 48,000 model-item evaluations on 6,000 questions, **pooling samples from another model family raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget**, while a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. The three-call contract performs within one point of pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples, automates 70% of items under the strict gate, and still acts on 16% of errors.

papers.title: Limits of local curvature for constructing search subspaces in segmentation models
papers.abstract: We examine how well subspaces constructed from local curvature represent the change in the gradient update field after a finite step in semantic segmentation models. The local response is the action of the curvature operator on the actual input displacement. In a study of 50 images and two models, we measure the ratio of the loss increase attained in a fixed subspace to that attained in the full space. This ratio decreases as the search radius increases. On ten images from the same sample, we compare the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the initial gradient with two rank-16 subspaces for both models. The two equal-rank subspaces are assessed at the same initial states, using the same actual steps and measured vectors. Adding generalised Gauss-Newton directions to the initial gradient reduces the mean relative error in representing the field change from 0.922 to 0.874 for the first model and from 0.819 to 0.763 for the second. At the same rank, including the response direction for the initial gradient nearly eliminates the error in representing the local response. The mean error in representing the field change does not decrease. A decomposition with fixed pixel weights shows that the finite-step remainder is comparable in norm to the field change and makes the largest diagonal contribution to the squared projection error of the field after the step. Evaluation of a search subspace should measure how accurately it represents the field change and the local response.
papers.summary: Subspaces built from local curvature are used to search for loss-increasing input perturbations, and this study asks how well they capture the change in the gradient field after a finite step in semantic segmentation models. Across 50 images and two models, the ratio of loss increase achieved in a fixed subspace to that in the full space falls as the search radius grows. Adding generalised Gauss-Newton directions to the initial gradient **reduces the mean relative error in representing the field change only from 0.922 to 0.874 and from 0.819 to 0.763** for the two models. Including the response direction nearly eliminates error on the local response but does not lower error on the field change, because the finite-step remainder is comparable in norm to the field change itself.

papers.title: A Sparse Low-Rank Biclique Decomposition for Graphs
papers.abstract: Low-rank plus sparse decompositions, such as robust PCA, typically model the low-rank component as dense and the sparse component as corruption. This viewpoint is poorly suited to graph adjacency matrices, where sparsity is structural and dense low-rank factors destroy the combinatorial and computational properties of the graph. We propose signed biclique decomposition (SBD), a sparse low-rank decomposition for integer-weighted graphs that represents the structured component as a sum of sparse signed binary rank-one factors, together with a sparse signed residual. The resulting representation remains discrete, interpretable, sparse, and compatible with standard linear algebra. We formulate fixed-rank and greedy SBD objectives and derive a gain-based greedy algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, SBD recovers block structure in noisy graphs, while its factorized representation enables efficient sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM). On real graphs with strong shared-neighborhood structure, SBD achieves compression factors above $10$ and SpMM speedups up to $6\times$ over cuSPARSE, suggesting a practical alternative to dense low-rank decompositions for graphs. Code is available at https://github.com/IAntoineV/sbd.
papers.summary: Low-rank plus sparse decompositions such as robust PCA produce dense low-rank factors, which suits graph adjacency matrices poorly because sparsity there is structural. Signed biclique decomposition (`SBD`) represents an integer-weighted graph as a sum of sparse signed binary rank-one factors plus a sparse signed residual, keeping the representation discrete and interpretable, with a gain-based greedy algorithm that carries theoretical guarantees. It recovers block structure in noisy graphs, and on real graphs with strong shared-neighborhood structure it achieves **compression factors above 10 and sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM) speedups up to 6× over `cuSPARSE`**.

papers.title: Beyond Alignment: Whitening Geometry, Profile Synthesis, and Heterogeneous Ensembles for Cross-Environment WiFi Action Recognition
papers.abstract: Cross-environment deployment is the central obstacle to practical WiFi sensing: a pipeline reaching 0.89+ top-1 in its training environments collapses to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with only K-shot labels. A ceiling analysis shows the collapse is not an alignment problem: the action signal is strong across seen environments (about 0.89 K10), environment identity is decodable from the encoder (0.965), and the failure concentrates in the encoder's extrapolation to the novel environment. A pre-registered falsification chain confirms that "align the domains" methods--training-time alignment, readout-level prototype alignment, adversarial confusion, and covariance/subspace alignment (CORAL -3.8pp, subspace -8.3pp)--degrade performance, and that source-domain statistics anti-correlate with cross-environment contribution. The effective levers lie elsewhere; we combine them into Dec-H: (i) closed-form source within-class whitening, provably re-geometrizing the readout's L2 regularization (+8.6pp, zero cost); (ii) profile-mixing augmentation (+1.0pp); (iii) few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit (+1.5pp; fixed preconditioners are 20/20 negative); (iv) heterogeneous decision ensembles (+1.7pp); homogeneous scaling and source-weighted stacking are saturated or harmful. Dec-H reaches 0.560 K10 (0.812 K40), +15.2pp over the baseline, consistent across all four environments and seeds; all thirteen configurations were pre-registered with frozen criteria.
papers.summary: WiFi-based action recognition that scores above 0.89 top-1 in its training environments collapses to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with only a few labelled shots in the new environment. A ceiling analysis and a pre-registered falsification chain show the failure is not an alignment problem: domain alignment methods such as `CORAL` and subspace alignment reduce accuracy. The authors instead combine source within-class whitening, profile-mixing augmentation, few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit, and heterogeneous decision ensembles into `Dec-H`. It reaches **0.560 with 10 shots, 15.2 percentage points over the baseline**, and 0.812 with 40 shots, consistently across all four environments and seeds.

papers.title: Rank2Replace: VLM-Ranked Slot Replacement for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
papers.abstract: Spurious correlations can give image predictors high in-distribution accuracy but poor generalization under distribution shift. We introduce $\textbf{Rank2Replace}$, which transfers knowledge of task-relevant evidence from pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to small predictors through training-time augmentation for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance and guides rank-dependent replacement with same-rank slot embeddings from another image. This augmentation retains the original image's label, encouraging reliance on preserved task evidence as incidental cues change, and supports combination with existing OOD methods. Across four datasets and six splits under shared frozen slot embeddings, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches macro-averaged average-group and worst-group accuracies of $80.43\%$ and $65.28\%$ without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning. Slot corruption improves both macro-averaged metrics for all fourteen OOD training methods. Combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches $81.96\%$ and $72.68\%$. Controlled ablations support the ranking and replacement design, with gains across five ranking VLMs and six extractor--predictor combinations. Permutation-invariant predictors further improve both macro-averaged metrics over their unaugmented counterparts while using VLM guidance only during training for efficient inference.
papers.summary: Image classifiers that latch onto spurious correlations score well in distribution but fail under distribution shift. `Rank2Replace` uses a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) to rank object-centric slots by task relevance at training time, then swaps slots with same-rank slot embeddings from another image while keeping the original label, pushing the small predictor to rely on the preserved task evidence. Across four datasets and six splits, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches 80.43% average-group and 65.28% worst-group accuracy without environment labels, and **slot corruption improves both metrics for all fourteen out-of-distribution (OOD) training methods tested**. Combined with slot ranking and `IRM` it reaches 81.96% and 72.68%, and the VLM is needed only during training.

papers.title: Self-Replicating Language Models
papers.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.
papers.summary: Whether language models can undergo Darwinian evolution is tested through several modes of self-reproduction: emitting a genome that trains an offspring, copying and mutating the model's own weights, and teaching a child model from its own samples. The experiments indicate that **small language models can replicate and evolve, improving under selection and adapting to narrow niches**. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model can drive its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship large language models (LLMs) can write such replicators, but replicating a large LLM by teaching its offspring is reported as technically and economically infeasible for now.

papers.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language agents call segmentation tools, and prior work has treated obtaining a good mask as the end of the job without checking whether the agent uses that evidence well. The authors build `Mask-Evidence MedVQA`, a 2.5K-example benchmark over four image types pairing each question with a ground-truth mask in multiple renderings, and find that the rendering of a fixed mask changes model behaviour and that even a ground-truth mask can flip initially correct answers to incorrect. Their harness `TUNE` (Tool Use is Not Enough) explicitly manages which evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. It **improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks**, and raises a fine-tuned `Qwen3.5-9B` backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 points on three public medical VQA benchmarks.

papers.title: Whose Risks Count? What 1,901 AI Incidents Reveal About Corporate Disclosures
papers.abstract: AI systems can harm people, yet the AI actors that provide or deploy them are rarely obliged to disclose these risks. US securities regulation is an exception. Companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose their material risks, including those of their AI systems, in filings that carry liability for misstatement. Materiality, however, is defined by what a reasonable investor would consider important, so harms to third parties enter disclosure only insofar as they become financial risks for the company. We test whether AI harms do so by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half belong to a risk type that the AI actor never disclosed, and this share varies with the kind of harm. Filings disclose the risk types of 67\% of system failures but only 2\% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2\% of incidents. Securities disclosure thus records the risks that AI actors face rather than the harms that people subject to AI bear. Public authorities that hold AI actors accountable for such harms could make them financially material. We release DISC, the Disclosure--Incident Securities Corpus, to support this work.
papers.summary: US companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose material risks, including those of their AI systems, but materiality is defined from an investor's perspective. To test whether harms to third parties make it into disclosure, the authors match 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings from 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half fall under a risk type the actor never disclosed, and **filings cover the risk types of 67% of system failures but only 2% of social system harms**. AI actors themselves report fewer than 2% of incidents, and the matched data is released as `DISC`, the Disclosure-Incident Securities Corpus.

papers.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
papers.abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.
papers.summary: Literature retrieval benchmarks for research agents mostly supervise on topical relevance or citation links, which do not capture which prior methods a paper actually uses as experimental baselines. `Lineage` defines an empirical lineage relation linking a prior paper to a source paper that uses its method as a comparison baseline, and builds graphs of these relations with a pipeline called `Lineage-Constructor`. Drawn from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, the benchmark contains 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 retrieval systems show that **performance drops sharply with lineage distance**, and isolated hits often fail to recover closely connected comparison neighborhoods.

papers.title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting
papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: https://zhixuanli.github.io/projects/li2026protocast
papers.summary: Neural weather forecasters learn local patterns implicitly, which makes it hard to interpret how those patterns shape a forecast and can lead to similar predictions for locations that evolve differently. `ProtoCast` keeps a prototype bank per variable group, matches local features and their temporal change against those prototypes, and applies sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators as corrections before a gated attention block exchanges features across groups. Prototypes are refit before every training epoch, with slot tracking keeping each prototype tied to its operator. Experiments on `GlobalForecast` and `TyphoonTracking` show improved accuracy, and **deleting individual prototypes links their local feature contributions to changes in prediction error**.

papers.title: TableRoute: Capability-Aware Routing for Scalable Table Question Answering
papers.abstract: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.
papers.summary: Table question answering with large language models is hard to scale because tables range from compact to million-token sizes, and each fixed strategy (reading the full table, reducing it, or executing code over it) fails in a different regime. `TableRoute` first generates validated question-table evidence and identifies the operations a question needs, then routes each instance to one of the three strategies based on serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles those operations. Across `WikiTQ`, `WTQ-L`, `BirdQA`, and `TableBench`, it **consistently improves accuracy across table scales while reducing online token cost**.

papers.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.
papers.summary: Memory systems for personalized agents typically store and retrieve interaction history, leaving the agent to work out which user preferences still hold and where they apply. `HabitusMem` instead treats memory as the assistant's belief about a latent, evolving preference state: a trained writer produces text records for a frozen agent, each belief carrying its evidence, scope, and status. Across two agent families it **achieves the best results among memory systems on both `PersonaMem-v2` and `VitaBench 2.0`**. Controlled analyses attribute the answering gain to learned conditioning on the current request, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

papers.title: Decoupled Knowledge Retrieval and Compact Memory Enable Reliable Lifelong Model Editing
papers.abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.
papers.summary: Memory-based editors add new facts to deployed large language models without touching base parameters, but their storage grows linearly and retrieval degrades as edits accumulate. `BiSpace` decouples the two steps: it routes queries and finds relevant edits in an external semantic space, then injects the corresponding knowledge into the model's internal representation space through sparse, storage-efficient updates. It **shrinks each entry's storage to about 10.2% of the original** and stays resilient over sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark it improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods.

papers.title: HALTT: A HAte Lexicon Through Time
papers.abstract: Automated hate speech detection degrades over time as everyday vocabulary is weaponized into covert slurs while retaining original benign meanings (polysemy retention). Existing lexical semantic change detection (LSCD) frameworks struggle with this phenomenon due to a lack of standardized, sense-delineated diachronic resources. We propose a multi-stage framework to construct and validate a diachronic lexicon of semantically shifted hate speech terms. Filtering > 20,000 candidates, our pipeline combines historical (1770-1964) and modern (2001-2024) corpus frequency grounding, masked definition-level scoring to mitigate LLM temporal bias, and a dual-persona reasoning prompt paradigm. We release HALTT, a grounded lexicon of 19 polysemous terms with literal and derogatory senses, analyze shift typologies, and establish evaluation protocols for downstream diachronic benchmarking.
papers.summary: Hate speech detectors degrade over time as everyday words acquire covert derogatory senses while keeping their benign meanings, a pattern that lexical semantic change detection (LSCD) frameworks handle poorly for lack of sense-delineated historical resources. The authors build a multi-stage pipeline that filters more than 20,000 candidates using frequency grounding in historical (1770-1964) and modern (2001-2024) corpora, masked definition-level scoring to reduce LLM temporal bias, and a dual-persona reasoning prompt. The result is `HALTT`, **a grounded lexicon of 19 polysemous terms with both literal and derogatory senses**, released with an analysis of shift types and evaluation protocols for downstream benchmarking.

papers.title: Full Rank and Stable Sampling of $\tanh$ Networks
papers.abstract: We study the recovery of feedforward $\tanh$ networks of fixed architecture with $P$ parameters from finitely many point evaluations. First, we characterize the set of parameters where the differential of the realization map has full rank and show that it coincides with the regular parameters in the sense of Vla{\v{c}}i{\'c} and B{\"o}lcskei (2021). Second, we make use of this characterization to prove that almost every tuple of $2P+1$ sampling points yields uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of this parameter set. Third, we prove that for exact observations, projected gradient descent and projected Gauss--Newton converge locally from sufficiently close feasible initial guesses. The same evaluations also determine the realized function for arbitrary parameters and identify parameters in the characterized set up to permutations and sign changes of hidden neurons. Finally, we develop a general framework for real-analytic networks that highlights the role of full rank in stability and local reconstruction.
papers.summary: The question studied is when the parameters of a fixed-architecture feedforward tanh network with P parameters can be recovered from finitely many point evaluations. The authors characterize the parameters at which the differential of the realization map has full rank, showing this set coincides with the regular parameters of Vlacic and Bolcskei, and then prove that **almost every tuple of 2P+1 sampling points gives uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of that set**. For exact observations, projected gradient descent and projected Gauss-Newton converge locally from sufficiently close feasible initial guesses, and the same evaluations identify parameters up to permutations and sign changes of hidden neurons. A general framework for real-analytic networks is also developed.

papers.title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
papers.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions.
