During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
papers.summary: Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) for traffic scene understanding get little guidance from terminal rewards on intermediate decisions, and they replan from scratch on similar tasks. `StarTV-Agent` trains with Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (`RSPO`), which combines process and terminal advantages, and Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (`WDL`), which supplies validated teacher demonstrations on the student's weak questions. At inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (`LAWR`) takes a fast path by selecting a stored workflow and binding task-specific arguments, falling back to a slower `ReAct`-based path when none fits. Across three benchmarks it reports up to 8.0% relative performance improvement while **cutting token consumption by up to 52.1%**.

papers.title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
papers.abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.
papers.summary: Deep Hedging learns option hedging policies with neural networks, but the models are opaque and typically need large training sets. `X Hedging` replaces the networks with `LightGBM` tree ensembles, using an optimization scheme that trains the tree models sequentially and introduces stochasticity through random training orders so they fit a reinforcement-learning-style hedging setup. In controlled experiments it **matches Deep Hedging's performance while being cheaper to compute and substantially more robust when training data are limited**, and it offers more user-centered explainability.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
papers.abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.
papers.summary: Micro-Doppler radar allows contactless human activity recognition (HAR), but how well models hold up under deployment shift is underexplored. The study compares full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) under subject-disjoint cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer, and pairs the self-supervised `DINOv3` backbone with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (`PiSSA`). Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer and frozen features under-adapted across orientations, while `DINOv3-PiSSA` ranked first among PEFT methods in every setting. Under the authors' protocol, its Small variant **matched the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art in-distribution with 4.5x fewer total parameters and only 3% trainable**, with transfer gains over a size-matched baseline growing with shift severity (2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points).

papers.title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
papers.abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.
papers.summary: The `ID` algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution is computable from observational data and, if so, returns a formula of nested products, ratios, and summations of conditional probabilities. By following the trajectories of the algorithm's recursive calls, each ending in a tail that alternates lines 7 and 2 and then an exit, the authors show that line 4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation while the tail builds everything inside it. They further show that **a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and an ancestry test on the original graph decides beforehand whether a topological order can avoid this**. A bound on nesting depth and a simple dimensional count that every output must satisfy are also derived.

papers.title: Coherent belief and opinion propagation produces more echo chambers: corrected version
papers.abstract: The occurrence of echo chambers is a well-known phenomenon in social networks. Echo chambers are groups of agents satisfying three properties: homogeneity, i.e., sharing the same opinion, segregation, i.e., listening primarily to agents of the same group, and reinforcement, i.e., increasing opinion similarity over time. Opinion dynamics models have been used to explain how echo chambers occur through agents updating their opinions. However, social network users also exchange beliefs supporting their opinions. Here, we aim at identifying the effect of propagating beliefs together with opinions on the formation of echo chambers. For that purpose, we complement an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations. Beliefs and opinions are also maintained coherent guided by values that agents share. We introduce measures, applying to either beliefs and opinions, to identify echo chambers based on the three properties. This model is used to simulate opinion and belief propagation with varying initial conditions and agent tolerance for different opinions/beliefs. Results confirm the occurrence of echo chambers observed in previous opinion dynamics studies in a different setting and with a stricter measure. They also demonstrate the occurrence of echo chambers with belief propagation. Finally, they show that connecting opinions to beliefs and maintaining their coherence increases the number of belief echo chambers, but that they involve a reduced number of agents.
papers.summary: Echo chambers in social networks, defined by homogeneity, segregation, and reinforcement, are usually modeled through opinion updates alone, although users also exchange the beliefs that support their opinions. The authors extend an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations, keep beliefs and opinions coherent through values that agents share, and define measures that detect echo chambers in either beliefs or opinions. Simulations over varying initial conditions and tolerance levels reproduce opinion echo chambers under a stricter measure and show they also arise with belief propagation. **Linking opinions to beliefs and keeping them coherent increases the number of belief echo chambers, though each involves fewer agents**.

papers.title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.
papers.summary: Quantum error correction needs a classical decoder that infers corrections from noisy measurements both accurately and quickly. The authors express several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a domain-specific language (DSL) and search over it with grammatical evolution. Simply re-parameterising `BP+OSD` (ordered statistics decoding) and `BP+LSD` (localized statistics decoding) with damping, before any search, makes each 17.1 to 41.0 times faster at a higher error rate. Evolution then finds decoders on a better time-error front, including one that makes **23% fewer logical errors than `BP+OSD-0` with damping at 0.64x its time**, and the two fastest evolved decoders generalize across noise levels, code sizes, and round counts.

papers.title: Trustworthy Geospatial AI Workflows: Reproducible Maritime Analytics and Forecasting on Open-Source AIS Data
papers.abstract: Publicly available geospatial data provide increasing opportuni- ties for data-driven maritime analytics and predictive modelling. However, their availability does not necessarily imply that the underlying observations are equally suitable for downstream AI applications. Properties of the data source and observation pro- cess, including provenance, reporting regularity, spatial coverage, observation density, and missingness, can affect how geospatial data are interpreted, processed, and ultimately used by predictive models. At the same time, trustworthy geospatial AI requires ana- lytical workflows in which these processing decisions can be made explicit and reproduced. This paper presents a reproducible mar- itime geospatial AI workflow built around damast, an open-source data-processing and machine-learning library developed at Simula Research Laboratory. Using AIS observations from multiple public data providers as a case study, we demonstrate metadata-aware validation, reusable processing pipelines, maritime trajectory con- struction, and reproducible machine-learning experimentation. The predictive stage is model-agnostic and is instantiated in this study using a Transformer-based vessel-trajectory forecasting model. Building on these implemented capabilities, we further outline an envisioned extension toward trustworthiness-aware geospatial AI. The extension introduces explicit characterization of source- and data-level properties and their relationship with downstream model performance. This distinguishes capabilities demonstrated in the current workflow from trustworthiness-oriented components identified for future development. Overall, the study demonstrates how reproducible open-source infrastructure can provide a practi- cal foundation for developing more transparent and trustworthy geospatial AI workflows.
papers.summary: Publicly available vessel-tracking (AIS) data vary in provenance, reporting regularity, coverage, density, and missingness, and these properties affect how suitable the data are for predictive models. The authors present a maritime analytics workflow built on `damast`, an open-source data-processing and machine-learning library, demonstrating metadata-aware validation, reusable processing pipelines, trajectory construction, and reproducible experiments with a Transformer-based vessel-trajectory forecasting model. **The contribution is a reproducible, model-agnostic workflow over AIS data from multiple public providers rather than a new forecasting result**. An extension that would relate source- and data-level properties to downstream model performance is outlined as future work and is not implemented.

papers.title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.
papers.summary: LLM agents can optimize RTL hardware designs using EDA tool feedback, but the search procedures that drive them are largely hand-engineered. `Meta-RTL` evolves the optimization harness itself from a minimal loop, holding the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with `Dr. RTL`, the evolved harness reduces aggregate WNS/TNS timing violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution it **transfers to 10 unseen `IC-RTL` designs, cutting aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%**.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.
papers.summary: Published accuracy figures for machine-learning forecasts of solar photovoltaic (PV) output are hard to compare, because many studies use random splits, omit a reference forecast, and present feature attributions without stating their limits. The authors review the main method families, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and lay out a reproducible workflow combining automated model search with explainable AI, tested on an open dataset from a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto forecast one day ahead. Over a full test year the best models reach **a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence**, and the choice of input features mattered far more than the choice among strong algorithms. Conformal calibration raised coverage of nominal 80% intervals from 64.5% to 81.7%, and SHAP rankings were stable across retraining periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed.

papers.title: One Schedule Does Not Fit All: Adaptive Inference Schedules for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models typically use a fixed denoising schedule across workloads. We show that the cheapest schedule that preserves quality depends on the task, model, and sampler. We propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a deployment rule with an explicit error guarantee. Given candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and guardrails against degeneration, TCDA uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify which candidates meet both the utility and guardrail criteria. It deploys the cheapest certified candidate or falls back to the full schedule. The probability of deploying an infeasible schedule is asymptotically at most alpha. Candidates include early prefix decoding, state-reusing continuation, reduced time grids, and confidence-threshold decoding. Across seven datasets and two model families, TCDA certifies reductions in denoiser evaluations by factors of 3.4 on XSum and 2.0 on WMT14 for ELF-B; 8.0 on WMT14 and 4.1 on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B; and 1.33 on OpenWebText for both ELF-M and ELF-L. A validation protocol fixed before generation confirmed every selection on fresh seeds. Across 500 calibration splits, false certification remained below 2% in every setting at a nominal level of 5%. Certified schedules vary across tasks and model scales. Trajectory measurements suggest that when decoded tokens commit is more informative for schedule selection than the remaining latent discretization error. We also find that the ELF reference sampler draws its time grid at random, so reproducible schedule comparisons for unconditional generation require fixing the grid.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models usually run a fixed denoising schedule, yet the cheapest schedule that preserves quality depends on the task, model, and sampler. Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (`TCDA`) takes candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and guardrails against degeneration, and uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify which candidates qualify, deploying the cheapest certified one or falling back to the full schedule. Across seven datasets and two model families, it certifies reductions in denoiser evaluations of **up to 8.0x (`LLaDA-8B` on `WMT14`)**, along with 4.1x on `GSM8K`, 3.4x on `XSum` for `ELF-B`, and 1.33x on `OpenWebText`. False certification stayed below 2% across 500 calibration splits at a nominal 5% level, and a pre-registered validation protocol confirmed every selection on fresh seeds.

papers.title: The Price of an Explanation: What Demanding Verifiable Artifacts Costs, and What It Buys Back
papers.abstract: Generative models produce many candidate solutions but provide no intrinsic signal by which to rank them. One mitigation is to demand a \emph{verifiable artifact}: a program that can be executed against the available evidence. A common concern is that requiring executable verification incurs costs in both solution quality and computational budget. We measure these two costs on the $120$-task ARC-AGI-2 evaluation set. Demanding a verifiable artifact from an LLM reduced the score from $93$ to $68$ of $120$ tasks ($77\%$ to $57\%$). Of those $25$ tasks, $21$ were reached by no program-producing configuration we ran, at any budget, by sampling or by search; yet for $27$ of the $28$ tasks that only the answer-only arm solved, some program arm held a program that reproduced every demonstration and still failed the test. The bottleneck is obtaining an explanation that \emph{generalizes}, not finding one. A short evolutionary search over two already-sampled programs, at no additional model cost, beats best-of-$2$ sampled code by $9.2 \pm 1.4$ tasks, and over a single sampled program beats $1$-shot sampling by $9.9 \pm 1.3$. Moreover, because a program can be checked against the training examples, any program-producing protocol can terminate early once a task is explained: under the same stopping rule, best-of-$n$ sampling declines up to $38\%$ of its budget and the evolved arm up to $49\%$, whereas an answer-only baseline cannot terminate early. Applying the same methodology to decoder synthesis for quantum error correction yields interpretable decoders evaluated against a certified panel of published decoders on held-out exam shots.
papers.summary: Requiring a generative model to output an executable program that can be checked against the available evidence, rather than a bare answer, is often assumed to cost both solution quality and compute. On the 120-task `ARC-AGI-2` evaluation set, **demanding a verifiable artifact reduced the score from 93 to 68 tasks (77% to 57%)**, and 21 of the 25 lost tasks were reached by no program-producing configuration at any budget. For 27 of the 28 tasks only the answer-only arm solved, a program arm held a program that reproduced every demonstration yet failed the test, indicating the bottleneck is generalization rather than finding an explanation. A short evolutionary search over already-sampled programs beats best-of-2 sampling by about 9.2 tasks at no extra model cost, and checkability lets program-producing protocols stop early, declining up to 38% to 49% of their budget.

papers.title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
papers.abstract: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.
papers.summary: Clinical large language models are usually judged on final-answer accuracy, which lets invalid reasoning, confident hallucination, and spurious demographic shortcuts go undetected. This critical review covers how clinical hallucination arises, how multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors, process reward models as step-level supervision, and neuro-symbolic grounding with logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs. It finds that **symbolic veto layers offer guarantees only relative to their encoded knowledge, with reported safety gains coming from single studies in mostly simulated or small-sample settings**, while process reward models remain bounded by their training data. The authors propose a framework mapping each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point and argue that certification should audit reasoning trajectories as well as benchmark accuracy.

papers.title: From Cases to Criteria: Reusing Evaluation Knowledge for Task-Specific Rubric Generation
papers.abstract: Query-specific rubrics make LLM evaluation more fine-grained and transparent, and generating high-quality rubrics requires both identifying the target query's evaluation scope and specifying concrete checks. Historical rubrics provide reusable evaluation experiences, yet existing approaches reuse either complete query-rubric cases or aggregated criteria and dimensions without explicitly connecting recurring evaluation requirements to their criterion-level evidence and source-query context. This can preserve irrelevant task details or lose the broader evaluation structure. In this paper, we introduce RubricDuo, which organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph linking evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries, where reusable evaluation requirements across queries are abstracted by shared concepts. Given a target query, RubricDuo first combines concepts relevant to the target query with retrieved historical cases to draft a rubric with broad coverage. It then revisits each draft criterion, retrieves concept-linked historical criteria and their source queries, and adapts applicable evidence to refine the criterion. Experiments on RubricBench and HealthBench demonstrate that RubricDuo achieves the overall best performance among the evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging.
papers.summary: Query-specific rubrics make LLM evaluation more fine-grained, but existing ways of reusing past rubrics either copy whole query-rubric cases or aggregate criteria without tying them back to their evidence and source queries. `RubricDuo` organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph linking evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries. For a new query it drafts a broad rubric from relevant concepts and retrieved cases, then revisits each criterion and refines it using concept-linked historical criteria and their source queries. On `RubricBench` and `HealthBench` it **achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging**.

papers.title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
papers.abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.
papers.summary: Enterprises moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to self-hosted open-weight models often validate rollouts with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. The authors present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and test the design choices linking its stages. **Replaying captured traces stays within 1.18x of recorded input tokens at the 95th percentile, whereas live re-runs reach 4.98x**, so a small set of recorded sessions gives a repeatable per-session load. A code-coverage analysis of `vLLM` shows live, replayed, and synthetic workloads each exercise serving paths the others miss, and in a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on `llm-d`, captured workloads supported about half the optimal concurrency and about 60% of the throughput seen with public traces.

papers.title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
papers.abstract: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using four representations trained on WikiText-103: two count-based PPMI configurations and two Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings reveal systematic linguistic organisation at multiple geometric scales and its sensitivity to representation choices.
papers.summary: The geometry of embeddings for lemma–dependency-relation pairs is examined using four representations trained on `WikiText-103`: two count-based `PPMI` configurations and two Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (`SGNS`) configurations. Globally, the authors analyse dependency-relation centroids with within-lemma centring and compare them to part-of-speech (POS) distributions; locally, they measure cross-relation consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usage. They find that **global geometry is strongly structured by the POS of the context across all four representations**, while broad lexical similarity is partly preserved across relations and immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially. `PPMI` representations show more cross-relation consistency than `SGNS` ones.

papers.title: Many Solutions, One Answer: Search Order Shapes the Default Solutions of Language Models
papers.abstract: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to give the same one.We study four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with exactly known solution sets.Repeated samples concentrate on one default solution far beyond uniform sampling, and different models often share it.Yet models usually produce even rarely sampled solutions when added clues uniquely identify them.On held-out symbolic puzzles, we compare visiting entities in name order with visiting those with the fewest initial candidates first. Both searches try values in the stated order. Where their pre-specified predictions differ, the latter matches a larger share of responses in all four models, by 26 to 40 percentage points.Reversing the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts responses towards the solution that the new order favours, on both testbeds. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order raises breadth (the effective share of solutions in use) by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic. The largest observed validity losses are 3 and 4 percentage points, respectively. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in each of the three main models.
papers.summary: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to return the same one, and this study asks why, using four open-weight models on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution `ZebraLogic` variants with exactly known solution sets. Responses concentrate on a default solution that is better predicted by a search visiting the entities with the fewest initial candidates first than by name-order search, by 26 to 40 percentage points, and reversing the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts answers accordingly. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order **raises the effective share of solutions used by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on `ZebraLogic`**, with validity losses of at most 3 and 4 points. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than simply instructing the model to choose randomly in each of the three main models.

papers.title: LIFT: Latent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Cell Fate Dynamics with Single Cell Snapshots
papers.abstract: Lineage tracing links cell states through clonal ancestry, but does not generally identify unique source-descendant pairings. Learning from such data therefore requires a model of conditional outcomes, rather than only the terminal population distribution. We introduce LIFT, a latent flow framework for probabilistic cell-state generation from lineage-informed couplings. Variational inference encodes alternative outcomes in a latent space, while a conditional prior enables sampling from the initial state alone. A Mean Flow decoder predicts future cell state directly, requiring one decoder evaluation per sampling, which makes it convenient to predict cell fate through large scale Monte-Carlo sampling. This construction combines a representation of one-to-many relationships with efficient sampling and an analysis of conditional prediction error. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate LIFT's ability to recover both population distribution and cell fate probabilities.
papers.summary: Lineage tracing links cell states through clonal ancestry but does not identify unique source-descendant pairings, so predicting cell fate requires modelling a distribution of outcomes for each starting state. `LIFT` is a latent flow framework that encodes alternative outcomes in a latent space via variational inference, uses a conditional prior so sampling needs only the initial state, and decodes with a `Mean Flow` decoder that requires one evaluation per sample, making large-scale Monte Carlo fate prediction cheap. In experiments on synthetic and real datasets, the authors report that it **recovers both the population distribution and cell fate probabilities**.

papers.title: A Lightweight Hybrid Approach for Milling Force Reconstruction from Internal Machine Signals
papers.abstract: Data-driven monitoring based on milling force can enable advanced manufacturing services including process optimization and condition monitoring. However, industrial implementation is often hindered by costly and intrusive hardware and large training data requirements. This paper therefore presents a hybrid approach using machine-internal signals and machining metadata to enable force-based monitoring on brownfield machines without additional sensors. Commonly available machine signals have relatively low sampling rates and cannot directly represent high-frequency milling-force variations, especially at higher spindle speeds. Instead of learning the complete force signal, which would increase model complexity, data requirements, and overfitting risk, a supervised machine-learning model predicts only the average milling force from selected machine-signal features and machining parameters. This low-frequency estimation parameterizes a static milling force model that reconstructs the force behavior over one spindle revolution. Although the static model does not reproduce all dynamic effects, it captures the force distribution, load levels, and angular regions of highest tool engagement. The approach is evaluated on one milling machine across varying process parameters, engagement conditions, cutting tools, and two workpiece materials. Dynamometer measurements are required only for development and validation. Ridge regression achieves an $R^2$ of $0.984$ and $0.991$ for average-force prediction on the test data ($\bar{F}_x$ and $\bar{F}_y$). The reconstructed force behavior over one spindle revolution achieves an $R^2$ of $0.962$ and $0.982$ ($F_x$ and $F_y$) compared with the reconstruction based on measured force features. The method provides a cost and computationally efficient basis for process monitoring, tool condition assessment, and process optimization on existing machines.
papers.summary: Force-based monitoring of milling normally needs costly, intrusive sensors, and the low sampling rates of machine-internal signals cannot capture high-frequency force variations. The proposed hybrid approach has a supervised model predict only the average milling force from machine-signal features and machining parameters, then uses that estimate to parameterise a static milling force model that reconstructs the force over one spindle revolution. Evaluated on one milling machine across varying process parameters, tools, and two workpiece materials, **ridge regression reaches R² of 0.984 and 0.991 for average-force prediction in the x and y directions**, and the reconstructed per-revolution force reaches R² of 0.962 and 0.982 against a reconstruction from measured force features. Dynamometer measurements are needed only for development and validation.

papers.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
papers.summary: Post-training language models with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) tends to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode, so repeated outputs are nearly identical and pass@k accuracy stalls or degrades. `ROAM-GRPO` augments `GRPO` by detecting well-solved problems during training and routing them to an off-mode track, where the model is prompted for distinct solution strategies that an LLM judge checks for validity and distinctness before they are self-distilled into the policy. Training `Qwen3.5-2b` on a 1,000-problem subset of `MATH` level 5, the method **raises peak pass@16 by 4.7%** and increases the embedding cosine distance among correct answers by roughly 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.

papers.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
papers.summary: Planning with latent world models is expensive at test time because comparing candidate action sequences requires recursive rollouts. `Fast-JEPA` constructs a goal-directed plan to guide the search and directly predicts the outcome of complete candidate sequences, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across `PushT`, `Reacher`, `Cube`, and `TwoRoom` it achieves **96.50% average success with 2.41x faster planning than `INTACT`**. The authors also introduce `DynaGoal`, a benchmark for planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and response delays, on which the method reaches 73.83% success on `DynaGoal-Shift` and 87.67% on `DynaGoal-Deadline`.

papers.title: Hellinger Decision Trees for Density Ratio Estimation: Finite-Sample Guarantees
papers.abstract: Density ratios play a central role in two-sample comparison, distribution-shift adaptation, and generative-model evaluation. However, estimating a density ratio through separate estimation of the underlying densities can be unnecessarily challenging. In this paper, we develop a direct approach to the log density ratio estimation by minimizing a balanced Hellinger risk over additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees, trained using Newton boosting. We establish finite-sample guarantees for the estimator produced by the algorithm and derive an explicit convergence rate. Under suitable tail and H\"{o}lder smoothness conditions, together with an additional assumption on the progress made at each boosting iteration, our rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical minimax-optimal $ \mathscr{L}^{2} $ rate for function estimation. A key technical contribution is an optimization analysis that exploits the special exponential structure of the Hellinger risk. In particular, we show that the decrease in the second-order Taylor approximation (which is computable) of the empirical risk controls the actual decrease in that risk, yielding a direct optimization guarantee for the boosting algorithm. This allows us to establish statistical convergence guarantees for the algorithm's output without relying on an idealized empirical-risk minimizer. Experiments on synthetic data corroborate the predicted convergence behavior, while experiments on public datasets demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed estimator.
papers.summary: Estimating a density ratio by separately estimating two densities can be unnecessarily hard, so the authors estimate the log density ratio directly by minimising a balanced Hellinger risk over additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees trained with Newton boosting. They prove finite-sample guarantees and, under tail and Hölder smoothness conditions plus an assumption on per-iteration boosting progress, a convergence rate that **matches the classical minimax-optimal L2 rate for function estimation up to logarithmic factors**. A key step shows that the computable decrease in the second-order Taylor approximation of the empirical risk controls the actual decrease, so the guarantees apply to the algorithm's output and not to an idealised empirical-risk minimiser. Experiments on synthetic and public datasets are reported to agree with the predicted behaviour.

papers.title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
papers.summary: Block sparse attention speeds up long-context prefill by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring which blocks to keep can itself be costly. Delta-Based Tile Scoring (`DTS`) is a training-free method that picks query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones, with a parallel chunked scan to speed up anchor selection. On `LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct` it keeps average `RULER` and `LongBench` scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention and cuts scoring-pipeline latency by 38% versus `XAttention` at 128K tokens. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs it achieves a **3.3x prefill speedup over a `FlashAttention-2` full-attention baseline at 512K tokens**.

papers.title: Gradient Boosting with Kolmogorov-Arnold Units for Interpretable Regression beyond Pairwise Interactions
papers.abstract: Interpretable models for tabular regression, such as the explainable boosting machine (EBM), restrict a prediction to main effects and pairwise interactions so that every part of it can be plotted. When the target depends on three or more inputs jointly, this restriction costs accuracy, and a black-box model with post hoc explanations becomes the usual fallback. Here we present MJBoost, a gradient boosting method whose weak learner is a single Kolmogorov-Arnold unit $g(\sum_p \phi_p(x_p))$ with penalized spline inner and outer functions. Each unit is fitted in closed form by alternating penalized least squares, starting from principal Hessian directions of the residual, and categorical and missing inputs enter the units directly. Because a unit depends on each input only through one inner function, the fitted model has an exact functional ANOVA decomposition into main effects, pair effects and a higher-order remainder, which one-dimensional convolutions compute. On synthetic targets of interaction order three to six, the test error of MJBoost is up to 13 times lower than that of EBM, and its decomposition recovers the true variance share of every order to within 0.04. On the 35 regression tasks of the OpenML-CTR23 benchmark, it has a lower test RMSE than EBM on 21 tasks and a higher one on 2 (geometric-mean RMSE -29.1%). On these tasks the main and pair effects of the fitted model explain a median 0.992 of its variance, so the model reads as plots where the data allow, and the decomposition measures the higher-order part where they do not. With Newton steps the same algorithm classifies: on 32 binary tasks of OpenML-CC18 its test log-loss is on par with that of EBM, and on 11 multiclass tasks its mean log-loss is lower than that of EBM on 8 and than that of tuned LightGBM on 7.
papers.summary: Interpretable tabular models such as the explainable boosting machine (`EBM`) restrict predictions to main effects and pairwise interactions, which costs accuracy when the target depends jointly on three or more inputs. `MJBoost` is a gradient boosting method whose weak learner is a single Kolmogorov-Arnold unit with penalised spline inner and outer functions, fitted in closed form, which yields an exact functional ANOVA decomposition into main effects, pair effects, and a higher-order remainder. On synthetic targets of interaction order three to six its test error is up to 13 times lower than `EBM`, and on the 35 regression tasks of `OpenML-CTR23` it has **lower test RMSE than `EBM` on 21 tasks and higher on 2 (geometric-mean RMSE down 29.1%)**. Main and pair effects explain a median 0.992 of the fitted model's variance on those tasks, and on `OpenML-CC18` classification tasks its log-loss is on par with `EBM` for binary problems.

papers.title: GaussTrans: A Gaussian Interface Framework for Multi-Layer Refractive Transport
papers.abstract: We investigate surface modeling of multi-transparent interfaces to achieve accurate light transmission. The interplay of errors in geometric structure, light paths, and observation results during the reconstruction of transparent media with a high number of layers makes this a challenging problem. Some existing techniques address the reconstruction of transparent scenes by reducing the number of layers or simplifying light paths; however, this limits their direct applicability to high-order transparent scenes. We propose GaussTrans, a compact framework for light transport in high-order transparent scenes, consisting of three components: Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection. Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces use a hybrid approach combining Gauss surfaces and fields to reconstruct different interfaces. Transport-Coupled Refinement reduces coupling errors by evaluating the entire light path. Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection combines primitive support regions to reduce errors in the intersection of interfaces and rays. In experiments on datasets such as RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher accuracy with relatively low spatial storage requirements.
papers.summary: Reconstructing scenes with many layered transparent interfaces is difficult because errors in geometry, light paths, and observations compound, and existing methods cope by reducing the layer count or simplifying light paths. `GaussTrans` combines three components: hybrid surfaces that mix Gaussian primitives and fields to represent different interfaces, a refinement step that evaluates the whole light path to reduce coupling errors, and a primitive-guided implicit intersection method to reduce ray-interface intersection errors. In experiments on datasets including `RefRef`, the authors report **significantly higher accuracy at relatively low storage cost**.

papers.title: Web search in Latin America: language models use less local and diverse news than search engines
papers.abstract: AI platforms are becoming a major gateway to news and current events. This shift risks amplifying existing geographical biases that favour narratives from wealthier countries over those from the Global South. This is particularly relevant in Latin America, which accounts for the largest share of AI usage in the Global South. We examine how information about Latin America changes when users shift from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. We construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, craft realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models. We vary query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign user scenarios. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines. Across user types, the share of domestic news returned by language models is inconsistent. For local users, while search engines already return only 41.3\% local news, language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less. Taken together, our findings suggest that LLM-based search can reproduce and, in some settings, amplify geographical hierarchies in the reach and visibility of news sources. We release an open dataset to support multilingual and geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search, and highlight implications for more equitable information systems design.
papers.summary: The study examines how news about Latin America changes when users move from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. The authors build a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, write realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models while varying query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign users. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources, and for local users, where search engines already return only 41.3% local news, **language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less**. The dataset is released for multilingual, geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search.

papers.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.
papers.summary: Audio LLMs often give poor timestamps for when a queried sound occurs, and the authors find that a few attention heads nonetheless track the queried sound: they shift with the query, follow the sound when it moves, and ablating them often hurts the model's timestamps. Intervals read directly from these heads beat the model's own answers, which motivates head-guided decoding, a training-free method that keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores candidate timestamps with a prior from the heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries across three audio LLMs, and on recordings released after the models were trained the method **raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56**.

papers.title: Power Setpoint Tracking for Large-Scale EV Charging: Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning with Self-Tuning Constraint Prices
papers.abstract: In power setpoint tracking (PST), an operator follows a purchased charging profile without overloading shared transformers or undercharging vehicles. PST is cast as a constrained Markov decision process that minimizes tracking error subject to overload and mean user-satisfaction constraints. Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning (TC-CPL) extends soft actor-critic with proportional-integral Lagrange-multiplier updates from measured violations, a residual on the incumbent dispatcher that is warm-started from its demonstrations, and a transformer-aware encoder shared by all ports. It observes no departure times or states of charge. Simulations (five seeds, 100 paired days) compare it with the incumbent, Round-Robin. On a 600-port, 122-substation district, raw overload falls from 3.59 to 0.0017 kWh/day (overloaded seed-days from 77% to 0.4%), and absolute tracking error falls by 27%. Delivered energy rises by 16%, and satisfaction rises from 0.959 to 0.989. On a 42-kW transformer with household load, overload falls from 1.86 to 0.0014 kWh/day and satisfaction rises from 0.974 to 0.985, but absolute tracking error is 22% higher. Against hand-set fixed multipliers, self-tuning is statistically indistinguishable on the district. On the single transformer, it raises satisfaction by 0.011 at similar overload, but a short sweep found a better-serving fixed pair. The overload multipliers stay below their cap.
papers.summary: In power setpoint tracking (PST), an electric-vehicle charging operator must follow a purchased power profile without overloading shared transformers or undercharging vehicles. Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning (`TC-CPL`) casts this as a constrained Markov decision process and extends soft actor-critic with proportional-integral Lagrange-multiplier updates, a residual policy warm-started from the incumbent dispatcher's demonstrations, and a transformer-aware encoder shared across ports, without observing departure times or states of charge. In simulation on a 600-port, 122-substation district, **overload falls from 3.59 to 0.0017 kWh/day** against the incumbent `Round-Robin` dispatcher, tracking error drops 27%, and satisfaction rises from 0.959 to 0.989. On a single 42-kW transformer overload also falls but tracking error is 22% higher, and self-tuned multipliers are statistically indistinguishable from hand-set fixed ones on the district.

papers.title: The Depth of a Prediction: Where Language Models Resolve a Word Predicts Human Reading Time
papers.abstract: Surprisal from a language model's final layer predicts how long people read a word, yet the model computes its prediction across many layers. We read each word's prediction at every layer with the tuned lens and summarize this layerwise surprisal trajectory by its resolution depth, the depth around which its change is centered. On eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora (81,957 words) and ten GPT-2, OPT and Pythia models, words that a model resolves later, and the words after them, are read more slowly than equally surprising words. Resolution depth improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy and the best single layer by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001), about a third of entropy's gain, and each model family gains, GPT-2 and Pythia through one corpus each. The net gain varies between corpora (random-effects mean 0.07, p = 0.37); against layer-shuffled depth, which adds as many coefficients, it is positive in seven of eight corpora (random-effects mean 0.23, p = 0.016), and untrained networks show no gain under the logit lens. Pooled over corpora, the effect holds with corrected word probabilities and beyond first-to-last-layer divergences, and a whole-trajectory functional regression adds no significant information beyond resolution depth.
papers.summary: Final-layer surprisal from a language model predicts human reading time, but the model forms its prediction across many layers. Using the tuned lens to read each word's prediction at every layer, the authors summarise the layerwise surprisal trajectory by its resolution depth, the depth around which the change is centred. Across eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora (81,957 words) and ten `GPT-2`, `OPT`, and `Pythia` models, words resolved later are read more slowly than equally surprising words, and resolution depth **improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy, and the best single layer by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001)**. The net gain varies between corpora, is positive in seven of eight against a layer-shuffled control, and is absent in untrained networks.

papers.title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation
papers.abstract: We tested whether energy estimates of open-weight large language models (LLMs) scale proportionally with an exactly stated food weight, and whether computing energy density times weight removes the error. Under a prespecified protocol, seven open-weight LLMs estimated the energy of 168 randomly drawn foods from the USDA Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies at nine stated weights, from 0.25 to 4 times the default amount. The primary outcome was the elasticity of the estimate with respect to weight (1: proportional scaling). A two-step estimate multiplied each model's own stated energy density by the weight in code. All seven models compressed their estimates, with elasticities from 0.548 to 0.979 (every 95% CI below 1); four compressed severely (0.548 to 0.709). These four overestimated a quarter of the default amount by 47% to 130% and underestimated four times it by 20% to 34%. Supplying the density restored near-proportional scaling in three of the four, and the two-step estimate cut the typical error factor at these extremes from 1.47-2.43 to 1.20-1.38. Compression persisted at full precision and grew in five of seven models under a plain question. The models hold the energy densities needed for proportional scaling and answer near a typical serving, reproducing the flat-slope syndrome of dietary recall. Accuracy at usual portions does not reveal it. Food-logging tools should compute the energy of weighed entries as density times weight, and evaluations should test fixed foods across stated weights.

papers.title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
papers.abstract: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.
papers.summary: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person to wear a new garment requires all rendered views to agree on garment details, but existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines edit views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics. `GS-VTON-MVT` is a three-stage framework that jointly inpaints a set of training views with a multi-view transformer using full cross-view self-attention, conditions a diffusion editor through a multi-modal `ControlNet` on the garment image plus depth and normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, and replaces fixed attention-blending weights with ones derived from camera-pose proximity. On `3D-VTONBench`, the authors report **improvements in FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference** over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

papers.title: Safe Subgame Resolving in Multiplayer Games
papers.abstract: Poker and other games with hidden information are too large to solve in one pass. Strong systems compute a complete blueprint strategy offline and refine it in real time inside the reached subgame. In 2p0s games, a safety theorem guarantees that subgame resolving never increases how much an adversary can gain by exploiting the resolved strategy relative to the blueprint strategy. With three or more players acting independently, no such guarantee exists yet, and heuristic resolving can increase the profile's best-response gap. We prove the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, a post-hoc certificate for any delivered update. The best-response gap of the resolved profile exceeds that of the blueprint by at most four terms. Two concern the resolver: the subgame value the blueprint promised without realizing ($A_i^{S}$) and the resolver's subgame solve error ($\varepsilon_i$). The other two are the opponents' best-response gains inside the subgame over their promised values ($\sum_q M_{q}$) and a structural tax ($\Theta$), which measures how much the players' total utility can change. The tax is zero in constant-sum games, including every rake-free poker variant. Constructions attain each term with equality. On three-player Leduc poker and on Kuhn poker with up to six players, resolving without a certificate raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of the updates. The certificate flags every such update and accepts 41% (Kuhn) and 86% (Leduc) of the standard resolving updates. A resolver that keeps the blueprint whenever the certificate exceeds the tolerance delivers no harmful update. The certificate needs only one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame, so real-time multiplayer solvers that refine a blueprint can attach it as a safety check. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/MultiPlayerSolver
papers.summary: Strong poker systems compute a blueprint strategy offline and refine it in real time within the reached subgame, which is provably safe in two-player zero-sum games but has had no guarantee with three or more independently acting players. The authors prove a conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving that works as a post-hoc certificate: the resolved profile's best-response gap exceeds the blueprint's by at most four terms, one of which is a structural tax that vanishes in constant-sum games such as rake-free poker. On three-player `Leduc` poker and `Kuhn` poker with up to six players, uncertified resolving raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of updates, while **the certificate flags every such harmful update and still accepts 41% (`Kuhn`) and 86% (`Leduc`) of standard resolving updates**. It costs one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame.

papers.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
papers.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents are being deployed faster than the legal infrastructure needed to govern them, and the authors argue that maturing protocols such as the `Model Context Protocol` and the `Agent2Agent Protocol` fix what resources an agent can reach but not the legal authority under which it acts. They term the resulting deficit the legal attribution gap, covering both liability when an agent causes harm and the allocation of rights generated by agentic activity, and argue it is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployments. The proposed Autonomy Under Law Architecture (`AULA`) **registers AI systems and data assets as legal objects anchored to identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments evaluated at runtime**. Each instrument can carry a legal context clause that applies the legislation, regulation, and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act.

papers.title: Seeing Beyond the Obvious: Complementary Semantic Guidance for Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning
papers.abstract: Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SalSPML) assigns each image its most salient positive label, leaving other classes unlabeled. Existing methods construct class-level Salient Prototypes from observed positives to guide the recognition of unobserved classes. However, since salient annotations favor visually prominent instances, these prototypes may not fully capture the visual diversity of hidden positives, resulting in insufficient positive supervision. To address this limitation, we propose CoST, a Coverage-guided Complementary Soft-Target Refinement framework that supplements Salient Prototypes with complementary class-semantic information. Specifically, CoST identifies semantically relevant candidates from unknown classes by leveraging task-learned category information and image-text semantic correspondence. The selected candidates are then aggregated into class-wise Coverage Prototypes to complement the semantic representations provided by Salient Prototypes. Furthermore, we introduce a ranking-based selective refinement strategy that identifies classes receiving stronger semantic support from Coverage Prototypes and selectively enhances their soft targets while preserving the base soft targets for the rest. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of CoST, with strong performance gains over existing baselines.
papers.summary: In Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SalSPML), each image is labelled only with its most salient positive class, and prototypes built from those labels tend to miss the visual diversity of unlabelled positives. `CoST`, a Coverage-guided Complementary Soft-Target Refinement framework, selects semantically relevant candidates from unknown classes using task-learned category information and image-text correspondence, then aggregates them into class-wise Coverage Prototypes that complement the Salient Prototypes. A ranking-based strategy enhances soft targets only for classes with stronger support from the Coverage Prototypes and keeps the base targets for the rest. The authors report **performance gains over existing baselines on multiple benchmarks**.

papers.title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.
papers.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) for vision-language models is revisited through policy improvement instead of the usual stability and forgetting lens. Using the performance difference lemma, the authors characterise changes in performance on past tasks through the current policy's expected advantages, which motivates replaying historical prompts with the current policy. Their Contrastive Likelihood Replay (`CoLiR`) allocates limited replay memory by contrasting likelihood gains on correct responses under the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy, using cached log-likelihoods and no extra response generation. Across three `Qwen3-VL` model sizes on `MRCL`, it achieves **the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods** while keeping new-task performance competitive.

papers.title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE
