papers.abstract: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts are highly sensitive to the fiber-orientation field supplied to the material model. In conventional workflows, that field comes from resin-flow analysis, which requires molding-specialist support and takes about 25 hours of work per part. We previously proposed a surrogate model that addresses this bottleneck by predicting the orientation field in about 3 minutes. This paper reports the implementation, validation, and operational design that turned the model into an engineering tool for Honda design workflows. We present staged validation from 2D plates to production parts, evaluation against a predefined engineering angular-error criterion, and the expert review that approved design use in March 2025; the system has since been transferred to the crash-safety group and is in initial, limited use in directed fracture-prediction scenarios. The developed system combines injection-gate setting support for cases in which gates are unknown (90% gate-count accuracy, mean position error 11% of flow length), voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and report generation in a single GUI. The complete orientation-preparation workflow takes about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the conventional 25-hour flow-analysis route, and can be run directly by crash CAE engineers without molding-specialist support. As evidence of practical impact, component-level crash analysis using the predicted orientation field reduced the absolute peak-force error from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%, while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region. The deployment lesson is that a surrogate model alone is not enough for practical adoption: gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and shareable reporting are what make the model usable as a design tool.
papers.summary: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts depend on a fiber-orientation field that normally comes from resin-flow analysis, which needs molding specialists and about 25 hours per part. The authors describe how a previously proposed surrogate model was turned into a tool for Honda design workflows, combining injection-gate setting support, voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash computer-aided engineering (CAE) model, and report generation in one GUI. The full orientation-preparation workflow takes **about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the 25-hour route**, and using the predicted field cut absolute peak-force error in a component-level crash analysis from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%. The authors conclude that the surrounding tooling, not the surrogate alone, is what made the model usable by crash engineers.

papers.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning few-step diffusion generators with black-box rewards is difficult because such a generator is a sampler rather than a score model, and because it must stay anchored to an undistilled teacher that shares no transitions with it. `Shadow Posterior Matching` (`SPM`) renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and derives reward credit from their shadow posterior, yielding a regression loss from the KL-regularized reward objective that both follows the reward direction and anchors outputs to the teacher. On 4-step generators, `SPM` reaches **higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step reinforcement learning methods**.

papers.title: Xing-Audio-NVVASR: Scaling and Refining Supervision for Joint Recognition of Speech and Non-Verbal Vocalizations
papers.abstract: Joint recognition of speech and non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) is hindered by scarce event-rich training data and inaccurate or missing event labels. We present Xing-Audio-NVVASR, an end-to-end recognizer trained through progressive data mining and iterative supervision refinement. Guided by unified acoustic criteria, two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations, flagging disagreements for teacher reannotation. To uncover shared omissions that model agreement may conceal, complementary breath detectors screen the entire corpus for human review. Human-confirmed labels accumulate across rounds and are preserved during subsequent refinement. Over five rounds, we refine annotations for 170,000 utterances from public corpora and incorporate 630,000 mined utterances. The resulting corpus of approximately 800,000 utterances is used to train a single 1.7B-parameter model that transcribes speech with inline tags for six NVV classes. Across four human-annotated benchmarks, Xing-Audio-NVVASR ranks first among nine models in both composite score and six-class Macro-F1. It achieves a mean composite score of 64.46, surpassing the strongest comparison model, StepAudio 3 Chat Preview, by 6.03 points, and exceeds the annotation teacher's breathing F1 by 14.40 to 31.57 percentage points. We plan to release the model weights, inference code, four evaluation benchmarks, annotation guidelines, and evaluation code.
papers.summary: Recognizing speech together with non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) is held back by scarce event-rich data and missing or wrong event labels. `Xing-Audio-NVVASR` is trained through five rounds of data mining and label refinement in which two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations, disagreements go to a teacher for reannotation, and breath detectors screen the corpus for human review, producing roughly 800,000 utterances for a single 1.7B-parameter model that emits transcripts with inline tags for six NVV classes. Across four human-annotated benchmarks it ranks first among nine models with a **mean composite score of 64.46, 6.03 points above `StepAudio 3 Chat Preview`**. The authors plan to release weights, inference code, benchmarks, and annotation guidelines.

papers.title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.
papers.summary: Simulation-driven design of real parts must work with few expensive solves, a design space of hundreds to thousands of CAD values, and coordinated redesign rather than local surface polishing, and existing optimisers satisfy at most two of these. Here `GPT-6 Astra` edits a magnesium stent through a CAD parametrisation of about 1,650 values with a budget of 15 nonlinear finite-element simulations, reading the full results of every solve. Within that budget it **lowered the strain objective by 32%, while the industrial shape optimiser `Tosca` improved the design by about a tenth and then stalled**. An earlier design from the same model, 25% lower on the objective, was checked in an independent higher-fidelity deployment model and showed 14% less strain and 63% less damage at its most damaged spot at full expansion.

papers.title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
papers.abstract: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.
papers.summary: Reasoning models understand multimodal tasks well but are too slow for sub-second control, while fast decision models lack task-specific experience. `System-One RSI` (Recursive Self-Improvement) pairs an online Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) loop, in which a decision model produces structured judgments that a decision tree turns into timed actions, with an offline loop in which a team of reasoning agents revises the prompt and tree, derives supervision from interaction records, and retrains the model. It needs only a small number of real episodes and no expert demonstrations, environment modification, or parallel simulation. With a 27B decision model, mean `Snake` score rises from 1.30 to 7.35, and in a `Black Myth: Wukong` combat scenario the **offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7%**.

papers.title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
papers.abstract: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.
papers.summary: Safety evaluations of AI assistants usually present signs of distress clearly in a single message, although people often reveal them gradually within ordinary conversations. Working with three community mental health support workers, the authors built nine scenarios involving depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse, defined a gold-standard response for each, and presented five cues either together or dispersed across a conversation in more than 7,400 conversations with six models. `GPT-5.5`, `Grok 4.3`, `DeepSeek V4`, and `Llama 4 Maverick` met the standard in 26-59% of conversations with concentrated cues but **only 3-6% when the cues were dispersed**. `Claude Sonnet 5` and `Claude Opus 5` showed a smaller gap, at 68-97% concentrated and 59-87% dispersed, with the best model still falling short in 13% of dispersed conversations.

papers.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
papers.abstract: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.
papers.summary: Judging whether a game-playing agent behaves like humans requires comparing full behavioral distributions across contexts rather than average outcomes. The proposed framework computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells and then discovers subgroup rules that pinpoint where agent and human play diverge. Session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes add little beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency expose real differences. On a commercial match-3 game, the method finds that **a playtesting bot diverges substantially from humans in some game modes while showing no detectable divergence in others**, and the implementation is released as open source.

papers.title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
papers.abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.
papers.summary: Global Workspace Theory (GWT) holds that information becomes conscious when broadcast to specialized processes that use it, but building a workspace into a network does not show whether a trained module actually combines a broadcast message with its own knowledge or merely forwards an answer computed elsewhere. The authors introduce a causal protocol whose central test transplants a message from a different input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying, and recombining it each predict a different answer. Among trained workspace models the test finds all three behaviors, and in `AFGW`, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields **the answer recombination predicts in 97% of cases**. The tests also carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer.

papers.title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
papers.abstract:
Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load.
  We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache.
  Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models that mix self-attention with recurrent layers can only reuse a cached prefix at positions where the recurrent state was saved, and existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each checkpoint, adding scheduler overhead. `FrontierReplay` exploits the observation that prefix reuse in chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search almost always ends at predictable structural boundaries: it logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs during an uncut prefill and uses a state-only replay kernel to build checkpoints 6-37x cheaper per token than recomputation. Against existing exact caches it lowers **median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89%**, raises 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improves goodput by up to 4.26x. Unlike approximate replay methods, it preserves exact task accuracy, avoiding accuracy drops of up to 17% on long contexts.

papers.title: ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek
papers.summary: Video agents built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically fetch clips reactively based on local saliency, without a global temporal plan. `ForeSeek` instead forms visually grounded expectations about unseen parts of the timeline, verifies them with targeted observations, and treats failed expectations as signals for backtracking, supported by a two-stage training framework for foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. On five long-video benchmarks it reaches competitive or superior accuracy while observing **2.5-4.4x fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent**.

papers.title: Serialization Tax in Shared-Latent Exchangeable Decisions
papers.abstract: Accurate item probabilities can produce inaccurate group-level decisions. A system may score each item separately, yet act on whether enough hidden items succeed: show a slate, defer a panel decision, or inspect a batch. When items share an uncertain latent state, independent marginalization preserves means but removes dependence from the aggregate posterior. We call this error the serialization tax. For binary items sharing one success rate, classical convex-order comparisons give a more dispersed exact count law than any independent completion with the same total mean. We quantify variance and total-variation gaps, derive threshold separation under margin conditions, and connect posterior approximation to decision regret. Separate results cover non-binary outcomes, heterogeneous items, and sufficient posterior resolution. TaxScore identifies large hidden blocks with unresolved uncertainty near a decision boundary for routing to richer posterior heads. On pre-specified, hidden-target-free MovieLens 1M/10M audits, existing shared-latent heads improve high-score negative log-likelihood (NLL)/utility from 0.673/0.696 to 0.629/0.723 and from 0.670/0.691 to 0.639/0.715. Routing gives 0.006--0.012 full-population utility gains, with matched controls identifying their sources. Our code is available at https://github.com/SiminChang/Serialization-Tax-in-Shared-Latent-Exchangeable-Decisions.
papers.summary: Systems that score items independently can make poor group-level decisions, such as whether to show a slate or inspect a batch, because items sharing an uncertain latent state are correlated and independent marginalization discards that dependence. The authors call this error the serialization tax and show that, for binary items with a shared success rate, the exact count distribution is more dispersed than any independent completion with the same mean; they quantify variance and total-variation gaps and link posterior approximation to decision regret. A `TaxScore` heuristic flags large hidden blocks with unresolved uncertainty near a decision boundary for routing to richer posterior heads. On `MovieLens` 1M and 10M audits, such routing yields **full-population utility gains of 0.006-0.012**.

papers.title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
papers.abstract: Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy -- the loss incurred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic groups of decision-subjects (DS) -- on static data, where reducing one often comes at the expense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder without increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never lowers any group's acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM's break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which may lower the advantaged group's acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group. Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs, allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.
papers.summary: Fairness in machine learning is usually assessed on static data, where lowering the decision-maker's loss and lowering unfairness across groups trade off against each other, even though decisions change the population they act on. In a model where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, the authors ask when a policy that is Pareto-optimal before deployment can be beaten by a fairer one once each is evaluated on the population it induces. They show that under Rawlsian fairness, **a sufficiently high fairness weight reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged subjects at the break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the decision-maker than rejecting them**; egalitarian fairness needs an additional condition on the advantaged group. They also caution that with accuracy-based loss, the decision-maker's gains can come from declining qualification among decision subjects.

papers.title: SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-Glasses Pipelines
papers.abstract: Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM). Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space, and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework, not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.
papers.summary: Camera-equipped glasses can turn an exam page into a query to a vision-language model (VLM), raising the question of whether the document itself can be designed to make such captures less useful. `SEOYUN` is a framework for exam documents that induce the model to refuse, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions, and it contributes a threat model, analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol that separates digital, simulated, and physical inputs and distinguishes refusal from correct-answer leakage. A candidate corpus and rendering harness are prepared, but this version reports **no model-performance measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results**, so the authors present it as a research framework rather than a validated defense.

papers.title: Fixing the Twin, Not the Detector: Sim-to-Real Roadside LiDAR Detection from Digital-Twin Data
papers.abstract: Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different objects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We describe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026 Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track (0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain came from correcting differences between the twin and the real site rather than from the detector. We align the twin's coordinates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, generate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guarantees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typically keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain, while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.
papers.summary: Detectors for roadside LiDAR trained on digital-twin data face a different sensor, different objects, and different annotation conventions at the real site. The described pipeline, which placed first on the `LUMPI` track of the `UrbanTwin` Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge and fifth on its `V2X-Real` track, trains `CenterPoint` models only on synthetic data using a single 8 GB laptop GPU and gets most of its gain from correcting the twin: aligning coordinates, point density, and box conventions, generating missing pedestrians and riders, and rebuilding objects at real size. A non-learned resampling to real per-cell point density lifts `LUMPI` realism **from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames**. Component-wise reporting shows that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences keep a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain on the test set, while choices fitted to a few validation objects do not transfer.

papers.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
papers.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.
papers.summary: Little is known about how practitioners respond in practice to the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), whose obligations for general-purpose model providers have applied since August 2025. The authors collected over five million records from `Hugging Face` repository cards, discussions, and commits across Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and manually coded the records that explicitly mention the Act. They find that **explicit references remain rare, with just over 1,500 records mentioning the Act**; cards mainly assert compliance or shift responsibility to downstream users, discussions report alleged violations, and commits update supporting artifacts. Compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved, which the authors take as a case for platform-level checks and templates.

papers.title: Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.
papers.summary: Skateboarding requires a humanoid robot to coordinate its body with a passive, movable board while also pushing against the ground, and existing approaches rely on human demonstrations or analytic steering models that need system identification. The authors present a model-free deep reinforcement learning framework that uses no prior data and combines task rewards with terminations that block exploits such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, or separating from the board. Applied to the `K1` humanoid, the shifting prevalence of these terminations during training **produces an implicit progression from stance control to sustained robot-board locomotion**.

papers.title: When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
papers.abstract: Can ranking a batch of antipodal query pairs recover a gradient direction with fewer evaluations than using within-pair signs alone? We study fixed-center recovery in $d$ dimensions for a linear signal plus an unknown differentiable even nuisance, counting function evaluations and feedback rounds separately. Shared pair offsets create an information hierarchy: Mirror retains within-pair signs, Reverse couples reversed cross-pair orders to cancel offsets, and Full enforces all ranking inequalities. Relative shell variation is the nuisance range over the query sphere normalized by the linear-signal scale. When it is at most $c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$, Reverse localizes every consistent direction to angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations in one round at fixed confidence, without a variation bound supplied to the decoder. This matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, versus the $\Theta(d/\varepsilon)$ one-round sign-only minimax cost on the same class. Over well-conditioned positive-definite quadratics with no common relative-curvature bound, the $R$-round minimax cost is instead $\Theta(dR(\varepsilon^{-1/R}-1))$, even with cumulative rankings. We extend validity beyond exact evenness under supplied error bounds. Matched-endpoint experiments certify information beyond signs and short cycles. On two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, short-cycle recovery attains lower terminal mean gaps than the tested batch-capable controls. An additional optimization benefit from fitting the complete ranking remains unestablished.
papers.summary: The question studied is whether ranking a batch of antipodal query pairs can recover a gradient direction with fewer function evaluations than using only within-pair signs, for a linear signal plus an unknown even nuisance in d dimensions. The authors define a hierarchy of decoders, `Mirror`, `Reverse`, and `Full`, that use increasing amounts of ranking information. When the nuisance variation is small enough, `Reverse` reaches angular accuracy epsilon with **roughly d + sqrt(d/epsilon) evaluations in one round, versus order d/epsilon for sign-only methods**, matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Without a curvature bound on well-conditioned quadratics the advantage disappears, and experiments on two ridge tasks show lower terminal gaps for short-cycle recovery, while any extra benefit from fitting the complete ranking remains unestablished.

papers.title: SlotFlow-GB: A Neural Framework for Trans-Dimensional Inference of Overlapping Galactic Binaries
papers.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe the millihertz gravitational-wave sky, including millions of long-lived Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands of which are expected to be individually resolvable throughout the mission's lifetime. Extracting these sources requires jointly determining their number and physical parameters from strongly overlapping signals, posing a computationally demanding trans-dimensional inference problem. We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework that constructs a learned approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior, producing a probability distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual binaries in a single evaluation, without requiring their number to be specified in advance. We demonstrate this framework using year-long LISA simulations containing up to ten binaries within a 2 $\mu$Hz frequency interval, focusing on a high-SNR regime in which source overlap, rather than individual-source detectability, is the primary challenge. The inferred source count differs from the true count by at most one in 94% of cases, while the model identifies individual binaries even when their signals overlap strongly in frequency. A complete evaluation, including parameter sampling, takes just 41 ms per band on one NVIDIA GH200 GPU, or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. We further demonstrate that these distributions can be used to initialize subsequent likelihood-based inference, connecting fast amortized predictions with joint parameter estimation.
papers.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe millions of Galactic binaries whose gravitational-wave signals overlap strongly, so both the number of sources and their parameters must be inferred jointly. `SlotFlow-GB` is a neural framework that learns an approximation to this trans-dimensional posterior, outputting a distribution over source count and per-binary parameter densities in a single evaluation. On year-long simulations with up to ten high signal-to-noise binaries in a 2 microhertz band, the **inferred source count is within one of the true count in 94% of cases**, and a full evaluation takes 41 ms on one GPU or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. The outputs can also initialize subsequent likelihood-based inference.

papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
papers.summary: Post-training low-rank compression of large language models should preserve input-output behavior rather than just approximate weights. `Complete-SVD` minimizes the L2 distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally; linearizing the network and applying a Kronecker-factored approximation reduces this to a weighted singular value decomposition with a closed-form solution, with the intractable output-side factor estimated without bias from random probes. With uniform ranks and `WikiText-2` calibration it achieves **the lowest `C4` and `PTB` perplexity in every matched setting**, and it improves `IFEval` instruction-following accuracy over prior output-aware methods. A Kullback-Leibler variant, `KL-SVD`, raises downstream accuracy but worsens cross-corpus perplexity.

papers.title: Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration: Bootstrapping Generative Auto-bidding from Narrow Support
papers.abstract: Auto-bidding is a core algorithmic component in online advertising auctions. In practical cold-start settings, iterative training is commonly used to compensate for low-quality, narrowly supported historical data. Unfortunately, in iterative training, representative diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods fail to sustain extrapolation beyond the narrow data support and stagnate at a suboptimal level. In this paper, we theoretically attribute this stagnation to Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse: the weak radial return signal is overwhelmed by a curvature-induced penalty. To break this stagnation, we propose \textbf{Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE)}, which introduces a guidance handoff: as the return signal collapses, scarcity subsequently takes over as an exploratory signal to elevate the SNR above a critical threshold. Specifically, ISGE iteratively alternates between a \emph{Judger} that assigns scarcity scores to trajectories and an \emph{Explorer} that performs guided generation of high-scarcity and high-return trajectories, thereby bootstrapping from the narrow support with such self-generated trajectories. Extensive experiments on the industrial AuctionNet benchmark demonstrate that ISGE, starting from cold-start datasets, effectively surpasses the performance of the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations. Code is available at https://github.com/alimama-tech/ISGE
papers.summary: Diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods for advertising auctions stall when trained iteratively from narrow cold-start data, which the authors attribute theoretically to Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse, where a weak return signal is overwhelmed by a curvature-induced penalty. `Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration` (`ISGE`) hands guidance over to a scarcity signal as the return signal fades, alternating between a Judger that scores trajectory scarcity and an Explorer that generates high-scarcity, high-return trajectories to expand the data support. On the `AuctionNet` benchmark, `ISGE` starting from cold-start datasets **surpasses the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations**, and code is released.

papers.title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.
papers.summary: Knowledge graphs are incomplete and SPARQL answers only from stored triples, while large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts but return names rather than graph identifiers and need one call per variable binding. `GenSPARQL` extends SPARQL 1.1 with an operator, `GENOP`, that binds LLM-generated values to query variables during evaluation, using a similarity join to map generated names to graph entities and a planner that calls the LLM only for bindings that survive the other patterns and filters. In an evaluation with three open-weight LLMs on graphs built from `Wikidata`, the embedding similarity **maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs with only one incorrect match**.

papers.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.
papers.summary: Automating spreadsheet tasks with locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs) requires both task reasoning and workbook understanding, plus correct use of predefined operation interfaces. `SheetAlign` structures the work around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement it: task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in the actual workbook, stage-isolated learning trains program generation and review with edit-progress rewards, and at inference programs are selected by agreement among resulting workbook states. On `SpreadsheetBench`, the grounded interface alone **raises `Qwen3-4B` accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without any training**, and the full system reaches 32.8% there and 30.1% on `Domain-Spreadsheet`.

papers.title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.
papers.summary: Deciding when a large language model (LLM) judge can statistically replace human annotators is handled by the Alternative Annotator Test (`Alt-Test`), but that test assumes every item is labelled by the same annotators. `AltRA-Test` removes this requirement with a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations per item, and swaps one for an LLM annotation, supporting replacement when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the all-human panel. The authors prove the test is consistent at asymptotic level alpha and evaluate it in simulations and on 18 LLMs, 5 prompting techniques, and 20 datasets spanning text, image, audio, and video. About 100 items often suffice, and on real data **LLMs pass the test in only about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task**.

papers.title: Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated Biologically Plausible Network
papers.abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.
papers.summary: Whether spiking neural networks can be trained for humanoid locomotion while staying biologically plausible is examined on the Unitree `H1-2` humanoid. A biologically inspired spiking network is trained under schemes of decreasing biological fidelity: a frozen reservoir with a linear readout, reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), eligibility propagation (`e-prop`), and backpropagation through time as a non-biological baseline, all by distilling a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. **`e-prop` reaches a 100% survival rate, matching backpropagation through time**, while the fixed reservoir and reward-modulated STDP plateau at roughly 43.7% and 11%. Brief bipedal stepping is also demonstrated on the full-size robot.

papers.title: Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
papers.abstract: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select. Those switches can alter the answer scores in ways that derivatives do not capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these extra effects, then adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, our method reduces the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60\% on Qwen3.6 and 47\% on Gemma4, relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.
papers.summary: Gradient-based attribution estimates how changing a model's internal computations shifts its preference between answers, but in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select, an effect derivatives miss. The proposed predictor uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these routing-switch effects and adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, it **cuts the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60% on `Qwen3.6` and 47% on `Gemma4`** relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.

papers.title: Same Judgement, Different Scores: Numerical Scoring Topology in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as automated evaluators to reduce the cost and time required for human annotation. However, the role of scoring-scheme design in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation remains underexplored. To address this problem, we introduce numerical scoring topology, which characterizes the structural design of a scoring scheme in terms of its scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement. Building on this definition, we conduct the first systematic study of how numerical scoring topology influences zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across diverse benchmarks and judge models. Our results show that numerical scoring topology systematically affects judge scores, calibration, and robustness, particularly in judgment-intensive evaluations. Shifted and narrow ranges tend to induce some of the largest score deviations across many settings. We further find that stronger and larger judge models generally achieve higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to scoring-topology changes. These findings suggest that numerical scoring topology should be treated as an integral component of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation and highlight the need for more principled and standardized scoring protocols.
papers.summary: How the design of a numeric scoring scheme affects the reliability of large language models used as automated judges has been little studied. The authors define numerical scoring topology, covering a scale's width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement, and run a systematic study of its effect on zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across benchmarks and judge models. Topology systematically shifts scores, calibration, and robustness, especially on judgment-intensive tasks, with **shifted and narrow score ranges producing some of the largest score deviations**. Stronger and larger judge models show higher discriminative validity and more robustness to these changes.

papers.title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
papers.abstract: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.
papers.summary: Comparing internal representations across trained models normally requires running each candidate on reference inputs and collecting activations. This work asks whether representation similarity can instead be predicted directly from a model's parameters, using a graph metanetwork that maps each internal site to an embedding of its upstream computation while accounting for hidden-unit permutations and attention-basis transformations. The authors derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection, and find empirically that the learned predictors give low-regret layer retrieval and **select useful stitching connections despite never being trained on stitching outcomes**.

papers.title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
papers.abstract: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.
papers.summary: How outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) shifts a model's balance between its pre-training prior and new observations is studied in a puzzle world where both are exactly known, using small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL converts that hedging into decisions in whichever direction the reward favours, but when the right action is rare each run either learns it everywhere or not at all. Which runs take off is predicted before training by the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins, with **about 35 such groups giving even odds of success**. The count holds across group sizes of 4 to 256, learning rates, optimizers, `GRPO` variants, and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.
papers.highlight_summary:
When an agent's learned rule stops working, it must weigh its pre-trained prior against fresh evidence, and it is unclear whether outcome-reward RL makes it more stubborn or more responsive. In a synthetic puzzle world where the prior and the optimal decision are exact, RL turns calibrated hedging into decisive choices, but only for actions the base model already tries often enough to be seen winning.

- Small `nanoGPT`-style models (10.7M parameters by default, 1.3M to 85M in ablations) are trained from scratch on 9 million games played by a scripted Bayesian player, then post-trained with outcome-reward `GRPO` on puzzles where a default tool may have silently stopped working.
- Base models match the Bayesian posterior to within two percentage points, and RL then pushes decisions toward the optimal policy in both directions (the bet on the alternative tool after two failures rises from 56% to 77%), closing **74% to 95%** of the reward gap to optimal while making the model less calibrated.
- When the correct switch is rare in the pre-training corpus, each run is all or nothing: of 210 runs, **138 learn no rule and 53 learn all nine**, and when the switch appears in 1 of 232 corpus decisions or fewer, 0 of 90 runs learn it and RL suppresses it further.
- Take-off is predicted before training by the expected number of groups containing at least one winning switch, with about **35 successful groups** giving even odds, which explains why groups of 256 took off in 1 of 10 runs versus 9 of 10 for groups of 4 on the same 102,400 attempts, and why 4 to 8 times the budget recovered a supposedly undiscoverable switch in 15 of 20 runs against 15.1 predicted.
- The world is synthetic and templated, only `GRPO` variants are tested, the threshold of 35 is specific to this setup (a lower learning rate or `SGD` needs two to three times as many groups, across 910 robustness runs), the cross-recipe fit does not extrapolate to new settings, and `OLMo-3-7B` could not play whole games reliably enough to test the count on a real pre-trained model.

papers.title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
papers.abstract: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.
papers.summary: Controller area networks (CANs) in vehicles and industrial systems lack built-in security, and masquerade attacks that mimic legitimate message patterns are hard for existing intrusion detection systems (IDS) to catch. `PhantoMasq` models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical signal features and classifies each graph with graph convolutional networks, learning representation and classification jointly. On the `ROAD` dataset, with a split that keeps overlapping windows out of both train and test, it reaches mean AUC-ROC of 0.831 to 0.999 across five attack types and **beats a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline on all five by 0.13 to 0.36 AUC-ROC**. Processing takes 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU.

papers.title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models
papers.abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
papers.summary: Training hybrid physical and neural models online requires gradients through long simulated trajectories, and adjoint methods or backpropagation through time (BPTT) have memory and compute costs that grow with the window length, while truncated BPTT biases the gradient. The proposed approximations keep the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory but compute exact pullbacks only at sparse anchor states, propagating sensitivities in between through the identity (`Zero-order`) or a frozen reused pullback (`Pullback Reuse`). Tested on an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a turbulence closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic flow, and bias correction in a multilayer ocean model, **peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime by up to fourfold** with comparable training accuracy.

papers.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
papers.abstract: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.
papers.summary: Content recommendation on a large marketplace site must match heterogeneous content types to sparse, fast-changing user behavior at the retrieval stage. `LSER` (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), deployed on autodesk.com, derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and feeds them as auxiliary user-side features into the retrieval user tower alongside existing sequence encoders, with a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes user vectors. An ablation across the full multi-content-type catalog indicates that **adding the LLM-derived embeddings as retrieval signals is feasible in production and can improve model performance**.

papers.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
papers.abstract: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.
papers.summary: Most interpretability methods measure pairwise interactions between components and cannot describe how the exponentially many input-to-output paths in a network interact, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones. `Complete Path Contribution` decomposes a network's output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths, which sum to give contributions for any circuit at any granularity, and comes with an algorithm that **finds the k strongest paths with runtime empirically linear in k rather than exponential in depth**. Applied to image classification networks it quantifies excitatory-inhibitory interactions behind decisions, and in an interpretable model of the mouse retina it shows how dynamic receptive fields emerge from such interaction motifs between cell types.

papers.title: How Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity Shape Decentralized Learning: A Spectral Analysis
papers.abstract: Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to consensus dynamics.
papers.summary: Analyses of decentralized federated learning usually assume doubly stochastic aggregation, which hides how irregular network topologies give some nodes more influence.
