A spectral framework separates two mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode sets the consensus trajectory and node influence, while the remaining eigenmodes govern how disagreement spreads and decays. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, **a node's stationary influence is shown to be proportional to its degree plus one**, with a bound tying model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. Experiments show nearly identical learning dynamics across topologies with identically distributed data, while network size and connectivity matter when data is unevenly distributed across nodes.

papers.title: HiUni: Harmonizing Understanding and Generation in Shared Visual Space
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.
papers.summary: Unified multimodal models typically use separate visual representations or backbone computation for understanding and generation. `HiUni` instead extends a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) by reusing the same language-aligned vision transformer and dense Transformer backbone for both tasks, confining task-specific computation to the output side. A `Pixel Diffusion Head` handles direct pixel-space generation and a lightweight `HiGate` pathway restores fine spatial detail lost to semantic abstraction. The model **keeps a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while achieving competitive image generation and editing**.

papers.title: Pareto-Optimal and Strategyproof Data-Sharing Between Competitors
papers.abstract: We study data-sharing among firms competing in the same market through the quality of their predictive models. We model firms' profit through two main components, precision and market share, where the former depends on the firm's own number of datapoints and the latter depends on the endowments of all firms. We characterize Pareto-optimal contracts as those in which at least one firm receives all of the other firms' datapoints. We then propose a parametric family of data-sharing contracts and show that, under any of them, the relative market shares of all firms remain constant, eliminating the negative effect of sharing data with competitors and equalizing all firms' gains relative to the no-sharing scenario. We further show that one contract within this family satisfies both Pareto-optimality and strategyproofness against firms attempting to under-declare the size of their initial endowment. Finally, using a real-world dataset, we empirically test the gain in profit for all firms under the contract described above, and show that data-sharing is particularly beneficial when the machine learning task is harder or when firms' initial endowments are closer to homogeneous.
papers.summary: Firms that compete through the quality of their predictive models face a tension when sharing data, since profit depends on both their own model precision and their market share relative to rivals. The authors characterize Pareto-optimal contracts as those in which at least one firm receives all other firms' datapoints, and propose a parametric family of contracts under which relative market shares stay constant and all firms gain equally relative to not sharing. **One contract in the family is both Pareto-optimal and strategyproof against firms under-declaring their data**. Experiments on a real dataset show sharing helps most when the learning task is harder or initial endowments are more similar.

papers.title: SenseAlign: Learning Decision-Aligned Predictive Representations for Active Urban Sensing with UAVs
papers.abstract: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.
papers.summary: Coordinating a drone fleet to inspect a large urban road network requires both forecasting traffic dynamics and deciding under partial observation. `SenseAlign` is a reinforcement learning (RL) framework in which a privileged teacher agent sees future ground-truth traffic, and a student with an auxiliary traffic-prediction branch is trained so that the teacher's action distribution under the student's predicted future matches that under the true future, shaping the latent space for decisions rather than prediction alone. On the real road network of central Barcelona with 1570 road segments, it **consistently outperforms the baselines across multiple utility formulations**, with no added inference cost.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
papers.abstract: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.
papers.summary: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) maps tissue stiffness via shear wave speed (SWS) but suffers from slow acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. The proposed framework chains a model-based, neural-network-regularized image reconstruction module with a phase-gradient inversion (`k-MDEV`), giving an end-to-end trainable pipeline that estimates SWS maps directly from undersampled k-space data. On retrospectively undersampled brain data it **reduces normalized error by 30% compared with total variation minimization**, supports accurate SWS quantification at acceleration factors up to 19, and generalizes to in vivo data.

papers.title: Loss-Guided Tsetlin Machines: Making the Learning Objective Explicit
papers.abstract: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has no explicit notion of a loss function. Its learning signal is fixed to an implicit, margin-based update rule (MBUR), with no way to choose an objective function suited to a specific task. This paper introduces Loss-Guided TM, which replaces MBUR with an explicit and swappable loss function. In our proposed method, clause feedback and weight updates are driven by the loss, while keeping the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic unchanged. The approach incorporates cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross entropy (SCE), and asymmetric loss (ASL). We evaluate Loss-Guided TM across six datasets that span multiclass, multilabel, and binary classification tasks. With a suitable loss, Loss-Guided TM matches or improves accuracy and F1 over MBUR on five of the six datasets. The gains are greatest for the imbalanced multilabel datasets, where ASL improves macro F1 by up to 9 percentage points. With CE, Loss-Guided TM is also significantly better calibrated than MBUR on all six datasets, reducing calibration error by a factor of 3 to 11. A qualitative inspection shows that the clause-based global interpretability, examined at the per-class level on image and text data, is preserved when using the Loss-Guided mechanism. These results show that our explicit TM learning objective allows direct targeting of uncertainty calibration, data imbalance, and task structure, opening the TM to the broader literature on loss functions.
papers.summary: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) learns through a fixed, implicit margin-based update rule (MBUR) and offers no way to choose a task-specific objective. `Loss-Guided TM` replaces MBUR with an explicit, swappable loss that drives clause feedback and weight updates while leaving the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic unchanged, with cross entropy, symmetric cross entropy, and asymmetric loss as options. Across six multiclass, multilabel, and binary datasets it matches or improves on MBUR on five, gains up to 9 points of macro F1 on imbalanced multilabel data, and with cross entropy **reduces calibration error by a factor of 3 to 11 on all six datasets**. Clause-based interpretability is preserved.

papers.title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.
papers.summary: Because response length drives latency and cost in vision-language models (VLMs), adversarial images that prolong generation pose an availability risk, but prior attacks needed gradients, logits, or token-level feedback. `ChronoPatch` is a black-box attack that observes only the final response: it finds visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then shrinks the perturbation with decision-based optimization. On four open-source VLMs it raises inference latency by 47.86% to 293.34% and GPU energy by 41.44% to 249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. On three commercial VLM APIs it **increases client-observed latency by 1.82x to 2.29x with only 500 queries per API**.

papers.title: Sage-Evolve-Preview:Adaptive Observation for Post-Training Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.
papers.summary: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops repeatedly intervene, train, and evaluate against a fixed anchor benchmark, but using only the anchor's aggregate score as feedback leads to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. Adaptive observation (`AdaObs`) keeps the anchor objective fixed while changing what the loop observes: at a plateau a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks, feeding validated increments back into training. Across eight anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, it **raises the mean score from 66.4 to 73.7 under a matched data budget** over the anchor-only `FixedObs` baseline, and the evolved harness also improves the seven-task average on `PostTrainBench` across two agent backends.

papers.title: Can World Models Predict Rice Growth? Toward Agricultural World Models
papers.abstract: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? We introduce agricultural world modeling, the task of predicting how the same plant will look at a requested horizon of days to months, from one photo of it, its cultivar, and its camera view. In preliminary analysis, even state-of-the-art image generators get this wrong: they often grow the plant too little or give it the color and form of the wrong growth stage. We argue that they do not work out the plant's developmental state, which the photo reveals only indirectly. We therefore propose AgroWM, which reasons about development before it draws growth. Its reasoning module, PhenoClock, works out the current growth stage, predicts the future one, and writes a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, plant area, and color; its generation module, the Rooted Renderer, then edits the photo to follow this script, adding new organs and colors to the photographed plant. Because pixel scores can prefer an unchanged copy of the photo, we instead check each forecast's traits and developmental timing against the plant's own later photos. On rice, 54.6% of the forecasts of AgroWM are matched to the target stage (Stage R@1), against 34.8% for GPT Image 2.5, 24.0% for Qwen Image 2.1, and 47.4% for the strongest domain-specific baseline, the same backbone fine-tuned without Growth Scripts; 9 to 20 weeks ahead, it still reaches 46.4%, against 35.7% for that baseline. On maize, a crop with a different body plan and stage scale, the same design again scores best on all four measures.
papers.summary: Existing image generators asked to show how a crop will look weeks or months later tend to grow the plant too little or give it the appearance of the wrong growth stage. `AgroWM` first reasons about development with a module called `PhenoClock`, which estimates the current growth stage, predicts the future one, and writes a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, plant area, and color; a second module, the `Rooted Renderer`, then edits the photo to follow that script. Forecasts are scored against the same plant's later photos rather than by pixel similarity, and on rice **54.6% of `AgroWM` forecasts match the target stage, against 34.8% for `GPT Image 2.5` and 47.4% for the same backbone fine-tuned without Growth Scripts**. The same design also scores best on all four measures for maize.

papers.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantization methods are usually calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity, which hides failures on long tool-calling sessions with contexts of 100K tokens or more: existing quantizations of `Qwen3.8-27B` at or below 3 bits per weight solve at most 72% as many `DeepSWE` tasks as the full-precision BF16 model. `NariQ` is a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens the BF16 model generated during agent sessions. At **3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight it stays level with BF16 on the long-horizon agentic benchmarks `DeepSWE` and `Terminal Bench`**, as well as on `AIME` and `RealWorldQA`, while the 2.0-bit checkpoint falls behind. The quantized files are released in GGUF format with inference through a `llama.cpp` fork.

papers.title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
papers.abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.
papers.summary: Operations research (OR) problems such as routing, scheduling, and network design usually need algorithms tailored by specialists, and it is unclear whether large language model agents can design ones that scale. In the `FrontierOR` benchmark's one-shot evaluation, **the strongest model matches the `Gurobi` solver (objective within 1% and no slower) on only 39% of large instances**. The `FrontierOR Challenge` asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms across many optimization problems, releasing 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems in a first stage and new unseen problems in a second. Submissions are ranked in a sandboxed, open-source-only track and a self-hosted track, with each feasible solution scored by the ratio of its objective to a frozen reference on hidden instances.

papers.title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) normally trains reasoning models under a fixed cap on rollout length, and the authors show this cap changes behavior rather than only training cost. Across `Qwen3.5-4B`, `Gemma4-E2B`, and `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B`, trained models beat their base models near the training budget but **stop improving with more tokens and fall below the base model at larger inference budgets**, an effect the authors call budget internalization. Stronger KL regularization or forcing an answer on truncated rollouts restores some test-time scaling at the cost of in-budget accuracy. Supervised fine-tuning on artificially truncated traces reproduces the effect while fine-tuning on naturally short traces does not, tying it to length-censored post-training rather than to reinforcement learning specifically.

papers.title: RegionAgent: Two-Stage Preference Optimization for Regional Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration capabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uniform operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incomplete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using preferences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage preference learning in improving restoration quality.
papers.summary: Images with different degradations in different regions are poorly served by restoration methods that apply the same operation everywhere, and successive restoration steps on one region can interfere with each other. `RegionAgent` trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to choose a region-specific restoration action at each iteration, using two stages of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): a step-level stage driven by immediate restoration feedback and a trajectory-level stage driven by scores of complete action sequences. To supply the supervision, the authors build a preference dataset of 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs. Experiments across multiple datasets report strong results on mixed and single degradations, and ablations indicate that **both stages of preference learning contribute to restoration quality**.

papers.title: Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks for a Universal Fluid Gibbs Free Energy Equation of State
papers.abstract: Over the past three centuries, many thermodynamics researchers have worked to develop fluid equations of state with both high accuracy and broad applicability, proposing various theoretical frameworks and models. Building on these efforts, this study uses Gibbs free energy as the starting point and introduces thermodynamically consistent neural networks to construct a fluid equation of state based on Gibbs free energy (GEoS). This approach establishes a novel machine learning framework that provides a unified representation of fluid states. GEoS performs well on the vapor- and liquid-phase density test sets, with average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25% and 3.96%, respectively. It outperforms conventional volume-translated cubic equations of state and existing machine learning models, demonstrating its effectiveness. Further analysis using the UMAP dimensionality reduction method shows that most molecules in the test set belong to extrapolation systems, confirming the strong generalization ability of the model. Finally, the test results show that the PC-SAFT equation fitted using GEoS maintains high predictive accuracy, providing a reliable basis for its practical application in industry.
papers.summary: Fluid equations of state trade accuracy against breadth of applicability, and this work builds one from Gibbs free energy using neural networks constrained to be thermodynamically consistent. The resulting model, `GEoS`, gives a single representation of fluid states and reaches **average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25% and 3.96% on vapor- and liquid-phase density test sets**, ahead of volume-translated cubic equations of state and earlier machine learning models. A `UMAP` analysis indicates that most test molecules lie outside the training distribution, and `PC-SAFT` parameters fitted from `GEoS` outputs keep high predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
papers.abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.
papers.summary: Disagreement between a predefined reward and expert judgment is treated here as a source of candidate materials rather than as a failure. Using electronic flat bands as the test case, the authors find that experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score but that **their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels**. They learn expert preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model; the learned preferences match the score on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere, favoring reported compounds with partially flat bands such as KCo2As2 and CoGa that the score would discard. The framework is also extended to synthesizability and phonon properties.

papers.title: Invertible Transport Between Sample-Only Distributions via Projected Characteristic Functions
papers.abstract:
Many useful latent distributions can be sampled but do not have a tractable density. Such distributions may be represented by empirical collections of real-world observations or generated by scientific simulators and black-box generative models. These sample-only priors cannot be used directly in likelihood-based normalizing flows, which require evaluating the prior density. We propose Projected Characteristic-Function matching (PCF), a density-free framework for learning an invertible map between a data distribution and a prior specified only through samples.
  Our method aligns distributions using projected empirical characteristic functions, eliminating the need for density estimation, adversarial training, or paired observations. To address the non-uniqueness of the transport map, we introduce an optional transport regularizer that selects lower-displacement transformations while preserving endpoint alignment.
  We benchmark PCF on controlled transports, sample-efficiency studies, and high-dimensional alignment tasks. PCF matches the accuracy of kernel MMD on the controlled benchmark and on raw-pixel MNIST--USPS at a cost linear in the batch size, and it is more sample-efficient, achieving lower endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs across library sizes. By avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation, it reduces discrepancy memory by 29.8% and trains at batch sizes where kernel MMD exceeds GPU memory. These results show that PCF provides accurate and efficient invertible transport, particularly in sample- and memory-limited settings.
papers.summary: Likelihood-based normalizing flows need a prior with a tractable density, which rules out priors available only as samples from real observations, simulators, or black-box generators. Projected Characteristic-Function matching (`PCF`) learns an invertible map between data and such a sample-only prior by aligning projected empirical characteristic functions, without density estimation, adversarial training, or paired data, and adds an optional regularizer that prefers lower-displacement maps. It matches kernel maximum mean discrepancy (`MMD`) in accuracy on controlled transports and raw-pixel `MNIST`-`USPS` at a cost linear in batch size, and **achieves lower endpoint error than `MMD` in 13 of 15 paired runs**. Avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation cuts discrepancy memory by 29.8% and permits batch sizes at which kernel `MMD` runs out of GPU memory.

papers.title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
papers.abstract: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.
papers.summary: Encoder backbones for semantic segmentation are often picked without systematic comparison, so this study trains all 52 combinations of four decoders (`U-Net`, `FPN`, `LinkNet`, `PSPNet`) and 13 backbones from six families under one protocol on the `BDD100K` driving dataset. The best pairing, `FPN` with `EfficientNet-B4`, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), and only two of the 52 models exceed the 56.9% reported with the benchmark. **The backbone's effect depends strongly on the decoder: the same `EfficientNet-B4` scores 42.6% mIoU with `PSPNet` but 62.6% with `FPN`**, and the spread between best and worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points for `U-Net` to 42.5 points for `FPN`.

papers.title: Learning to Think with Images Faithfully via Adaptive Data Selection
papers.abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.
papers.summary: Thinking with images (TwI) lets vision-language models crop and zoom into details, but the authors find that such models often call the zoom tool without actually relying on the returned region. They trace this to training questions that can be answered without zooming, a problem that worsens as the model improves, and respond by continually selecting training questions where correct zoomed evidence still helps, backed by a synthesis pipeline for verifiable small-object questions and a reward favoring tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The method improves reasoning faithfulness and raises visual search accuracy by **+11.6% on `V*`, +7.9% on `HR-Bench 4K`, and +9.4% on `HR-Bench 8K`**. It also outperforms the compared TwI baselines on multimodal hallucination benchmarks.

papers.title: Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function Across Architectures
papers.abstract: Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this complementary form of transfer through a learn-freeze-transfer protocol, in which the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run, and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activation represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures (standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.
papers.summary: Transfer learning normally reuses weights; this work asks whether a learned activation function can be transferred instead. `FAct`, a five-parameter activation built from a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series and initialized to approximate `GELU`, is learned jointly with a Vision Transformer (`ViT`) on `ImageNet-1K`, then frozen and inserted into networks trained from scratch. In a same-architecture `ViT` it improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over `GELU`, and across four smaller architectures (`ViT`, `Swin Transformer`, linear-attention `ViT`, `MLP-Mixer`) and four image-classification datasets it has **the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings**. With learning rate and weight decay tuned separately per activation, it still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings.

papers.title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
papers.abstract: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 39% of public peer reviews published in Oct-Nov 2026 (78% on a subset of reviews from Nature), and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.
papers.summary: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt with no tools, web access, or candidate lists, frontier models are tested on whether they can tell if a human or an AI wrote it, which lab's model if AI, and which person if human. The latest models match trained detectors such as `Pangram` on the human-versus-AI question, and `Opus 5.5` names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models. **`Claude Fable 5.2` correctly names the author of 39% of public peer reviews from October-November 2026 and the username behind 69% of comments from highly active Reddit users**. Accuracy depends on how much of the author's writing appeared in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and the authors report that defenses are limited.
papers.highlight_summary:
Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt — no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples — frontier models can now tell whether a human or an AI wrote it, name the lab behind AI text, and often name the specific person behind human text. The capability comes entirely from parametric knowledge, which makes anonymity far more fragile for anyone with a sizeable public writing footprint.

- The same minimally modified prompt drives all three tasks, asking for a prediction, quoted evidence, decisive factors and a confidence level, and it is tested on 72 models from 13 labs for detection and on five frontier models for attribution.
- On 36K documents from 24 benchmarks, `Gemini 4 Carbon` detects **97%** of fully AI-generated texts, matching `Pangram 4.1` at the same **0.01%** false positive rate on English human text, while `GPT-6.1 Sol` reaches **90%** on detecting AI-originated ideas against 87% for `IdeaLens`.
- `Opus 5.5` and `Gemini 4 Argon` name the correct lab for **98%** of texts from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, but reach at most 35% on the other eight labs, with `Kimi K3` and `GLM-5.3` texts almost always attributed to Claude, consistent with reported distillation.
- `Claude Fable 5.2` names the reviewer of **56%** of 398 private peer reviews, **78%** of `Nature`-family reviews, and the username behind **31%** of recent Reddit comments (**69%** for accounts with more than 500 posts in the past year), and it is right **87%** of the time when its stated confidence is 25% or higher.
- Accuracy depends on how familiar the model says it is with the writer, falling to under 2% for authors it does not know and to 1–4% on reviews flagged as AI-generated, and the private-review set comes from only six writers, while defenses are weak because models rarely refuse and AI paraphrasing only partially helps.

papers.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
papers.abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $\alpha$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $\alpha$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.
papers.summary: Program analyses that track data through a large language model (LLM) call have no code describing which prompt placeholders the output actually uses, so they either taint every output with every input or pay a second model to label each call. The authors prove, and mechanize in `Lean 4`, that to first order a placeholder influences a transformer's output only through the attention that reads it, and that a faint reading cannot certify the absence of a flow. Their tool `Sightline` reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns which reads count as uses, and calibrates pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction of true flows. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, at a 1% target miss rate it **misses about 1% of true flows while pruning 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline**, and in information-flow control for an LLM agent it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

papers.title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity
papers.abstract: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.
papers.summary: Attention heads are known to specialize in stages during training; this work instead asks how specialization depends on the amount of training data. Empirically, heads tuned to syntactic relations in `BERT` emerge as the dataset grows. In a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention, the authors establish that **head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, marked by a non-analyticity in the test error**. Depending on data structure and regularization, it can occur through a cascade of transitions that recover progressively weaker latent features, a statistical form of simplicity bias, and the authors relate these transitions to the stagewise emergence of heads in online learning.

papers.title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
papers.abstract: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.
papers.summary: Causal discovery on multivariate time series is hampered by autocorrelation, distribution shift, and the cost of high-order conditional independence tests. Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (`ITPD`) is a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for nonstationary time series that builds the global graph by finding each variable's parent set in turn, using temporal priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to replace higher-order tests with lower-order ones. With an exact oracle it performs the fewest tests with the smallest average conditioning sets among baselines, and in simulations it sits on the Pareto frontier of F1 and wall-clock time. On graphs with 2000 nodes it runs **2.3x, 9.1x, and 40.9x faster than iterative `IAMB`, `DF-PC`, and `PCMCI`, respectively**.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
papers.abstract: Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing remains challenging because experimental datasets are limited and process-property relationships vary across materials and operating conditions. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) govern process stability and defect formation. Conventional ML models typically use dimensional process parameters, which represent laser-material interactions only implicitly and may limit cross-material transfer. This study evaluates whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, combining laser processing conditions with material thermophysical properties, improve melt pool prediction over raw process parameters. We systematically benchmark seven models: four classical ML methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2). Experiments span 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets, covering regression of melt pool width and depth and classification of melting modes. Dimensionless features yield comparable or superior predictive performance in most settings, with the largest gains in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). Tabular foundation models generally achieve stronger classification performance than classical baselines, particularly for multi-material datasets. These findings indicate that combining physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular models can improve data-efficient melt pool modeling and support more transferable process-window identification in LPBF.
authors: Md Habibor Rahman (University of South Carolina)
papers.summary: In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode determine process stability, but models trained on raw process parameters transfer poorly across materials and experimental data are scarce. This study tests whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, improve prediction, benchmarking four classical methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, `XGBoost`) against three pretrained tabular foundation models (`TabPFN`, `TabDPT`, `TabICLv2`) on 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined datasets. Dimensionless features perform comparably or better in most settings, with the largest gain in **cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96)**. The tabular foundation models generally classify melting modes better than the classical baselines, particularly on multi-material data.

papers.title: FastRoverVLA: Fast Vision-Language-Action Execution for Off-Road Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
papers.summary: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) driving models are expensive to query at every trajectory update, yet reusing an old prediction leaves its commands out of step with the vehicle's actual motion. `FastRoverVLA` is a training-free interface that keeps a buffer of speed-curvature actions between visual predictions, realigns it with measured motion at each update, writes the corrected remainder back, and decides how long to reuse a plan from a roughness score. Over a 3 s horizon it reduces final displacement error (FDE) by 18.0% on `ORAD-3D` and 36.7% on `RELLIS-3D` while calling the model on only 6.0% and 4.8% of updates, and it **cuts `Qwen3-VL` request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8** under serial replay. Control experiments identify persistent state correction as the main source of the accuracy benefit.

papers.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for AI scientists mostly test whether agents can run a given workflow or choose among predefined measurements, not whether they can design their own experiments. `TwinLab-Bench` covers 52 tasks from physical science, life science, and engineering laboratories with more than 100 experimental action types, and scores the agent's report against a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task is served by its own `TwinLab` agent, which acts as the environment and executes the designed experiments by reading the lab's raw materials and calling calculators built from its records; this nearly eliminates readings that deviate from real records and inconsistent answers to repeated requests. The tasks remain hard for frontier models: **the strongest, `Claude Fable 5.2`, averages a score of only 45.0**.

papers.title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.
papers.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) is usually evaluated with final aggregate metrics, which can hide temporary performance loss while an agent adapts to new tasks. The authors introduce a simple, inexpensive benchmark that varies observation representations while keeping environment dynamics and rewards fixed. With it they demonstrate a stability gap: **performance on earlier tasks drops substantially when new tasks are introduced and then partly or fully recovers, even though the agent has complete access to past tasks**.

papers.title: STAGE: Spatio-Temporal Augmented Graph Expansion for Weakly Supervised Cross-Tweet Event Causality Discovery
papers.abstract: Causal relations in disaster-related social media of- ten span independent posts, making cross-tweet causal discovery difficult to supervise and model at scale. We propose STAGE, a framework that separates scalable cross-tweet weak-supervision construction from spatio-temporal relational learning over event occurrences. Starting from local causal seeds, STAGE retrieves semantically related event occurrences across tweets and uses a causal scorer to construct weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs. These pairs supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network over semantically enriched event representations and a spatio- temporal context graph. We evaluate STAGE on California Wildfire and Hurricane Harvey using human-gold cross-tweet test sets and 15 baselines. Compared with local-only supervision, the constructed cross-tweet supervision improves STAGE AUPRC by 0.340 on Wildfire and 0.107 on Hurricane. STAGE achieves in-domain AUROC of 0.885 on Wildfire and 0.710 on Hurricane. Cross-disaster experiments reveal asymmetric transfer, highlighting sensitivity to dataset-specific spatio-temporal shifts. These results demonstrate the value of scalable cross-tweet supervision combined with relational event modeling for causal learning across fragmented disaster reports.
papers.summary: Causal relations between events in disaster-related social media often span separate posts, which makes them hard to label and model at scale. `STAGE` starts from causal seeds found within single tweets, retrieves semantically related event mentions across tweets, and uses a causal scorer to build weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs; these supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network over enriched event representations and a spatio-temporal context graph. Evaluated against 15 baselines on human-labeled test sets for `California Wildfire` and `Hurricane Harvey`, the constructed cross-tweet supervision **improves AUPRC by 0.340 on Wildfire and 0.107 on Hurricane over local-only supervision**, with in-domain AUROC of 0.885 and 0.710. Cross-disaster experiments show asymmetric transfer between the two datasets.

papers.title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.
papers.summary: Skills reused by LLM agents can work on one operating system and fail on another because OS assumptions are scattered across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and entrypoints, and finding these failures by running everything everywhere is costly. `SkillBridge` is a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis that screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases (1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows), dynamic validation with root-cause review on selected cases, and repair of the contract field responsible. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, and a retrospective Linux/macOS analysis finds **38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, versus about 865 expected under uniform random selection**.

papers.title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
papers.abstract: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.
papers.summary: An updated release of `fosf`, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, adds flexible `SPARQL` query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. The language is extended with a similarity relation among sorts, and a translation engine compiles OSF terms into standard `SPARQL` after a fuzzy, ontology-aware rewriting step that uses sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations. The rewriting **returns approximate solutions, so queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the ontology still yield relevant results**.

papers.title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
papers.abstract: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.
papers.summary: Manual reading of analogue gauges in manufacturing introduces human error, so the authors build an automated gauge reader and compare three hybrid pipelines: `OpenCV` with `Scikit-Image`, `OpenCV` with `ResNet18`, and `OpenCV` with `VGG19`. The dataset contains 1,848 pressure gauge images in the 0-10 BAR range, gathered through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation. **`ResNet18` reaches 97.3% accuracy, against 64.4% for `VGG19` and 63.8% for `Scikit-Image`**.

papers.title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.
papers.summary: Training-data auditing asks whether particular documents were used to train a large language model, a question behind privacy audits, copyright disputes, and benchmark-contamination checks, and membership signals are often concentrated in only a few passages of a long document. The proposed statistical framework combines complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination into document scores, then uses calibrated p-values and multiple testing to assess a whole collection and flag suspicious documents. Under stated exchangeability conditions the authors prove **finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for collection-level auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification**. Case studies cover `BookTection`, `Pile-arXiv`, `Cosmopedia`, and `HealthCareMagic` for both pre-training and fine-tuning data.

papers.title: dLoop: Looped Diffusion Language Models via Recurrent Latent Refinement
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate tokens in parallel but need many denoising steps, because only some predictions are reliable enough to commit after a single forward pass. `dLoop` restructures a pretrained DLM into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and repeatedly applies a parameter-shared middle block to the same partially masked state, giving extra latent computation before any commitment decision. On `GSM8K`, `MATH`, `MBPP`, and `HumanEval` it achieves **the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark, and no compared method beats it on both accuracy and tokens per forward pass**; it beats `Fast-dLLM` on both measures everywhere and `dParallel` on three benchmarks, while `d3LLM` is less accurate but has higher throughput. Mechanistic analyses indicate the extra loops mainly help slow, unstable trajectories.

papers.title: What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
papers.abstract: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether the internal reasoning format of a large language model can be deliberately changed, and whether doing so helps. Instead of Chain-of-Thought, models are fine-tuned to follow Question-Option-Criteria (`QOC`), a structured decision process built from explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria, developed over three generations from a basic decision core to statistically enriched reasoning. Across the reported experiments, **`QOC` fine-tuning improves answer quality over non-fine-tuned base models, with the largest gains once models are big enough to carry out the `QOC` computations reliably**.

papers.title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
papers.abstract: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources.
