These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.
papers.summary: Peer review depends on different readers finding different problems, and this study measures how much the critiques in reviews of the same paper overlap. At `ICLR`, **measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027**, with year-on-year rises also at `NeurIPS`, `ICML`, and the `F1000` and `PLOS` journals, and a third `ICLR` review added 5.46 new problems in 2027 against 6.12 in 2026. Applying `MELD`, a detector of LLM-generated text, shows that two flagged reviews of one paper overlap more than two unflagged ones, by 4.5 points at `ICLR` in 2026-2027 and by 5.4 points across five journal sources.

papers.title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
papers.abstract: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/\psi$, and $\Upsilon$. The network was never told which muons come from a resonance, it was only trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state particles. We use these features to alter aspects of the $Z$ boson: we change its mass between $\sim80$ and $105$ GeV, and removing such a feature from the neural network produces a broader $Z$ peak. In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spectrum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was built from the gradients of the neural network, and its selectivity was built using pattern recognition methods. A generative particle physics model trained on unlabeled data can be modified internally to change a physical quantity.
papers.summary: Mechanistic interpretability methods are applied to `ShellFlow`, a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data, to search for physics concepts inside it. The authors find internal features that represent resonances such as the Z, J/psi, and Upsilon, even though the network was only trained to generate final-state particle kinematics and was never told which muons come from a resonance. Using these features, **they shift the Z boson mass between roughly 80 and 105 GeV, and removing a feature broadens the Z peak, while the rest of the invariant mass spectrum stays mostly unchanged**. The features were built from the network's gradients, with selectivity established by pattern recognition methods.

papers.title: BADAS-3.0: Real-Time Driving Perception and Planning from One Camera
papers.abstract: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.
papers.summary: `BADAS-3.0` is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads that tests how far a driving model can get with one forward camera and real-time latency. From two seconds of video it predicts current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score, and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, it has **44% lower minADE_6 across five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B, six-camera `Alpamayo 2 Super`, which runs over 100x slower**; the gain comes from camera rigs neither model was trained on, and the two are on par on the rig they share. On two new open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of `Euro NCAP` scenarios, it has a higher pass rate than every published planner tested.

papers.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
papers.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png
papers.summary: Agent skills are usually natural-language instructions placed in context, which cannot be optimized continuously, while fine-tuning is model-specific and does not transfer between agents. `Skill.png` instead optimizes the pixels of an image by gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen vision-language model (VLM), producing a skill-like image input that any VLM can consume and that can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. It **outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized with frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (4 VLMs, 4 benchmarks) while using 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens**. Jointly optimized text-plus-image skills improve performance further, and an image optimized on an ensemble transfers across the models in that ensemble.

papers.title: A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger States Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
papers.abstract: Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating an \(N\)-photon \(D\)-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even \(N\ge4\) when \(D\ge N\). The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum \(\mathcal F\) of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex. Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an \((N-1)\times N\) matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes \(\omega\) and GHZ target \(\Delta\), the row--column imbalance yields \(\mathcal F(\omega)=0\) but \(\mathcal F(\Delta)\neq0\), contradicting the required equality \(\omega=\Delta\). Finally, we give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.
papers.summary: Photonic Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states made with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured, complex-weighted graphs, where producing an N-photon, D-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum graph. The authors prove that **no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even N of at least 4 when D is at least N**. The proof was discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in `Lean` using `AlphaProof Nexus`; it builds a weighted sum of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by vertex, and a row-column imbalance makes that sum zero for the graph amplitudes but nonzero for the GHZ target. A physical interpretation of the proof is also given.

papers.title: Scalable fault vulnerability analysis for ReRAM-based process-in-memory CNN accelerators
papers.abstract: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector multiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (\textit{SaH}) and stuck-at-low (\textit{SaL}) resistance states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accuracy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and measuring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate, it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerability at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our proposed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks, whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about $10^4\times-10^5\times$, enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only a few minutes or hours.
papers.summary: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) processing-in-memory accelerators run neural network matrix-vector multiplications efficiently, but permanent stuck-at-high and stuck-at-low faults corrupt the convolutional neural network (CNN) weights stored in the cells. Assessing this by fault injection is accurate but takes days or weeks for large networks. The authors propose an analytical framework that computes vulnerability scores at the weight, kernel, and layer level without exhaustive simulation, and report that the scores agree with fault-injection results while delivering **a speedup of about 10^4 to 10^5 times**, cutting analysis to minutes or hours.

papers.title: Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
papers.abstract: Textual recommendations generated by large language models (LLMs) can be difficult to inspect. This paper introduces \emph{Client Exits}, a lightweight mechanism for enriching LLM responses while separating semantic intent from client-specific presentation. The model inserts predefined, machine-interpretable markers into its output, and the receiving client decides whether and how to realize the corresponding enrichments. This allows supplementary information to be presented as graphics, text, speech, or other modalities without prescribing a concrete interface. We implement a prototype combining a finetuned Qwen model with a modified LibreChat client. Using the Question--Option--Criteria (QOC) approach including three XML-based client exits. We evaluate two QOC-oriented model variants trained on essentially the same examples, with client-exit annotations added for one variant. Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response. An LLM judge, informed about the mechanism without being instructed to favor it, prefers this model's answers in 66\% of the comparisons. These results demonstrate successful marker generation on the evaluated test set and support the feasibility of client-controlled enrichment.
papers.summary: `Client Exits` is a lightweight mechanism in which a large language model inserts predefined, machine-readable markers into its output and the receiving client decides whether and how to render the corresponding enrichment, as graphics, text, speech, or another modality. A prototype pairs a fine-tuned `Qwen` model with a modified `LibreChat` client, using the Question-Option-Criteria (`QOC`) approach with three XML-based client exits. Across 100 test questions the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response, and **an LLM judge prefers its answers in 66% of comparisons** against a variant trained on essentially the same examples without the annotations.

papers.title: Actor-Predictor Architecture for Reinforcement Learning with Formal Specification Objectives
papers.abstract: One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks. It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as $(a^n b^n)$, for which finite-automaton-based approaches are not applicable.
papers.summary: Enforcing temporal specifications in reinforcement learning usually means converting logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping, which restricts methods to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). `Actor-Predictor` instead trains a predictor to estimate whether a partial trajectory will go on to satisfy the specification, and feeds its learned features to the actor, which is optimized with `GRPO` and `RWR`. The authors show theoretically that with sufficient predictive accuracy the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. In grid world and `Isaac Lab` robotic tasks it outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks and **also handles non-regular specifications such as a^n b^n, where finite-automaton approaches do not apply**.

papers.title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
papers.abstract: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.
papers.summary: Most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture individual cells only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or very large. `C-LiTE` is a 22-million-parameter model for cell representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology that processes 64 x 64 pixel cell-centred crops with a 4 x 4 patch embedding and no upsampling, initialised from a pre-trained `ViT-5-S` through a pseudoinverse-based transformation of the patch embedding weights. It is pre-trained on 60 million cell crops from `TCGA`, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. Under frozen-feature evaluation on seven public datasets it reaches **a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, close to `CytoFormer` at 0.682 with roughly 30x fewer parameters**.

papers.title: Language-Oriented Semantic Modeling for Target Language Extraction
papers.abstract: Target Language Extraction (TLE) aims to isolate speech in a target language from multilingual mixtures. Existing approaches primarily rely on acoustic modeling with language identity labels, which provide only coarse categorical guidance. In this work, we propose a language-oriented semantic modeling framework that augments acoustic extraction with language-specific semantic representations. A pre-trained speech semantic model is adapted via language-aware prompt conditioning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to generate target-language-focused semantic representations from the mixture. {These capture high-level semantic structure of the acoustics and they} are integrated into the extraction model to provide structured semantic guidance beyond identity labels. Experiments on the CommonVoiceMix dataset show that incorporating semantic representations consistently improves over acoustic-only baselines, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR gain.
papers.summary: Target Language Extraction (TLE) isolates speech in one language from a multilingual mixture, and existing systems rely mainly on acoustic modelling guided by coarse language identity labels. The proposed framework adapts a pre-trained speech semantic model, using language-aware prompt conditioning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, to produce target-language-focused semantic representations that are fed into the extraction model. On the `CommonVoiceMix` dataset, adding these representations consistently improves over acoustic-only baselines, with **up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR gain**.

papers.title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics
papers.abstract: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.
papers.summary: Predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC) are two biologically plausible, local-learning alternatives to backpropagation whose relationship has been unclear. The authors show that **DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, exactly equivalent in shallow linear networks**, with systematic deviations growing with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. They call the approximation `Approx PC` and reduce its deviations by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. On `MNIST` and `FashionMNIST`, `Approx PC` performs comparably to PC trained with the same nudges, and its learned weights transfer directly to PC inference.

papers.title: Predicting Surface Displacement Fields of Laser Powder Bed Fusion Parts Using STL-Derived Graphs and Part-Level Descriptors
papers.abstract: Predicting part distortion before fabrication remains challenging in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), while thermomechanical simulation is computationally expensive for repeated design evaluations. This study presents a two-branch graph attention network (GAT) to predict three-dimensional surface displacement directly from STL-derived graphs. The first branch learns geometric relationships among connected vertices of a densified STL surface mesh, while the second incorporates 12 part-level descriptors of mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape. Displacement labels from ANSYS Additive Print simulations are mapped onto STL vertices using Gaussian-kernel weighted averaging. Evaluated on 117 parts using five-fold cross-validation split by part, the model achieves an R^2 of 0.946 and a mean absolute error of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude. Relative to a node-wise multilayer perceptron, GAT improves R^2 from 0.913 to 0.946; for build-direction displacement, R^2 increases from 0.903 to 0.939. GAT also outperforms GraphSAGE (R^2 = 0.936) and a graph convolutional network (R^2 = 0.934) across all five folds. Ablation experiments show that removing mass-distribution descriptors reduces magnitude R^2 to 0.900, while removing build-plate contact and overhang descriptors reduces it to 0.920. These results demonstrate the value of combining local mesh connectivity with global geometric descriptors to predict LPBF distortion, enabling faster design iteration and earlier identification of distortion-prone geometries.
papers.summary: Predicting distortion of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) parts before fabrication normally requires expensive thermomechanical simulation. A two-branch graph attention network (`GAT`) predicts 3D surface displacement directly from STL mesh graphs: one branch learns geometric relationships among connected vertices, the other takes 12 part-level descriptors covering mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape, with labels from `ANSYS Additive Print` simulations. On 117 parts with five-fold cross-validation split by part, it achieves **an R^2 of 0.946 and a mean absolute error of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude**, ahead of a node-wise multilayer perceptron (0.913), `GraphSAGE` (0.936), and a graph convolutional network (0.934). Removing the mass-distribution descriptors lowers R^2 to 0.900.

papers.title: Conformal Selection for Hierarchical Streaming Data
papers.abstract: Many real-world tasks involve making sequential decisions about whether to select candidates before their responses of interest are revealed. In this work, we address the online selection problem in the context of hierarchical data, where candidates arrive sequentially from different populations. This extends existing online conformal selection frameworks beyond the standard i.i.d./exchangeable data assumption. The primary challenge lies in constructing valid statistics for each candidate sequentially under the hierarchical data structure. To this end, we first develop Online Hierarchical Selection (OHS), a distribution-free method that enables principled candidate selection for hierarchical data streams. Specifically, we introduce methods to construct rank-based e-values for both between-group and within-group samples, and apply averaged e-values to the online e-BH procedure. We then develop OHS with feedback (OHSF), which boosts the power of OHS by leveraging potential response feedback. Theoretically, the proposed methods achieve false discovery rate control under mild hierarchical exchangeability and data arrival assumptions at any time. We also generalize methods to broader settings, such as data with covariate shift and selection under effect-related responses. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
papers.summary: Online conformal selection decides sequentially whether to select candidates before their outcomes are known, and existing methods assume i.i.d. or exchangeable data. This work handles hierarchical streams in which candidates arrive from different populations: Online Hierarchical Selection (`OHS`) builds rank-based e-values for between-group and within-group samples and applies averaged e-values to the online `e-BH` procedure, and `OHSF` raises power by using response feedback. The methods are distribution-free and **control the false discovery rate at any time under mild hierarchical exchangeability and data arrival assumptions**, with extensions to covariate shift and effect-related responses. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets are reported.

papers.title: Rigel-Ladon: An Option-Count Law for a One-Pass Decision Encoder, Tested on Held-Out Option Counts and Held-Out Schemas
papers.abstract: Laya is a small neural network that reads a text, a question and K written options, and returns one probability per option in a single pass. We ask how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether that can be predicted. We score nested option sets (every K-option question contains the smaller ones) on four question pools, for the released model (Base) and our fine-tune (FT), and score every item against each single rival. FT trained on one 12-option topic question (in-family); a 12-option HR (department-routing) question is out-of-family. Logit accuracy (the log of correct over incorrect answers) is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88. Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 (a log-linear rule: 1.6 and 6.7). Taking the slope from the topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy on HR predicts its other K within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base). On a 35-label pool of five schemas the law fails (5 to 11 points). Independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected: the gold-versus-rival log-odds shifts by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per doubling of K, yet pairwise answers reproduce K-way accuracy within 4.7 points. Order averaging (averaging over several orderings of the options), shortlists, a temperature law and calibrated prediction sets did not transfer (FT's 90% sets cover 84% on HR). 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held. Caveats: one model family and LLM-labelled synthetic text.
papers.summary: `Laya` is a small neural network that reads a text, a question, and K written options and returns one probability per option in a single pass; the study asks how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether the decline can be predicted. For the released model and a fine-tune, logit accuracy is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88, and **a law fitted on K up to 6 predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 points**; borrowing the slope from a topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy predicts an out-of-family HR routing question within 0.3 to 0.7 points. The law fails by 5 to 11 points on a 35-label pool spanning five schemas, independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected, and order averaging, shortlists, a temperature law, and calibrated prediction sets did not transfer. Only 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held, and the authors note the results cover one model family and LLM-labelled synthetic text.

papers.title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
papers.abstract: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.
papers.summary: Automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering needs more than code that runs, because syntactically valid models can still violate engineering requirements. `OceanCoder` fine-tunes `Qwen3-8B` on 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 task categories, then uses a three-layer verification framework (input checks, analysis completion, output plausibility) as graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (`GRPO`). On a new benchmark with out-of-distribution tasks and real engineering cases, **Pass@1 rises from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO**, exceeding a closed-source comparison model.

papers.title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
papers.summary: Key-value (KV) caches reused across denoising steps become a memory bottleneck for long video generation with diffusion transformers. Temporal Rotation Quantization (`TRQ`) fits, online and without gradients, an orthogonal transform per block of temporally adjacent cache vectors that flattens per-channel means, parameterized as a tree of 2x2 planar rotations stored in two bits each plus a shared Hadamard transform; a greedy fit is proven globally optimal for this objective. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, **`VBench` subject consistency improves over `QVG` from 90.38 to 92.02 on `LongCat-Video-13B`** and from 86.33 to 87.61 on `HY-WorldPlay-8B`, with fused Triton kernels released for inference.

papers.title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.
papers.summary: Agents answering from incomplete records must decide whether missing information means unknown or false, and existing evaluations entangle this with other reasoning demands. `ClosureBench` runs each base scenario under three closure contracts (OWA, CWA, and LCWA), changing only how missing information is treated, and counts a model correct only if it answers every variant correctly; agent extensions cover action choice, source scope, and updates. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy ranges from 71.18% to 99.86%, but **accuracy on scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract ranges from 18.23% to 99.31%**, with the largest discrepancies under LCWA.

papers.title: One Framework to Diagnose Them All: A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination
papers.abstract: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified along three crossed axes: a human-validated cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy. It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set (Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the profile: discourse-level omission defeats judges and most teams alike, whereas only a minority over-flag negative controls. The judges' verdict probabilities rank items well (ROC-AUC 0.74-0.95) but are overconfident (ECE 0.04-0.29). An open competition on Alikbachan drew 222 teams and 3,566 submissions, and a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th percentile. Of the 25 teams in both phases, 24 regress on Phase 2 (mean $-17.6$ points) while every zero-shot judge improves, and Phase-1 rank barely predicts Phase-2 rank (Spearman $\rho=0.35$), so a Phase-1 leaderboard alone would have crowned a different winner.
papers.summary: Hallucination resources for low-resource languages tend to fragment into incomparable datasets, one per failure mode. `Alikbachan` is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified by cultural-distance band, six task types, and a 32-mode taxonomy, with a harvested 2,516-item set (Phase 1) and a gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2), evaluated with four zero-shot LLM judges and an open competition of 222 teams. Judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata and are overconfident, and **24 of the 25 teams in both phases regress on Phase 2 (mean -17.6 points) while every zero-shot judge improves**, with Phase-1 rank barely predicting Phase-2 rank (Spearman rho = 0.35).

papers.title: Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?
papers.abstract: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, for one architecture.
papers.summary: The question studied is how far `Laya`, a 421M-parameter encoder that scores named answer options in a single forward pass, can be compressed before its decisions diverge from its own full-precision outputs. Decision flips and expected calibration error (ECE) are measured under bf16, grouped low-bit rounding, layer deletion, CPU dynamic int8, early exit, and distillation, on synthetic in-family items and out-of-family questions from `ARC`, `MMLU`, and `HellaSwag`. Flips are consistently higher out of family (bf16: 0.2% versus 2.2%; deleting 6 layers: 0.9% versus 9.1%), CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, and **at equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than layer deletion**; a single label-free temperature restores ECE from 39.2% to 3.6% after deletion. The data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, and only one architecture is tested.

papers.title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.
papers.summary: Shaping how language models reason is hard because full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning overconstrains outputs while trajectory-level reinforcement learning gives weak credit assignment. Edit-based training has an editor locate the first point of failure in a model's own sampled completion and propose a minimal replacement span, with supervision applied only to those edited spans, either offline or online. Applied to `Qwen3-32B` on the `ReasonIF` benchmark, the method **substantially improves compliance with reasoning instructions over both baselines while largely preserving skills on untargeted tasks**.

papers.title: DeepQuest: From Knowledge Gaps to Scientific Discovery in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Automating experiments does not necessarily advance scientific understanding. Research agents must identify meaningful knowledge gaps, determine what available data can resolve, and assess whether their findings advance existing knowledge. We introduce DeepQuest, a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease research. DeepQuest transforms unresolved questions from domain reviews into traceable, testable hypotheses and prioritizes them through data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking. It couples iterative experimentation with two-level auditing that separates experimental reliability from knowledge contribution relative to two frozen literature corpora. On OASIS-3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses and outperforms the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three language-model reviewers. The full framework achieves an audit-assessed scientific finding rate of 95.24%, outperforming both general-purpose executors and domain-specific research agents. This scientific finding rate remains stable across literature corpora and evaluator model families. Representative findings concern neuropsychiatric symptoms and dementia risk, longitudinal amyloid spatial stability, and neocortical tau-associated clinical impairment, with key associations supported in independent ADNI and AIBL cohorts. These results show how aligning knowledge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing can turn automated research into traceable, evidence-supported scientific discovery. Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeepQuest-3066/
papers.summary: `DeepQuest` is an AI-scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease research that turns unresolved questions from domain reviews into testable hypotheses, screens them for data feasibility, ranks them with groupwise Elo, and audits results separately for experimental reliability and knowledge contribution against frozen literature corpora. On `OASIS-3` it produces 42 feasible hypotheses and beats the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three language-model reviewers. The full framework reaches an **audit-assessed scientific finding rate of 95.24%**, with key associations supported in the independent `ADNI` and `AIBL` cohorts.

papers.title: Context as a Resource
papers.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.
papers.summary: Always-on personal agents that funnel interleaved tasks into a single session suffer cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling, while router-and-ticket hierarchies lose information in prose handoffs and merge blindly, reaching only a 33.3% mean on true-conflict repository merges. `ClonAct` is a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks with a non-generative context memory-management unit, in-place context cells, a footprint-aware bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a shared trunk. Across three multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, the trial merge gate **lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, which `ClonAct` attains with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens**, and under surge streams it matches the top completion rate (95.0%) with the lowest median wait.

papers.title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation
papers.abstract: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.
papers.summary: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations are computationally expensive and require expertise. `Perfumer` is an LLM-based agent that couples `Quantum ESPRESSO` with two predictive models: a pre-relaxation model that yields a **2.75-fold overall speedup over `Quantum ESPRESSO` alone**, and a band model combining a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head that returns 12 band energies at any wavevector. Trained on 125,153 band structures, the band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 held-out materials in about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores, and the agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows.

papers.title: TRCF: Temporal-Reference Complementary Forecasting for Irregular Multivariate Time Series
papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting supports healthcare monitoring, environmental analysis, and activity recognition. Channel-independent (CI) approaches capture each variable's temporal patterns but do not explicitly use observations from other variables. Channel-dependent (CD) modeling exploits relationships among variables, yet asynchronous measurements make these relationships difficult to learn. Incorporating cross-variable information while preserving each variable's irregular history therefore remains a key challenge. We propose Temporal-Reference Complementary Forecasting (TRCF), a framework that augments a compact CI forecaster with a complementary CD branch. ANCHOR aggregates observed values and timestamps at shared temporal locations, retaining observation support to form compact CI features. BRIDGE constructs complementary features through history completion. It first estimates each variable's historical values from its own observations, then uses differences between other variables' observed and estimated values at nearby times to correct missing entries. The completed history preserves observed values and is encoded to supply context alongside the direct CI representation. Finally, the two representations are fused, combined with the query-time embedding, and passed to a shallow multilayer perceptron for forecasting. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that TRCF achieves the lowest mean squared error and mean absolute error in the main benchmark comparison, while reducing measured peak inference memory by 17.28% to 87.98% relative to APN.
papers.summary: Forecasting irregularly sampled multivariate time series forces a choice between channel-independent (CI) models that ignore other variables and channel-dependent (CD) models that struggle with asynchronous measurements. Temporal-Reference Complementary Forecasting (`TRCF`) augments a compact CI forecaster with a CD branch that completes each variable's history by correcting self-estimated values using nearby residuals from other variables, then fuses both representations in a shallow multilayer perceptron. On four real-world datasets it achieves the lowest mean squared and mean absolute error in the main comparison while **reducing peak inference memory by 17.28% to 87.98% relative to `APN`**.

papers.title: Mamba Flow Matching Neural Processes: Linear-Time Inference for Irregularly Observed Spatial Fields
papers.abstract: Interpolating a spatial field, such as daily maximum temperature, from sparse, irregularly located observations recurs across the environmental and health sciences. Standard Gaussian-process kriging refits hyperparameters and solves an $O(N^3)$ system for every new field. When many related fields are observed, such as daily maps from one sensor network, neural processes (NPs) instead learn the interpolation map from past fields and predict a new field in one forward pass. Joint-predictive variants, which sample whole fields rather than independent per-location values, typically use self-attention over context and query points, costing $O(K^2)$ in the combined point count $K$ and limiting practical use to a few thousand points. State-space models offer a linear-time alternative, but a direct state-space adaptation compresses the context into one hidden state before reading queries, reducing what the decoder sees. We propose MambaFlowNP, a linear-compute joint-predictive NP trained with conditional flow matching. A multi-directional Mamba-2 scan reads context and query tokens in one shared sequence, so each query's velocity is read from its own scan position rather than a compressed context summary, and because queries only read the scan state, predictions are consistent across query sets. MambaFlowNP is competitive with the strongest attention-based joint-predictive baselines on synthetic Mat\'ern Gaussian-process benchmarks, and on regional to continental-scale NOAA temperature interpolation it attains the lowest RMSE and CRPS and near-nominal coverage on every tier, while running 114--784$\times$ faster than the strongest joint-predictive baseline. A single forward pass scales to $10^6$ points on one NVIDIA L40S GPU in under a second. This makes joint prediction feasible for continental-scale, irregularly sampled sensor networks; predictive quality is evaluated up to $K=5{,}580$.
papers.summary: Neural processes that sample whole spatial fields from sparse, irregular observations typically use self-attention with quadratic cost in the number of points, limiting them to a few thousand points. `MambaFlowNP` trains a joint-predictive neural process with conditional flow matching and uses a multi-directional `Mamba-2` scan over context and query tokens in one shared sequence, giving linear compute and predictions that are consistent across query sets. It is competitive with attention baselines on synthetic Matern Gaussian-process benchmarks and attains the lowest RMSE and CRPS on NOAA temperature interpolation while **running 114-784x faster than the strongest joint-predictive baseline**; a forward pass scales to 10^6 points in under a second on one GPU, though predictive quality is evaluated only up to 5,580 points.

papers.title: Beam Model Technical Report
papers.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.
papers.summary: `Beam` is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with **501.3B total and 23.4B active parameters** built for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads, claimed to deliver frontier-level reasoning at 3-4x less inference compute than comparable models. It was pretrained on 23.8T tokens, given a 1M-token context window through a two-stage midtraining phase, and post-trained with an asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign of over 100M rollouts on 10.5K GPUs across 4 weeks, with capabilities reported to keep improving as RL compute increased. Serving relies on FP8/NVFP4 quantization and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (`DFlash 2`), and the model refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless ones.

papers.title: Learning from Context: Leave-One-Out Prediction in Jump Diffusions
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion models generate discrete data through stochastic dynamics in an embedding space. We consider jump diffusions that additionally reset coordinates to embeddings of categorical values. A coordinate's own corrupted state can make prediction easy, potentially reducing the pressure to learn dependencies between coordinates. We study leave-one-out (LOO) prediction, in which each coordinate is predicted from the corrupted states of the other coordinates. We show that, under stated assumptions, jump diffusions with complete coordinate resets and state-independent clocks preserve the prescribed marginals when reset destinations use exact LOO probabilities and the drift uses the full endpoint posterior. We further show that this drift can be constructed from LOO probabilities by analytic likelihood completion without additional network evaluations. We evaluate unrestricted, LOO, and completed predictions on Text8 and LM1B text generation and ZINC250k molecular graph generation. LOO-based variants improve key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls on all three datasets. Controlled interventions assess reliance on local inputs and context, and we analyze the effect of analytic likelihood completion.
papers.summary: In jump diffusions for discrete data, which add coordinate resets to continuous embedding-space dynamics, a coordinate's own corrupted state can make prediction easy and weaken the pressure to learn dependencies between coordinates. The authors study leave-one-out (LOO) prediction, where each coordinate is predicted from the corrupted states of the others, prove that under stated assumptions the prescribed marginals are preserved, and show the required drift can be built from LOO probabilities by analytic likelihood completion with no extra network evaluations. In experiments, **LOO-based variants improve key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls on `Text8`, `LM1B`, and `ZINC250k`**.

papers.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents repeat procedural mistakes such as mis-paginating an API or resolving the wrong entity. The authors describe a pipeline, shipped in the open-source `altk-evolve` library and deployed in IBM's `CUGA` agent, that mines short lessons from an agent's own trajectories, consolidates them into guidelines, and injects all or a selected subset at inference, evaluated on `AppWorld`. The central finding is that **the right amount of memory depends on the model**: `DeepSeek-V3.2` gains +9.5 points of task completion with its full 191-guideline set, whereas `gpt-oss-120b` reaches 51.2% with all 199 guidelines but 55.4% with a selected subset of about 29 (from a 39.9% baseline). The report also documents failures encountered along the way, including a backfiring high-support guideline, silently dropped provenance, a swallowed API error, and a baseline confound.

papers.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
papers.summary: Standard attention computes a full dot product between every query and key. Hidden Sparse Attention (`HiSA`) keeps the projections intact but computes only part of the dot product according to a static, parameter-free rule derived from token positions and the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), making attention sparse along the hidden dimension rather than over tokens. In LLMs trained from scratch, the partial product **improves performance over the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products**, and it speeds up decoding and reduces memory at inference, with an extension to `FlashAttention-3` kernels. The authors also show that dense attention learns to suppress the score components `HiSA` drops.

papers.title: World Models Favor Learned Priors over Visual Evidence
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to simulate physical interactions, but training a separate model for each environment limits scalability. Cross-environment prediction requires identifying the current physical rule, which appearance alone may not reveal. We therefore study visual calibration: using object motion and interactions in a short video as direct evidence to infer the current rule and predict motion under that rule from a different initial state. However, differences in data availability across physical conditions can yield a long-tailed training distribution, biasing models toward common rules even when evidence supports rare ones. To study this challenge, we introduce TailWorld, which evaluates the transfer of demonstrated rules across initial states while independently controlling training imbalance and calibration informativeness. The benchmark compares predictions with two reference futures from the same prediction initial state, one following the demonstrated rule and the other a common rule, to measure prediction bias toward common dynamics. We further propose Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT), which learns how different rules affect object motion, infers the current rule from calibration interactions, and applies it to prediction from a new initial state. RIFT explicitly controls the influence of training frequency on rule inference, allowing sufficiently informative observational evidence to support rare rules. Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across varying training imbalances and distribution shifts, with gains in predicting rare dynamics.
papers.summary: World models that must work across environments need to infer the current physical rule from a short calibration video, but long-tailed training data biases them toward common rules even when the evidence points to a rare one. `TailWorld` is a benchmark that independently controls training imbalance and calibration informativeness and compares predictions against two reference futures, one following the demonstrated rule and one a common rule. The proposed Rule Inference for Transfer (`RIFT`) method infers the rule from calibration interactions while explicitly controlling the influence of training frequency, and **improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across imbalance levels and distribution shifts, with gains on rare dynamics**.

papers.title: From Benchmarks to the Bench: Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional Drug-Target Screening
papers.abstract: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Drug-target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug-target pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates. Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.
papers.summary: Drug-target interaction (DTI) models rank huge numbers of drug-target pairs, but only a handful of top candidates can be tested experimentally. Comparing the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 FDA-approved drug structures and 614 human proteins, the authors find that **pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons**, and that some overlap reflects recurring preferences for the same candidates rather than target-specific signal. Checks against published kinase inhibition data show some systems' hit yields barely change when recommendations are matched to different drugs or targets, and retraining one architecture with different seeds yields a mean Top-10 overlap of about two candidates despite similar test performance.

papers.title: Evidence from a Multi-Regime Causal Discovery Benchmark: UCMT Algorithms, Comparative Performance, and Controlled Ablation Studies
papers.abstract: We present an internal, pre-registered evaluation of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family alongside established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, complemented by a separately pre-registered, controlled study of UCMT v2 Global components. The contribution is both empirical and methodological: a family-stratified comparison of three actively developed algorithm configurations and targeted evidence about which internal stages affect their outcomes. In the main benchmark, UCMT v2 Global has higher directed F1 than NOTEARS and DAGMA in selected real, semi-synthetic and Gaussian-network comparisons at the paired-run level, while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings. The BOSS-based UCMT v4 produces a CSuite-specific directed-F1 improvement over BOSS (mean paired difference +0.279; pair-level Holm p < 0.001), but the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188). In a separate fixed-skeleton ablation, UCMT v2 Global exceeds an adapted R^2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on standardized iSCM data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, dataset-level Holm p = 0.031); absolute orientation accuracy is 0.563 and there is no established broad advantage over RESIT, ANM or DirectLiNGAM. Controlled ablations show that sparsity and BIC-based refinement materially affect some outcomes, whereas the examined arbitration and automatic regime-selection mechanisms do not yield confirmed general improvements. We report performance shortcomings, multiple-testing correction, runtime costs, evaluation limitations and reproducibility checks. The results support UCMT as an implemented and empirically investigated algorithm family, not a claim of overall superiority, independent validation or demonstrated commercial impact.
papers.summary: A pre-registered internal evaluation compares the `UCMT` family of causal discovery algorithms with established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, alongside controlled ablations of `UCMT v2 Global` components. `UCMT v2 Global` achieves higher directed F1 than `NOTEARS` and `DAGMA` in selected settings but trails leading permutation-search methods in others, and the `BOSS`-based `UCMT v4` improves over `BOSS` on `CSuite` at the pair level (+0.279) but **the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188)**. Ablations indicate sparsity and BIC-based refinement matter for some outcomes while arbitration and automatic regime selection show no confirmed general benefit, and the authors explicitly make no claim of overall superiority.

papers.title: A Complete Geometric Message-Passing Architecture for Point Clouds
papers.abstract:
Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality, and a large family of machine learning architectures has been developed to respect their natural symmetries to rigid motions and permutations. A principled way to compare these architectures, which vary widely in complexity and cost, is through their expressive power. That is, an architecture is complete if it can distinguish any two inputs not related by the symmetries it respects. Simple distance-based message-passing networks are known to be incomplete, and while there exist complete alternatives, they typically rely on computationally intensive mechanisms like high-order representations of the rotation group or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman-type tests.
  In this work, we devise a novel, simple, equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, and prove that it is complete. We complement our theoretical result with experiments showing that our architecture separates challenging point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish. Our results suggest that high-order equivariant features may not be necessary to enhance the expressivity of point cloud architectures, and can help settle completeness for other equivariant architectures for which such results are currently unknown. We give initial evidence for this by proving completeness of a slightly modified version of SEGNN.
papers.summary: An architecture for 3D point clouds is complete if it can distinguish any two inputs not related by rigid motions and permutations; simple distance-based message passing is known to be incomplete, and existing complete alternatives rely on costly high-order rotation-group representations or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman-type tests. The authors devise **a simple equivariant message-passing architecture and prove that it is complete**, and show experimentally that it separates point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot. They also prove completeness of a slightly modified version of `SEGNN`, suggesting high-order equivariant features may not be necessary for expressivity.

papers.title: Simulation-pretrained autoencoders versus PCA for compressing multimode fibre transmission matrices
papers.abstract: Multimode optical fibres can image through a thin, flexible probe once their transmission matrix (TM) has been measured, but a TM is large and must be re-measured whenever the fibre moves. A compact model of feasible TMs would make storing and re-estimating them cheaper, so we ask how compactly TMs can be represented, and from how few measured TMs. Here we benchmark a permutation-equivariant autoencoder, pretrained on simulated fibres and adapted to measured TMs, against principal component analysis (PCA). At 62x compression, adapting the pretrained autoencoder with just two measured TMs reconstructs the TM of a 50um fibre well enough to focus light at 98% of the ideal enhancement, and it stays accurate when the TMs are shifted by 25 pixels or zoomed by 10%, which quickly degrades a linear basis. It is not, however, a better compressor: PCA is about ten times more accurate when fitted on all 163 real TMs (1.1% against 11.9% error on held-out TMs) and is already more accurate from ten. The autoencoder's value is as a prior when few or no real TMs exist: with none it reaches 29% error, against 91% for PCA fitted on the same simulation. Transfer to a different fibre is only partial. The most important extension, not yet tested, is to recover pixel-basis TMs from fewer measurements than a full TM, which would turn the pretrained prior from a compressor into a measurement-saving tool.
papers.summary: Imaging through a multimode optical fibre requires its transmission matrix (TM), which is large and must be re-measured whenever the fibre moves. A permutation-equivariant autoencoder pretrained on simulated fibres and adapted to measured TMs is benchmarked against principal component analysis (PCA) for compact TM representation. At 62x compression, adapting with just two measured TMs focuses light at 98% of the ideal enhancement and tolerates shifts and zooms, but **PCA is about ten times more accurate when fitted on all 163 real TMs (1.1% versus 11.9% error)**. The autoencoder's advantage is as a prior when few or no real TMs exist, reaching 29% error with none against 91% for PCA fitted on the same simulation.

papers.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
papers.abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.
papers.summary: Evidence produced by EU-funded projects is scattered across deliverables and reports, making it hard to find relevant context for water-governance and climate-resilience decisions. The authors rebuild documents from three projects (`IMPETUS`, `NATALIE`, `InnWater`) into hierarchical section trees with structured metadata, index them with two embedding models fine-tuned on water and climate data, and place a `ReAct`-style controller on top that allocates retrieval budget across domain collections until a stopping criterion is met. On a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the system improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by **26.7% (relative)** over a single-domain embedding baseline.

papers.title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
papers.abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation.
