Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.
papers.summary: Flow matching can transport heavy-tailed or multimodal source distributions to data, but finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources have been limited. The authors prove a nonasymptotic convergence result for Euler discretization with linear interpolation, assuming a source with a positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance, and an L-Lipschitz score. With the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, the sampler reaches total variation error ε in **roughly L·d·TotVar/ε iterations (up to log factors)** under a mild second-moment condition on the target. The assumptions cover multivariate Student's t sources with more than two degrees of freedom and Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, and allow targets without smooth densities or bounded support.

papers.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
papers.abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-H\"older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.
papers.summary: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) fix randomly drawn hidden-layer parameters and fit only the output coefficients, which turns regression into a linear sieve problem over a random approximation space. The authors prove that **such random sieves cannot stay uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows**, because the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix vanishes at a rate set by the covering geometry of the parameter space. They then build approximation, ridge-regularized estimation, and inference theory that tolerates this ill-conditioning, including Gaussian limits for linear functionals and consistent ridge-adjusted variance estimators for studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the conditioning decay and the finite-sample behavior of the procedures.

papers.title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
papers.abstract:
The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases.
  The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.
papers.summary: This thesis compares rule-based, optimization-based, and machine-learning methods for controlling batteries, heat pumps, and other residential energy systems across three simulation cases and one real-world experiment. It introduces `TreeC`, a method that learns human-readable decision-tree control strategies and performs competitively with model predictive control and reinforcement learning. In the hardware experiment both `TreeC` and model predictive control did worse than in simulation, owing to unrepresentative training data and unreliable real-time inputs respectively. For electrified Belgian dwellings, the algorithms cut costs, but **on average the savings do not yet outweigh the cost and effort of deploying them**.

papers.title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
papers.abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $\alpha$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($\theta_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $\alpha$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/\alpha)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.
papers.summary: Best-of-N style inference-time alignment spends a fixed sampling budget on every prompt, and existing adaptive stopping rules rely on heuristic thresholds with no statistical control over stopping too early. The authors cluster candidates by final answer using a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test, showing that a version based on Wald's sequential probability ratio test loses its guarantee because the leading answer shifts during sampling. Their method `e-RWSC` instead runs a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer, which **bounds the probability of ever certifying a non-majority answer by a user-chosen tolerance α**, uniformly over time. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models show the predicted inverse-KL scaling of sample cost and better accuracy than baselines at substantially lower token cost.

papers.title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
papers.abstract: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
papers.summary: Vision-language navigation systems usually fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) on navigation data to predict geometric goals, which can change its weights substantially and erode general visual abilities. `ZeroVLN` skips that supervised fine-tuning: the VLM conveys movement decisions in natural language through a semantic tool-calling interface to a separate action expert, and the two are then improved jointly with closed-loop reinforcement learning. Trained on the same navigation episodes, it **substantially outperforms supervised-fine-tuning-based hierarchical methods on `VLN-CE` (continuous environments) benchmarks** while making only minor changes to the VLM's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard vision-language navigation pipelines fine-tune the VLM "brain" on navigation data to emit geometric goals, which shifts its weights and wrecks its general visual abilities. `ZeroVLN` instead has the brain issue natural-language tool calls to a separate action expert and improves both through closed-loop reinforcement learning, with no navigation-domain supervised fine-tuning of the brain.

- A `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` brain calls `run_action_head(target, where, plan)`, `turn`, or `stop`, and a 12-layer flow-matching action expert turns each movement request into continuous motion, predicting 16-step action chunks but executing (and being supervised on) only the first 4 steps before replanning.
- Training is two-stage: the expert is first fit, with the brain frozen, to reference trajectories planned from the brain's own requests using a privileged mesh-derived semantic map, then brain and expert are jointly optimised with a shared trajectory-level advantage over success, first-arrival, distance-progress and information-discovery rewards.
- Using only **34,445 training episodes**, it reaches **51.3 / 52.7 / 51.4% success rate** on `SAGE-3D` / `R2R-CE` / `RxR-CE`, ahead of same-backbone, same-data `NaVILA` (23.5 / 46.5 / 48.7) and `DualVLN` (21.2 / 15.4 / 17.7), with joint RL responsible for most of the gain (`R2R-CE` success rises from 17.0% to 52.7%).
- The brain's weights move by only **0.01497%** versus 3.21% for `DualVLN` and 7.67% for `NaVILA`, and it retains **59.16%** mean accuracy on twelve general visual benchmarks against the base model's 59.47%, while both fine-tuned baselines score zero.
- Path efficiency is the cost: SPL on `R2R-CE` and `RxR-CE` is **29.2 and 28.1** versus `NaVILA`'s 41.8 and 43.0, success still trails published systems trained on far more data such as `JanusVLN` (60.5% on `R2R-CE`), and training depends on privileged scene geometry plus 512 long-horizon rollouts per RL step.

papers.title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
papers.abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.
papers.summary: Simulating fibre-reinforced composite structures with local defects requires a material-scale model at every integration point, which is prohibitively expensive with concurrent multi-scale schemes. The authors design a surrogate that combines a material-architecture encoder, a spiking neural network memory block tracking the long-term irreversible material state, and transformer blocks for the short-term strain state, trained in three stages ending with recursive fine-tuning to suppress error drift. Coupled to a non-linear finite element solver and benchmarked against experiments on `IM7/8552` laminates, pristine and wrinkled, under tension, compression, and transverse shear, it yields **prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%**.

papers.title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.
papers.summary: Egocentric video datasets cover many everyday activities but rarely include the synchronized whole-body motion needed to teach humanoid robots to move and manipulate at the same time. The authors build `Awaken-Human`, about 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video paired with whole-body human motion across more than 100 skills, and train `Awaken-HI`, a vision-language-action model that predicts both human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. More human pretraining data lowers held-out robot action error along an empirical scaling law, and after adaptation to a T800 humanoid the model reaches a **93.75% mean success rate across eight tasks**, outperforming `GR00T N1.7` and `π0.5`. The policy also generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training.

papers.title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items, responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do not.
papers.summary: Large language models can generate Q-matrices, the item-to-skill mappings used by diagnostic classification models in educational measurement, but evaluations have looked only at the final matrices rather than the basis for each assignment. Reasoning-Trace Analysis (`RTA`) has the model produce attribute-labeled reasoning steps via chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and then analyzes those steps to reconstruct and inspect each assignment. On 11 fraction subtraction items with responses from 536 examinees, CoT-derived matrices had a **mean overlap of .809 with the reference Q-matrix, below the .877 of directly generated ones**, and varied more across replications. Trace inspection tied disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were split into steps.

papers.title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
papers.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.
papers.summary: Deep-research agents running on a user's own device must rely on small language models, and guiding them at inference time usually means extra tool calls, unreliable self-evaluation, or per-model adaptation. `Seer` separates action proposal from learned consequence prediction: a tool-response simulator and a value estimator are trained offline on a shared corpus of real research trajectories and reused across agents, so candidate actions are scored in imagination and only the selected one is actually executed. `GAIA` accuracy rises **from 13.6% to 41.7% for `Qwen3.5-4B`** and from 22.3% to 50.5% for `Qwen3.5-9B`. The analysis suggests broader candidate coverage can offset imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the gains from wider imagined search.

papers.title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
papers.abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.
papers.summary: Sampling-free variational inference makes Bayesian neural networks cheaper to train, but existing approaches assume Gaussian output distributions, which can be inaccurate. `CF-Prop` propagates characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer without sampling, which gives a closed-form evidence lower bound for Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma likelihoods and a resulting training algorithm, `CF-VI`. On `CIFAR-100`, `CF-VI` has the lowest calibration error of the tested methods, **about 35% better than the next best**, and on a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset it captures tail uncertainty that other sampling-free and Monte Carlo methods severely underestimate.

papers.title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
papers.abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.
papers.summary: Long-running agents accumulate external memory stores whose growing record count raises retrieval overhead and whose longer retrieved contexts raise generation cost, while pruning or consolidating records risks losing evidence or producing longer units. `MemFolder` addresses both in sequence: `RecordFolder` merges compatible records using entity grounding, semantic and entity affinity, and temporal chaining, and `ContextFolder` encodes the grouped records into compact text, revising the encoding when verification shows key facts cannot be recovered. Applied to `Mem0`, `RecordFolder` **retains 99.0% of the original average performance with 50% fewer records** across `LoCoMo`, `PersonaMem`, and `LongMemEval`, 1.9 percentage points above the strongest baseline. Results are also reported on the multimodal `M3-Bench-web` and `M3-Bench-robot` benchmarks.

papers.title: Asuka-FM: A System-Architectural Co-Design Framework for Efficient Text-to-Image Pretraining on Consumer Hardware
papers.abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
papers.summary: Pretraining text-to-image Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) from scratch on one consumer GPU runs into quadratic attention costs, compilation graph breaks from variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and a throughput wall from the frozen Variational Autoencoder. `Asuka-FM` combines a dual-stream DiT backbone without AdaLN, token sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (`SPRINT`) that cuts attention FLOPs by over 50%, aspect-normalized rotary position embeddings with square-crop training to keep tensor shapes static, and a 10M-parameter pixel-space detailer head. The authors report that a roughly 206M-parameter model can be pretrained on a single RTX 4090 in **about 160 GPU hours for under $55**, scoring 0.588 on `GenEval` and 78.96 on `DPG` at 256px and 0.609 and 78.51 at 512px.

papers.title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
papers.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.
papers.summary: Learning to defer (L2D) systems hand difficult decisions to a human expert but typically assume that expert's reliability is fixed, ignoring shifts over time from fatigue and cognitive biases. `EDA-L2D` conditions the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes through a sequence model, so the policy can anticipate reliability fluctuations. Across image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection, including irregular shifts in expert reliability, the authors report that it **adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to temporal patterns in expert reliability**, improving overall system performance and deferral decisions.

papers.title: Should Belgians Install an Advanced Energy Management System in Their Electrified Dwelling ?
papers.abstract:
As dwellings electrify and more complex electricity pricing spreads in Belgium, the question arises: What are the potential benefits of installing an advanced energy management systems in an electrified Belgian dwelling ?
  To answer this question, we simulate 500 representative Belgian dwellings in which fossil systems are replaced by controllable electric technologies: space heating via air-to-air heat pumps, domestic hot water via electric boilers, and private transport via electric vehicles with home chargers. Photovoltaic systems are assigned according to current adoption rates.
  We evaluate two advanced energy management systems (EMS): model predictive control (MPC) and TreeC, a machine learning method using decision trees to model the EMS strategy. These are compared to a rule-based controller (RBC) that mimics default operation and an MPC with perfect forecasts (MPC P) as an upper bound. Performance for these EMSs is assessed for 2023 under a real contract with hourly prices and a monthly peak tariff.
  Average annual savings versus RBC are 82.5 EUR, 116.6 EUR, and 177.4 EUR for TreeC, MPC, and MPC P, respectively. All EMSs deliver similar thermal comfort (26-31 Kh). MPC saves more, while TreeC achieves higher EV charge completion (93.3% vs 88.8% for MPC, with a max charge of 95%) and a smoother aggregate load across the 500 dwellings. Savings remain modest relative to EMS purchase (280-680 EUR) and subscription (0-360 EUR/year) costs which is not favourable towards widespread adoption.
  The data and code to reproduce this study are available at https://github.com/EVERGi/should_belgians_install_advanced_ems_paper.
papers.summary: To gauge whether advanced energy management systems pay off in electrified Belgian homes, the authors simulate 500 representative dwellings with heat pumps, electric boilers, and electric vehicle chargers for 2023 under a real contract with hourly prices and a monthly peak tariff. They compare model predictive control (MPC) and `TreeC`, a decision-tree-based machine learning controller, against a rule-based baseline and an MPC with perfect forecasts as an upper bound. Average annual savings over the baseline are **82.5 EUR for `TreeC`, 116.6 EUR for MPC, and 177.4 EUR for the perfect-forecast bound**, with similar thermal comfort and higher vehicle charge completion for `TreeC`. These savings are modest next to purchase costs of 280-680 EUR and subscriptions of up to 360 EUR per year.

papers.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
papers.summary: Existing robot manipulation benchmarks either mix reasoning and execution in the same tasks or test them separately, so a failure cannot be traced to reasoning, execution, or the combination of the two. `Mind2Act World` provides 30 simulated manipulation tasks across five application domains in 180 configurations, organized into three views: Mind (decisions from past observations), Act (precise, timely execution), and Mind2Act (closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions), plus a harness that attributes failed episodes to one of the three. Evaluating multimodal agents, vision-language-action models, and world-action models, the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but **only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes**. Agents retain task state but struggle with sustained contact, while end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing manipulation benchmarks either entangle reasoning and execution in the same tasks or test them in separate assessments, so a failure cannot be traced to its cause. `Mind2Act World` organises its tasks into three views — `Mind` (history-based reasoning), `Act` (precise, timely execution) and `Mind2Act` (closed-loop composition, where action outcomes guide the next decision) — to show whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose the ones it has.

- The benchmark has **30 simulated bimanual tasks** (two ARX X5 arms in Isaac Sim) from five application domains, ten per view, each at three difficulty levels in `Clean` and `Random` scenes for **180 configurations**, plus **4,500 expert demonstrations (75.8 hours)** for fine-tuning end-to-end policies.
- Success is judged from physical predicates on hidden simulator state under a shared information contract for agents and end-to-end policies, and a diagnosis harness combining rule-based analysis with an LLM judge attributes each failed episode to `Mind`, `Act` or their composition and summarises the result in a per-model profile card.
- Across nine systems and 56,700 scored episodes (three multimodal agents, four VLAs including `π0.5` and `X-VLA`, and two WAMs), the strongest agent succeeds in **52.7%** of `Mind` and **39.0%** of `Act` episodes but only **12.0%** of `Mind2Act` episodes, and no end-to-end policy exceeds **3.6%** on `Mind2Act`.
- The failure profiles differ by architecture: the strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization.
- The authors note that the simulator pauses during inference, so timed successes do not reflect real-time performance, and that the views use different tasks of different lengths, so the gap between views does not by itself prove composition failure; agents were also run on only 5 instances per configuration against 50 for policies, and the harness was applied to just three systems.

papers.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs a classical decoder that keeps pace with syndrome measurements, and on superconducting processors existing real-time decoders give up accuracy for speed. `Rapids` is a streaming neural decoder co-designed with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and is trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code it decodes each syndrome round in under a microsecond on a single FPGA with a **logical error rate 240 times lower than existing real-time hardware decoders**. The design also extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, where it is 16 times more accurate than the real-time `Relay` decoder, and it scales across several FPGAs or custom silicon.

papers.title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).
papers.summary: Pretrained language models remain unreliable at exact multi-digit arithmetic unless they are fine-tuned or given an external tool. The authors present closed-form constructions that write deterministic arithmetic and Boolean circuits directly into a pretrained model's weights with no gradient steps, no training examples, and no runtime hooks, using analytical tricks to cancel normalization scaling and a small widening of the hidden dimension, all automated by a five-stage compiler. On 6-digit arithmetic, the modified `IBM Granite 4.2 3B` and `Qwen 3.5 4B` reach **99.17% and 100.00% accuracy, versus 42.2% and 61.7% for a `LoRA` baseline trained on 12.8K samples**, while changing at most 0.057% of weights. The authors report that natural-language behavior is preserved, with no out-of-distribution triggers of the circuit in 11,134 checks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Pretrained language models still fail at exact multi-digit arithmetic unless they are fine-tuned or handed off to an external interpreter. This work compiles closed-form arithmetic and Boolean circuits directly into the weights of pretrained models, using zero gradient steps, no labelled data and no runtime tool calls, while leaving natural-language behaviour intact.

- The circuit lives in `K` extra residual wires appended alongside the untouched language weights (`d→d+K` with a `sqrt(d/(d+K))` norm compensation), where a log-spaced two-layer `Mellin-GLU` gate bank cancels the unknown per-token `RMSNorm` scale across a more than 250× range.
- Cross-token routing uses signed Chebyshev `Indefinite-RoPE` attention on `Granite 4.2 3B` and memoryless `GatedDeltaNet` shifts on `Qwen 3.5 4B`, and a 5-stage declarative compiler synthesizes 4–8 digit signed add, subtract and multiply circuits without manual wire or layer assignments.
- On 1,200 six-digit problems in BF16, `Granite 4.2 3B` reaches **99.17%** and `Qwen 3.5 4B` **100.00%** ALU-prefix accuracy with 98% and 100% mid-sentence resumption, against 42.2% and 61.7% arithmetic accuracy and **0%** inline continuation for a same-backbone `LoRA` trained on 12.8K examples.
- The patches total 1.07M–2.39M non-zeros (under **0.06%** of weights), a block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 and 10.65 GiB, and both grafts pass **14/14** pre-registered noninferiority splits (N=4,392) with 0 of 11,134 out-of-domain false triggers.
- Scope is narrow and numerically fragile: there is no division and multiplication is capped by a digit budget, the exact-carry guarantee does not hold formally in BF16 (Granite needs an FP32 sidecar to reach 100%), stricter four-seed eight-format accuracy falls to 94.07% and 96.60%, uniform INT8/INT4 quantization of the circuit weights and `-ffast-math` kernels break it, and on `Gemma 4 E4B` only Boolean circuits were grafted, with the KV-shared upper layers failing.

papers.title: Bayesian optimization on amortized search space
papers.abstract: In real-world black-box optimization problems, a mechanistic simulator is often available that approximately predicts the behavior of the system as a function of the parameters being optimized. Here, we show how an amortized inverse map of such a simulator can be used in Bayesian optimization to restrict the search space while using a Gaussian process kernel that is aware of the original problem geometry. This allows for efficiently leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of the optimization problem. We characterize its approximation bias and information gain, and derive an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate under additional geometric and Gaussian Process assumptions. We illustrate the method with an application to drug dosing personalization in Parkinson's disease. We use, as a simulator, a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) model of a drug, a mechanistic model calibrated on population data with quantified parameter uncertainty. A dosing neural network is trained offline against the model, amortizing the map from patient PK/PD parameters to the regimen predicted to be optimal, and online Bayesian optimization then searches over this learned, low-dimensional representation rather than over raw dosages. Numerical simulations demonstrate the improved performance of our method in this application, as well as under simulator misspecification.
papers.summary: Many black-box optimization problems come with a mechanistic simulator that roughly predicts system behavior as a function of the parameters being tuned. The authors train an amortized inverse map of the simulator offline and run Bayesian optimization over that learned low-dimensional representation, using a Gaussian process kernel that respects the original problem geometry, and they derive a **regret rate that depends on the intrinsic rather than the raw dimension** under additional assumptions. In a Parkinson's disease dosing application built on a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model, numerical simulations show improved performance, including when the simulator is misspecified.

papers.title: Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics
papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
papers.summary: Data assimilation, the repeated estimation of hidden states and their uncertainty in partially observed nonlinear systems, is costly with conventional nonlinear filters and usually needs an explicit dynamical model. `Neural CGM` learns an encoder-decoder mapping into a latent space whose dynamics have a conditional Gaussian structure, which **permits closed-form assimilation updates in the latent space**, and a Gaussian decoder carries the latent posterior mean and covariance back to physical variables so that uncertainty enters the training loss. On benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems it gives accurate state estimation and forecasting at substantially lower online cost than conventional nonlinear methods, without knowledge of the governing equations.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Pass Search for Setpieces
papers.abstract: Set pieces produce about a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG), yet they are usually evaluated by what happened next. We present Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) for set pieces, which treats a corner or a lofted free kick as a distribution over plausible executions and plausible futures instead of a single realised event. From the pre-kick state, MCPS proposes counterfactual deliveries and counterfactual set-ups (where the attackers stand at the kick), plays each out many times in a world model (3D ball physics, a generative model of all 22 players, the keeper's come-or-stay decision and a Player-to-Touch model) and scores every future with a value model. On 249 deliveries from 30 Serie A 2025/26 matches, with every model applied only to matches it never saw, the best available delivery is worth 0.0085 xG more than the one kicked (+28 %), mainly because it reaches an attacker before the keeper. Searching where the attackers stand as well adds +0.0027 xG with the observed ball and +0.0033 on top of the best ball; designing their runs too adds +0.0007 more. We show how to keep such a search honest, and estimate how much more data each component needs before a club could rely on it.
papers.summary: Set pieces in football generate roughly a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG) but are usually judged only by what actually happened next. `MCPS` (Monte Carlo Pass Search) instead proposes counterfactual deliveries and attacker set-ups from the pre-kick state, plays each out many times in a world model (3D ball physics, a generative model of all 22 players, the keeper's come-or-stay decision and a Player-to-Touch model), and scores the outcomes with a value model. On 249 deliveries from 30 Serie A 2025/26 matches, evaluated out of sample, **the best available delivery is worth 0.0085 xG more than the one kicked (+28%)**, mainly because it reaches an attacker before the keeper. Also searching over where attackers stand adds a further 0.0027 to 0.0033 xG, and the authors estimate how much more data each component needs before a club could rely on it.

papers.title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
papers.abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{\lambda_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.
papers.summary: Critically damped Polyak (`CDP`) stepsizes are an adaptive stepsize rule that multiplies the classical Polyak rule by 4 and a mild damping factor, with the aim of biasing gradient descent toward flatter minima. The factor of 4 makes iterates oscillate evenly around the manifold of minimizers while damping drives convergence to it, so the method runs at the edge of stability and its projected iterates follow gradient descent on the log of the top Hessian eigenvalue along that manifold. The authors prove **the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction** on a broad class of locally quadratic objectives, and unlike normalized gradient descent the method converges to an interpolating solution at a finite learning rate. Empirically it flattens solutions about as much as Sharpness-Aware Minimization (`SAM`), including in nonlinear teacher-student networks and when fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
papers.abstract:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes.
  In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code.
  We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance.
  In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.
papers.summary: Continuous Integration (CI) builds run after every commit, which costs time and compute even for minimal changes. `BuildPredictor` is a random forest model that anticipates the build outcome from features such as changes to source code, build code, and code complexity. It reaches **a median Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.82 within a project and 0.86 in a holistic setting**, with historical build results being the most important features, and it reaches peak performance quickly as a project's history accumulates. Removing the hard-to-interpret historical build features still gives decent performance while making the model easier to interpret.

papers.title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
papers.abstract: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.
papers.summary: Real-time task guidance allows several acceptable responses and timings, and sometimes staying silent is best, yet existing benchmarks score systems against fixed synthesized dialogues. `FLUID` builds on naturally occurring human-human guidance from `WTaG` and `HoloAssist`, annotating each intervention with its supporting evidence, its necessity, and how flexible its timing is. That representation is used both to evaluate guidance flexibly and to build a real-time multimodal guidance agent. The agent achieves **the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timeliness, and latency among evaluated systems**, though it still overlaps with the user's speech more than desired.

papers.title: Multimodal Error Detection in Chest X-ray Reports: A Large Language Model Reading Image Evidence
papers.abstract: Rad-Linter checks chest X-ray reports against image-derived evidence to flag potential errors for review. A pretrained image classifier supplies scores for nine pathologies, and a 1.5B-parameter language model, fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,816 examples, checks their consistency with the report. We compare it with a keyword-and-negation rule baseline given the same reports and scores. Evaluation uses controlled report-score pairings from OpenI, with consistency labels derived from automatic report labels and score thresholds. Each counterfactual quad crosses two real reports with two real score vectors from other patients, creating two consistent and two inconsistent pairs. Every report and score vector occurs in both conditions, so either input alone permits only 50% accuracy. On 131 quads, Rad-Linter achieves 98.5% pair accuracy versus 80.5% for the rule baseline, and classifies all four pairs correctly in 94.4% of quads versus 56.5%. The checkers perform similarly on omission items, including unmentioned and negated findings; larger differences occur on the remaining item types, which require interpreting how findings are described. The same language model without fine-tuning remains near 50% accuracy. On a second set of 181 quads that also includes reports on which the automatic labelers disagree, pair accuracy is 93.4% versus 75.3%. These controlled results show that, given the same image-derived scores, a trained language model detects report-score inconsistencies more accurately than the tested rule baseline, with the advantage concentrated in interpreting how findings are worded.
papers.summary: `Rad-Linter` flags possible errors in chest X-ray reports by checking them against image-derived evidence: a pretrained classifier scores nine pathologies, and a 1.5B-parameter language model fine-tuned with `LoRA` on 1,816 examples judges whether the report is consistent with those scores. Evaluation uses counterfactual quads from `OpenI` that cross two real reports with two real score vectors, so that either input alone permits only 50% accuracy. On 131 quads, **`Rad-Linter` reaches 98.5% pair accuracy versus 80.5% for a keyword-and-negation rule baseline**, and gets all four pairs right in 94.4% of quads versus 56.5%. The advantage is concentrated in items that require interpreting how findings are worded, and the same model without fine-tuning stays near 50%.

papers.title: Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features: A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $\theta_i = 1/(1-\gamma\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.
papers.summary: Successor features let a reinforcement learning agent separate environment dynamics from task reward, but how well they work depends on the base features chosen. Borrowing the idea that entorhinal grid cells correspond to eigenvectors of the successor representation, the authors build the basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy, so that each successor feature is simply its base feature scaled by a closed-form factor of one over one minus the discount times its eigenvalue. No successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. In a two-goal gridworld with a uniform random walk as the reference policy, **these agents maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas `SimpleSF` and `DQN` lose most of their return at each change**.

papers.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
papers.abstract:
Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters.
  Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens.
  Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.
papers.summary: Decision models score candidate answers in a single forward pass without generating text, which is fast and gives confidence estimates but forgoes the benefits of explicit reasoning. `GLiDE` is a family of such models from 0.4B to 27B parameters built on `Qwen` hybrid language models, with causal masking removed from full-attention layers so that context, question, and candidate answers interact bidirectionally. Reasoning ability is transferred through soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, plus progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks and an optional parameter-free recurrent depth. All five sizes sit on the performance-versus-parameters Pareto frontier of a Hugging Face decision-model leaderboard, and **the 27B model scores 73.37 on the hidden set with 2.1% expected calibration error** after checkpoint averaging and recurrent depth, with the base 27B variant running at a median 92.9 ms on a single GPU.

papers.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
papers.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
papers.summary: Successful teacher trajectories used for post-training can still contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning (`Skill-FT`) uses natural-language skills to suppress such habits and elicit effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, and `AutoMaster` is an autonomous system in which an LLM agent designs these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and evaluation feedback. On terminal, search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, **`AutoMaster` improves mean performance over plain supervised fine-tuning on unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42 to 8.99 percentage points**, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and recipe held fixed. Keeping the skill instructions in the training demonstrations also beat removing them in all six settings, even though they are absent at evaluation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Successful teacher trajectories can still demonstrate bad habits such as unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, and superficial verification, so fine-tuning on them reinforces those habits along with the useful actions. `Skill-FT` appends natural-language skills to the teacher's system prompt to reshape its rollouts, and `AutoMaster` is an LLM agent that designs those skills and selects which demonstrations to train on.

- In an inner loop the agent pilots candidate skills in teacher rollouts, refines them, and selects trajectories, while an outer loop fine-tunes the student from the same initial checkpoint on 512 trajectories and feeds its evaluation scores and trajectories back to the agent over five rounds.
- With `DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview` as teacher and `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Qwen3.5-9B` as students, `AutoMaster` beats `Vanilla SFT` by **1.42–8.99 percentage points** across all six settings on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, `BrowseComp`, and `Doc2Repo`, with the largest gain on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` at 9B (**26.59% to 35.58%**).
- Keeping the skill instructions in the training input outperforms removing them by **2.15–4.01 percentage points** in all six settings, even though the supervised outputs are identical and students are evaluated without any skills.
- A `Task-Matched SFT` control using unguided rollouts on the same tasks trails by 1.08–10.11 points, and removing either skill guidance or data selection lowers the mean score in every setting, with both ablated variants falling below `Vanilla SFT` on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` at 4B (17.60% and 20.22% versus 22.47%).
- The evidence is weaker for the smaller student, where the 95% confidence intervals for `BrowseComp` and `Doc2Repo` include zero, and overall the evaluation sets are small (89, 185, and 50 tasks), the reported spread covers three evaluation runs of one checkpoint rather than training seeds, and the agent picks its final checkpoint after seeing benchmark evaluation feedback across rounds.

papers.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
papers.abstract: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access.
papers.summary: Citizens searching for government schemes must match everyday queries to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages. The system described here indexes aligned English-Marathi descriptions of Maharashtra government schemes and combines `BM25` lexical retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. On manually curated bilingual queries, `BM25` alone reaches a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864, and **hybrid retrieval with `MahaSBERT` raises MRR only modestly to 0.879**, while dense-only retrieval trails at about 0.66. Fusion also lifts precision from 0.781 to 0.808 at unchanged recall of 0.946.

papers.title: Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity
papers.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in expectation and with high probability.
papers.summary: Whether the simplest differentially private variant of stochastic gradient descent, Noisy SGD, achieves statistically optimal rates on strongly convex losses has been an open question. The authors bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth, strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi differential privacy. For strongly convex generalized linear models, these bounds match minimax lower bounds derived with the Score Attack framework, giving **the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression**, without the poly-logarithmic terms of earlier results. The same rates hold in expectation and with high probability.

papers.title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
papers.abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band.
